#6308. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

Archaeologists found a small cemetery full of high-status burials, two of which may be the graves of Germanic chieftains.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists excavating in northeastern France have unearthed a small fifth-century cemetery containing the graves of two Germanic chieftains and two warhorses. The burial ground is providing new information about the transitional period after the fall of the Roman Empire.

The burial complex was discovered near the city of Colmar, just a few miles from the Rhine River, which forms the border between France and Germany. This area had a Gallo-Roman village from the first to the third centuries, and archaeologists found several ancient houses, hearths, wells and craft areas, according to a Nov. 6 translated statement from the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap).

Archaeologists also uncovered a rare fifth-century cemetery at the site, which was used from about A.D. 450 to 500, a critical time period in Western Europe because of the collapse of the Roman Empire. While scholars have debated for centuries about why the empire fell, one key issue was the repeated occupation of Rome in the fifth century by Germanic tribes known as the Goths and the Vandals.

Several of the burials included gold-and-garnet accessories on weapons and clothing.

Archaeologists discovered 11 adult graves, three graves of children and two horse burials at the site, according to the statement. In two of the female burials, archaeologists found silver bird-shaped brooches, glass bead necklaces and a bone comb, suggesting that these may have been high-status women.

But two of the male burials, in particular, stood out because of their high-quality grave goods, including a sword with a partially preserved wooden scabbard, a shield, a javelin and a scramasax, a type of Germanic short sword, which was decorated with a gold-and-garnet accessory. The weapons are characteristic of the burials of Germanic chieftains or mercenaries, according to the archaeologists, and two horses were buried nearby with their harnesses.

Two horse burials were discovered in the cemetery.

In addition to the weapons and warhorses, archaeologists noticed evidence on the men's bones that hinted that the individuals were likely warriors. Two people suffered stab wounds that showed no signs of healing, which suggests they died quickly and violently, according to the statement. And another man's right knee bones had completely fused together, which would have prevented him from bending it. This condition, called ankylosis, commonly results from an improperly healed injury.

The archaeologists believe the warrior's grave goods weren't just for show, but further study of the skeletons is planned to confirm whether the injuries seen during the excavation could have been sustained in a conflict.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Few Germanic settlements and cemeteries from the fifth century have been found, so the newly excavated site should provide important information about the upheavals linked to the fall of the Western Roman Empire and how that political collapse affected communities on the edge of the empire.

#6306. Amazon’s New Kindle Paperwhite Is Here. Here’s What’s Different From the Last Version.

From slimmer designs to updated displays and charging features, here's what's changed with Amazon's latest e-readers.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Amazon has refreshed its Kindle lineup for 2026, introducing new versions of the popular Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition. Both e-readers have notable design updates, but if you already own a previous model, you might wonder whether it's worth upgrading.

The short answer? It depends on which Kindle you're using. Compared to the 2024 models, the latest Paperwhites offer a sleeker design, updated display technology, and some welcome improvements to everyday usability. The Signature Edition, in particular, gets a few extras that make it feel more like a premium device. Here's what's changed and what's stayed the same.

Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition

The most noticeable upgrade is the design and appearance. Amazon has made the standard Paperwhite thinner and slightly lighter, reducing its thickness from 7.8 millimeters to 6.8 millimeters. It also weighs approximately 204 grams, compared to the previous model's 211 grams. That might not sound like much, but a slimmer e-reader is always welcome when you're holding it for hours or slipping it into a bag.

The redesigned display construction also creates a more seamless, edge-to-edge look. Amazon uses a new display stack with an oxide thin-film transistor backplane, designed to deliver excellent contrast, deeper blacks, and crisp text. The screen is still 7 inches with a 300-ppi resolution, so don't expect a dramatic jump in sharpness over the 2024 model.

Another small but genuinely useful change is the power button's placement. Instead of sitting along the bottom edge, where it was easy to press accidentally, it's now positioned on the upper-right side.

And if battery life is your biggest concern, there's good news: Amazon still promises up to 12 weeks on a single charge, just like the previous generation. The new model also maintains its IPX8 waterproof rating and adjustable warm lighting.

The Signature Edition receives the same thinner design and updated screen construction, but Amazon has made a few additional changes to distinguish it from the standard Paperwhite.

For starters, it now has an aluminum back instead of the previous model's plastic construction, giving it a more premium look and feel. That upgrade comes with a trade-off, though: At approximately 229 grams, the new Signature Edition is actually a little heavier than its 214-gram predecessor.

The new model also introduces pogo-pin connectors for charging and accessories. These let the Kindle connect to Amazon's new charging stand and a magnetic Page-Turn Cover with physical buttons, which could appeal to readers who miss the page-turn buttons on older e-readers.

One important difference is that the 2024 Signature Edition supported conventional Qi wireless charging, while the 2026 model switches to the new contact-based pogo-pin system.

Amazon also highlights a double-tap feature that lets you advance pages by tapping the side or back of the device, making one-handed reading a little easier.

Otherwise, you'll still get 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. Both generations are waterproof, too.

If you're shopping for a new Kindle rather than replacing an older one, the decision mostly comes down to whether the Signature Edition's premium features are worth an additional $50.

The standard Paperwhite starts at $199.99 and includes 16GB of storage, adjustable warm lighting, and a 7-inch glare-free display.

For $249.99, the Signature Edition doubles the storage to 32GB, adds an aluminum back and automatic brightness adjustment, and supports the new pogo-pin charging accessories. It's also available in Seaglass Green, whereas the regular Paperwhite comes in Graphite.

Both deliver essentially the same core reading experience, so casual readers probably won't miss much by sticking with the less expensive version.

If you already own a 2024 Kindle Paperwhite or Signature Edition and it's working perfectly fine, you probably don't need to replace it. You're still getting the same screen size and resolution, excellent battery life, waterproofing, and access to Amazon's massive Kindle library.

However, if you're upgrading from an older 2021 Paperwhite—or you're shopping for your first e-reader—the 2026 models are worth considering. The thinner design, improved screen construction, and updated controls make the latest lineup more appealing.

For most readers, the regular Paperwhite will be more than enough. But if you read every day, want the premium aluminum design, or like the idea of a case with physical page-turn buttons, the Signature Edition is a worthwhile step up.

#6305. The 8 Best Gaming Mice for Precise Control

Pull triggers faster and enhance your aim for better performance in FPS and MOBA titles.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Any competitive PC gamer knows that a good gaming mouse can mean the difference between victory and defeat. Standard productivity mice aren't built for the fast-paced action of games like League of Legends and Apex Legends. Game console controllers, while comfortable, put you at a major disadvantage in competitive shooters like Fortnite.

Whether you play on one of the best gaming desktops, a handheld gaming PC docked at your desk, or a Mac, a gaming mouse gives you the fastest, most responsive connection to your game. If you want to map more actions to your mouse, improve your aim, and react faster, our top gaming mouse picks can help you reach the next level and leave your rivals in the dust.

We've been testing gaming mice and other PC peripherals for years, including recent coverage of the Logitech Mobi Fold travel mouse, the Logitech Alto Keys K98M mechanical keyboard, and the gaming-focused Kinesis Freestyle Edge RGB Plus split keyboard, as well as our roundup of the best ergonomic keyboards. For this update, we started from that past testing and coverage, then researched the newest models from Razer, Logitech, Corsair, and other major brands to see what has changed since our last update in 2023.

We judged each mouse on what affects gameplay, including weight, shape, sensor tracking speed, polling rate, switch type, battery life, and how many buttons you can program. We checked every claim against the manufacturer's published specs. We also looked at price and value, which is why the guide includes a budget pick alongside $150-plus flagships. Each pick suits a specific kind of player, whether that's a competitive shooter fan, an MMO player who needs a dozen thumb buttons, or a left-handed gamer tired of mice built for righties.

The Razer Viper V4 Pro weighs 49 grams and still runs up to 180 hours on a charge, which is about six weeks of play at four hours a day. It's light enough to steer with your fingertips, so small aim corrections in shooters are faster, and your wrist gets less tired over long sessions. The symmetrical body has no thumb rest or flared sides, so it suits claw and fingertip grips better than a full palm grip.

Razer's Focus Pro 50K sensor tracks at up to 930 inches per second, so the cursor stays where you aimed even when you swipe the mouse hard. The included wireless dongle supports an 8,000 Hz polling rate. At that rate, the mouse reports its position to your PC eight times as often as a standard 1,000 Hz mouse, so movements reach the screen a fraction of a millisecond sooner. At 8,000 Hz, battery life drops to about 45 hours.

The mouse doesn't support Bluetooth, so the only wireless option is the included USB dongle. That dongle uses up one of your computer's USB ports, and if you use the mouse with a laptop, you have to remember to bring the dongle too. The main buttons use light instead of metal parts to detect a click, so each press reaches your game a little faster than on a standard mouse. With no metal contacts to wear down, they also hold up longer. Razer rates them for 100 million clicks, which works out to more than 25,000 clicks a day for ten years.

The Logitech G305 Lightspeed is the cheapest wireless mouse in this guide, and you still get the same 1,000 Hz connection as a standard wired gaming mouse through Logitech's Lightspeed receiver.

The G305 runs on a single AA battery instead of a rechargeable one, and should last up to 250 hours. If you switch on Endurance mode in Logitech's G Hub software, that stretches to as long as nine months. A slot inside the mouse holds the USB receiver, so if you play on a laptop, you can toss the mouse in a bag without worrying about losing it.

The mouse’s HERO sensor tops out at 12,000 CPI, which is lower than the other picks in this guide but well above what most players use. The symmetrical shape is comfortable in either a claw or palm grip, and its six buttons can be remapped. The settings are saved to the mouse itself, so they carry over when you plug it into another computer.

The Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike lets you decide how far each main button must travel before it counts as a click. Instead of a standard switch, each button uses an electromagnetic field to sense how far you’ve pressed it, and you can choose from 10 click points. Set a shallow one, and your shot fires as soon as you press. Logitech says this cuts click delay by up to 30 milliseconds.

The buttons also support rapid trigger, which you can set to one of five reset points. A button resets as soon as you start lifting your finger instead of waiting for it to spring all the way back, so you can fire again sooner. With no mechanical switch inside, haptic feedback creates the click you feel.

The mouse weighs 59 grams, and Logitech moved that weight toward the center. It reports its position to your PC up to 8,000 times a second, over both the wireless receiver and the USB-C cable. The battery is rated for more than 135 hours, and the mouse can also charge on Logitech's Powerplay mouse pad, which is sold separately.

At 36 grams, the Corsair Sabre V2 Pro is 13 grams lighter than our top pick. With less weight to move on every flick, your wrist and arm don’t tire as quickly during long play sessions. The body is 119 mm long, so it's small and best suited for claw and fingertip grips.

It runs at the same 8,000 Hz polling rate as the Viper V4 Pro over the wireless dongle or the cable. It doesn’t quite match the V4 Pro’s battery, though. Corsair rates it for 70 hours at the standard 1,000 Hz and gives no number at 8,000 Hz, saying only that it lasts "a full day of scrims," meaning practice matches. When the battery runs low, you can plug in the included USB-C cable and keep playing; a full charge takes 90 minutes.

You don't need to download an app to set it up. Corsair Web Hub runs in your browser, so you can remap buttons, record macros, and adjust sensitivity. Corsair also includes grip tape and a spare set of skates, the slick pads on the bottom of the mouse, to swap in when the originals wear down.

The Razer Naga V3 Pro's left side features a magnetic plate that pulls off and swaps for one of two others. The 12-button plate is laid out like a phone keypad, which puts a dozen spells, macros, and mounts under your thumb in MMOs. The 6-button plate suits games like League of Legends, where you trigger a few abilities, and the 2-button plate clears the side for shooters. Depending on which plate is on, the mouse has 13, 17, or 23 programmable buttons.

Two small buttons next to the left click instantly change sensitivity. You can lower it for a careful shot, then raise it again to move around the map. The ring-finger button has a physical lock, so you can switch it off if you accidentally keep pressing it. In the scroll wheel's Smart-Reel mode, the wheel clicks in steps when you scroll slowly and spins freely when you flick it.

It connects via Razer's wireless dongle, Bluetooth, or a cable. On a charge, it lasts up to 155 hours on the dongle and 280 hours on Bluetooth. It weighs more than twice as much as the Viper V4 Pro, and its 1,000 Hz polling rate is an eighth of the rate on our first three picks.

Most mice sold as ambidextrous only have a symmetrical shape, so the thumb buttons still sit on the left side, where a left-handed player's pinky ends up. The Logitech G Pro 2 Lightspeed fixes that with magnetic side buttons. Pull them off one side, snap them onto the other, and you’re ready to go. You can also run buttons on both sides, for four to eight programmable buttons total.

Logitech's Lightforce switches use the same light-based sensing as the Viper V4 Pro's. They add a small mechanical part that gives each press the firmer, clickier feel of a traditional mouse button. The HERO 2 sensor is also used in Logitech's other Pro mice.

The battery lasts up to 95 hours, which is a lot for most of our other picks. You can recharge it over USB-C, or set the mouse on a Logitech Powerplay mouse pad, which charges it wirelessly while you play. Out of the box, it connects through the standard Lightspeed receiver. To match the 8,000 Hz rate on our first three picks, you'll need Logitech's Pro Lightspeed receiver, which is sold separately.

Beyond providing customization software for the internals, Mad Catz designed the R.A.T. 8 Plus so you can break it down and rebuild it to suit any hand size and shape. The pinky and palm rests are interchangeable across the three included versions. The thumb rest is also adjustable. Despite the forward-thinking customization, it’s a bit expensive, particularly for a wired gaming mouse. And the distinctive, somewhat retro design won’t appeal to everyone.

However, no other gaming mouse lets you tinker with nearly every component to create a truly unique fit. If you’re into swapping out your keyboard switches, building your PC, and modifying your tech, the R.A.T. 8 Plus allows you to explore your technical side by giving your mouse a full functional and aesthetic makeover on the fly.

Players with larger hands can sometimes feel like Goldilocks when looking for a mouse to fit their bear-sized mitts. Smaller gaming mice cause cramping and hand issues, whereas bigger mice lack precise control and satisfying buttons. This mouse was designed with that player in mind and blends bigger with better.

The Ironclaw has a grippy rubber body and a waxy scroll wheel for a satisfying, comfortable feel. Its refined dome conforms to the palm of bigger hands, and the contoured shape allows for easy button access. Those same buttons have ultra-durable Omron switches that can withstand up to 50 million clicks. Although it is on the heavy side, it feels substantial rather than cumbersome.

Wireless gaming mice now match wired ones on speed, and nearly every pick in this guide is wireless. The key component is the small USB receiver, or dongle, that comes in the box. It talks to the mouse on its own dedicated channel, which keeps lag low enough for competitive play. Some mice also connect over Bluetooth, which lets you pair with a laptop when the dongle isn't handy. Bluetooth responds more slowly, though, so it's better for browsing and casual games than for shooters. If you lose the dongle and your mouse doesn't support Bluetooth, you'll need a cable to keep using it.

A lighter mouse takes less effort to start and stop, so quick flicks and small corrections in shooters get easier. Competitive mice now weigh 36 to 60 grams. Mice with lots of buttons, like MMO models with side keypads, often weigh over 100 grams. That doesn't matter much in games where you aren't constantly swinging your aim around.

Right-handed mice are sculpted to support your palm and thumb. Symmetrical mice are flatter and smaller, which suits claw and fingertip grips, where only your fingertips and the back of your palm touch the mouse. If you're left-handed, look for side buttons that can move to the right side. A symmetrical shape alone still puts the thumb buttons under your pinky.

Polling rate is how often the mouse reports its position to your PC. A standard gaming mouse does this 1,000 times a second, and the newest models reach 8,000. At higher rates, each movement shows up on screen slightly sooner. Most players won't notice the difference, but competitive players chasing every millisecond might. Higher polling also drains the battery faster.

CPI, also called DPI, sets how far your cursor moves for every inch you move the mouse. A higher number doesn't mean better aim. Most players set it somewhere between 400 and 3,200, and the 30,000-plus ceilings in spec sheets go far beyond what anyone uses. Look at tracking speed instead, listed in inches per second (IPS). It tells you how fast you can swing the mouse before the sensor loses track.

Optical switches register a click when a beam of light is interrupted, which makes them faster and longer-lasting than older mechanical switches. A few newer mice let you set how far a button travels before it clicks, so a shot can fire with a lighter, shorter press.

Most gaming mice come with free software to remap buttons, record macros, and save profiles for different games. Some load the settings onto the mouse itself, so you don't have to set it up again on another computer. A few run entirely in a web browser, with nothing to install.

Neuroscientists say people can be "trained" to recognize when they're dreaming — in other words, lucid dreaming may be an acquirable skill.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During dreams, bizarre scenes you encounter can seem as tangible as reality; you feel as though you're really flying through the sky or being chased through a jungle of bright-purple trees. But in special cases, people realize they're in the midst of a dream as it's unfolding.

Called lucid dreaming, this phenomenon occurs when we suddenly regain our capacity for metacognition, or thinking about our own thoughts, in the middle of a dream. Lucid dreamers can sometimes even control the content or trajectory of their dreams. Now, researchers claim that they've found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they're awake.

In a study involving a few dozen participants, the scientists found that repeating this training twice a week for a month significantly increased how often participants experienced lucid dreaming. They say the approach could have practical applications as an intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder — but those applications are theoretical, for now.

If you could learn how to lucid dream, would you? Let us know in the poll below, and add your thoughts in the comments.

#6303. TCL A400U Designer Series TV Review: An Art TV That Puts Movie Night First

TCL's slim art TV gives you deep blacks and bright HDR, but its art mode isn’t quite as mesmerizing.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Frame TVs are built to look good when you’re not watching them. They’re designed to look like a painting, rather than a TV, with thin designs, wood frames, and a rotating set of digital art that lets it fade into the background of your home, unlike home theaters that often dominate the living room.

While appealing conceptually, most of these TVs do not provide the same performance as an equally expensive conventional TV. Specifically, very few of the models we’ve seen or tested have a feature called full-array local dimming, which allows the TV to brighten or darken different parts of the screen to optimize color and contrast. Without it, the whole backlight stays lit, so dark scenes look more gray than true black.

TCL's A400U Designer Series doesn't have that problem. Its QD-Mini LED panel has 836 local dimming zones, making the dark scenes actually look dark and moody instead of a faded gray. It also hits a claimed 2,500 nits at peak brightness, so HDR highlights, like explosions, really pop. And it still has that art TV look and feel: The body is just 1.57 inches thick, so it sits flush against the wall like a picture frame. Those are far better core specs than most Frame TVs, and at $1,600 for a 75-inch set, it costs far less than Samsung's Frame Pro ($2,800 for a 75-inch), the best-known art TV with a Mini-LED backlight.

While the A400U has the power to deliver a better picture when you’re watching, it also isn’t exactly an “art TV” as we’ve come to understand it. In fact, it’s missing a couple of the hallmarks. First of all, it doesn’t actually have a physical frame: It opts for a stylishly thin bezel that one might describe as artful. And the screen features a semi-glossy, low-reflection coating instead of the matte anti-reflection coating that has become a signature across most of the best art TVs, including Samsung’s Frame and Frame Pro, the Amazon Ember Artline, and the Hisense S7SG. Even TCL’s own A300L, a lesser version of this TV, has it. The matte coating is the X factor for art TVs: It makes digital art (especially paintings) look real at a glance. Without it, the A400U falls from possibly the perfect art TV to one that offers a different type of compromise: It’s a great set for folks who want the Frame aesthetic for an attainable price without compromising on TV image quality, at the expense of that “Frame TV” magic.

The A400U’s QD-mini-LED display panel combines two technologies that are fairly common in conventional TVs, quantum dots (that’s the “QD”) and mini-LED, which is a form of LED backlighting that puts thousands of tiny LEDs behind every inch of the screen. Since the TV supports local dimming, those lights are broken up into 836 groups or “zones,” which the TV can independently control, making them brighter or dimmer to more precisely produce whatever’s on screen. You’ll notice the difference most in dark scenes: Local dimming can accurately produce the lighting of a darkly candle-lit room, or even show what it’s like to see in the dark.

I watched Zach Cregger's Resident Evil, which is set entirely at night, and you can see right away how the Mini-LED’s local dimming zones come in clutch. When Bryan is driving through the snowy mountain roads, the night sky and surrounding forest stay black while the headlights and snow stay bright, so you only see what his headlights catch, which is exactly how a horror movie should look. When I watched the same scene on the Ember Artline, which does not have the tech, the whole backlight stayed lit, and the night sky turned a dull gray.

Quantum dots, which you may know best from “QLED” TVs that introduced them, enhance the screen’s color. There’s a layer of tiny nanoparticles in the display that glow a specific color when light hits them. When the backlight passes through the dots, the blue LED light turns into red and green. This allows the TV to produce deeper reds and greens than a standard LED TV, such as the red of Darth Vader's lightsaber or the green of the Hulk in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. TCL says the A400U covers 93 percent of the DCI-P3 color gamut, the color space where most movies and shows are mastered. That’s a respectable figure, though a step behind top-tier TVs. Top OLEDs like LG’s C6 cover 99 percent or more. Still, the colors on the A400U look rich and vibrant.

While the A400U’s display performance is impressive among Frame TVs, its performance does not compare to an elite mini-LED TV. I’ve praised the A400U for having 836 zones, but there are more than 2,000 in the 75-inch TCL QM8K, for example. With fewer, larger zones, excess light from bright spots on the screen can cloud the darker ones around them. (It’s no different from resolution or frame rate, really: Having more dimming zones creates a smoother gradient for the TV’s lighting.) That glow, called blooming, is pretty easy to spot around white subtitles on a black background, but it's a much smaller problem than the gray haze you get on a TV without full-array local dimming.

TCL claims the A400U hits 2,500 nits at peak brightness. That’s much, much better than the roughly 680 nits we measured on Hisense's S7SG. Most streaming content maxes out at 1,000 nits, so the A400U can show HDR highlights, like the flash of an explosion, at full intensity instead of dimming them.

The A400U has the build of an art TV. It comes with a flush wall mount that holds its incredibly slim body right up against the wall. The mount is fixed, though, so you can't tilt the screen down or swivel it toward a different seat. It also leaves no room behind the TV to reach the ports, so plugging in a new HDMI cable is a hassle. The A400U also has a center pedestal stand for setting it on a media console, but given its size, it looks much better on the wall.

But, as I mentioned at the outset, this TV doesn’t have a physical frame. Instead, the edge is a flat edge of black metal, which is closer to a minimalist frame than a chunky TV bezel. I like the look, and it suits the modern vibe TCL is going for, but it doesn’t quite give you that framed picture look. TK. Removing the frame is a strange omission: TCL makes a more affordable version of this TV, the A300L, which comes with a light-wood magnetic frame that snaps onto the edges of the screen.

In the same vein, TCL omits the ultra-matte anti-reflection coating found on most frame TVs, in favor of what the brand refers to as an “ultra-low-reflection coating.” The matte coating is the secret sauce for art TVs: It scatters light that hits the screen instead of bouncing it straight back at you, which cuts out any glare. In most cases, it does a pretty amazing job of making digital images look like a physical piece of art hanging on a wall. The A400U's finish is somewhere between glossy and matte, but closer to glossy. Combined with the bright backlight, that gives paintings a sheen and a glow that a print on the wall wouldn't have.

I put the A400U in the brightest room in my house, on the west wall. There's a small window right next to it and a huge window on the north wall, plus a door with a big glass pane directly across from the TV. The vaulted ceiling goes up about two stories and has more windows along the top. It's the worst spot in the house for a TV, but also the only space that could accommodate its size, which made it a good test.

The low-reflection coating and high brightness kept most of that light from washing out the picture, and glare was rarely bad enough to make me close the blinds. It can't block every reflection, though. When the screen is mostly dark, there isn't much light coming from the picture to cover up reflections, so the windows around the room show up more. During the day, that makes a movie like Resident Evil harder to enjoy. Brighter shows and movies look fine, and dark ones look much better after sunset or with the blinds closed.

When you aren't watching anything, the A400U can show pieces from TCL's Art Library, artificial intelligence–generated art, or your own photos uploaded through the TCL Home app, and none of it requires a subscription. Samsung's Frame TVs give you 30 free artworks a month and charge $5 a month for the full Art Store. TCL’s TV also has an Ambient Mode that plays moving scenes, similar to the looping landscape videos on the Ember Artline.

An ambient light sensor adjusts the screen's brightness to match the room, so a painting doesn't glow too brightly after dark. Unlike the Ember Artline, the A400U doesn't have a motion sensor, so it won't wake up and switch to art when you walk into the room. I usually turn art mode on whenever I'm done watching something, and I set it up to stay on for a few hours before shutting off.

The A400U runs at a native 144Hz and supports variable refresh rate (VRR) and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro. VRR matches the TV's refresh rate to the frames a console or gaming PC is putting out, which prevents tearing when a game's frame rate dips. I played Control Resonant and Marvel's Wolverine on my PS5. The detailed worlds in Control Resonant looked incredible, with sharp textures on the warped buildings and bright effects. In Wolverine, the fast action stayed smooth and clear, without the blur or stutter you'd see on a slower 60Hz screen.

Only HDMI 1 and 2 support 4K at 144Hz, while HDMI 3 and 4 top out at 4K at 60Hz. HDMI 1 is also the eARC port, which you need to send full-quality Dolby Atmos audio to a soundbar. If you plug a soundbar in there without passthrough, you’ll be left with one fast port, so a second console or a gaming PC would run at 60Hz. Since the flush mount makes swapping cables a pain, it’s worth figuring out which device goes in which port before you hang the TV.

The A400U runs Google TV and supports both Chromecast and AirPlay 2, so you can stream video from an Android phone or an iPhone. Google has added more ads over the years, but it's still faster than the Fire TV software on the Ember Artline, which lagged while scrolling through menus.

The built-in speakers are a pair of 10-watt drivers tuned by Onkyo, with Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X processing that simulates surround and height effects. When I fired up Top Gun: Maverick, I was impressed by how clear and detailed they sound for TV speakers. Dialogue was easy to follow without raising the volume, and the rumble of the jets filled the room. In other words, I wouldn't rush out to buy a soundbar.

With the A400U, TCL kind of wants to have its cake and eat it too. Its performance, design, and overall vibe are clearly meant to appeal to the art TV crowd, but it doesn’t have a frame or the matte coating, which are arguably the two defining qualities of the category. That isn’t necessarily a problem, though: It just makes this set a niche choice. This is a TV for people who want the aesthetics of art TV, but care enough about how movies and video games look that the standard Frame and other models like it may not live up to their expectations.

Ultimately, the Samsung Frame Pro still comes closer to letting you have it all—great performance and the true, matte-coated “frame” experience. It also has a Mini-LED backlight, along with the matte screen and a frame-style bezel that make art look like it’s actually hanging on your wall. But it costs $2,800 for a 75-inch model on Samsung’s site, compared with $1,600 for the 74-inch A400U.

If the Frame Pro’s price tag is a little too high, there are plenty of affordable alternatives with matte screens and magnetic wood frames that come much closer to looking like real paintings, including TCL’s own A300L and the Amazon Ember Artline. If you want an art TV you’ll also use every night for movies and games, the A400U gets you that for less than the Frame Pro, as long as you can live with art mode looking more like a TV.

Brandon Russell is a freelance writer covering gear and technology. He started his journey as a news writer at a small newspaper and later began reviewing smartphones, movies, and video games. In his free time, he enjoys the slower, more intentional experience of using a 35mm film camera and making short videos about movies he grew up watching.

Royal Caribbean's newest megaship is set to make its U.S. debut this weekend.

Passengers will board Legend of the Seas, the cruise line's third Icon Class vessel, at Fort Lauderdale's Port Everglades on Sunday for a pre-inaugural three-night trip to the Bahamas.

The cruise line added the departure ahead of the ship's previously announced Nov. 11 inaugural voyage from the cruise hub, giving travelers an early chance to experience its newest Icon Class ship.

The sailing will include a stop at Royal Caribbean's private island destination, Perfect Day at CocoCay, followed by a day at sea before returning to Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11.

At 248,633 gross tons, Legend of the Seas is the world's largest cruise ship, sharing the title with its two same-size Icon Class sisters, Icon of the Seas and Star of the Seas. The vessel can accommodate up to 7,600 passengers and approximately 2,350 crew members.

Like its sister ships, Legend of the Seas features eight neighborhoods, seven pools and a lineup of family-friendly attractions, including Category 6, a six-slide water park. The ship also introduces several new experiences, including the Hollywood-themed Hollywoodland Supper Club and additional dining options in the AquaDome.

Related: Royal Caribbean cruise ships from newest to oldest — a complete list

Legend of the Seas debuted in Europe in summer 2026, sailing seven-night Western Mediterranean itineraries from Barcelona and Rome before crossing the Atlantic to begin its Caribbean season.

Following two initial Bahamas sailings, Legend of the Seas will operate six- to eight-night itineraries from Fort Lauderdale to Western and Southern Caribbean destinations — including some places, like Aruba and Curacao, that don't normally see much action from Icon Class ships. Depending on the sailing, it'll also make port calls in Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic and Mexico. Plus, every sailing will visit Perfect Day at CocoCay.

Rates for six-night trips begin around $1,000 per person, and eight-night trips begin around $1,400. However, prices differ greatly based on your chosen itinerary, room type and dates of travel.

#6301. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

C. Le Quéré et al. A further acceleration of clean energy is needed for global CO2 emissions to peak and decline. Nature Climate Change. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41558-026-02821-8

This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6299. The ReelCharge ReelPro 200W Power Bank Is a Travel-Ready Charging Beast

This laptop charger has everything you could want in a travel power backup solution and only costs $120.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

ReelCharge, a relative newcomer to the portable battery pack market, has caught our eye this year with a few interesting options. Most notable among them is the ReelPro 200W, a compact but massively powerful laptop charger that can keep up with your travel charging needs better than any pack we’ve tested. It features an ample 27,000 milliampere-hour (mAh) battery capacity—about as much as you can get while staying under the FAA’s 100-watt-hour limit—and a maximum power output of 200 watts (W), including up to 140-watt charging on a single device. That beats most laptop wall chargers on speed. Best of all, it costs only $120, substantially undercutting flagship battery packs from legacy brands such as Anker and EcoFlow.

Throw in some premium features and a three-year warranty, and you have a power bank that truly feels like it's setting a new gold standard for high-end power banks that the competition will need to meet.

The ReelPro 200W looks like a bougie battery pack. It has a sleek housing with a matte finish, a glossy front panel, and a color LED display. A display is definitely a must for a high-capacity battery pack in the mid-2020s. It shows the battery’s remaining charge and the wattage going into each outlet, plus status checks on temperature and health. It’s neatly integrated into the pack’s glossy front panel, so it fades into it when turned off, giving it a pleasantly minimalist look.

The ReelPro can charge up to three devices—more than a little, but not the most we’ve seen. It has an integrated, retractable USB-C cable, which can loop around to become a wrist strap. There are also USB-C and USB-A ports for when you want to charge up multiple devices (and to charge the pack itself). Personally, I prefer a battery pack with an external cable to one with a retractable cord because this leaves more interior space for battery cells and allows for a larger capacity.

Having plenty of ports means little if the pack can’t power them properly, and that’s where the ReelPro 200 watts really impresses. As the name suggests, it has a total power output of 200W and can charge a single device at up to 140 watts. That’s as much as we’ve ever seen in a battery pack, and more than you’ll get out of premium wall chargers for laptops and other devices. Case in point: the official charger for the 16-inch MacBook Pro delivers the same amount of power.

Having that extra 60 watts of output means that when you plug in multiple devices, you’re less likely to see a slowdown in charging. I was able to charge my MacBook Pro and an iPhone 18 Pro Max at the same time at full speed. If you were to plug in three large devices (like laptops) at the same time, there would be a substantial drop-off in power going to the first device, but it can handle most common travel setups without that happening.

The result is a backup power solution that works just as well as plugging your devices into the wall, even when you need to charge multiple devices. On a recent weekend trip, I used it to charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro faster than its included 70-watt adapter, without exceeding 140 watts. It’s the kind of performance we all wish we could get from a battery pack, but never actually do.

This is a secondary concern, but I think it’s worth pointing out that ReelCharge offers a best-in-class three-year warranty on the ReelPro 200W. That’s a lot of protection for any piece of tech, and far longer than most competitors: Anker, for example, backs battery packs with an 18-month warranty, which is better than average. Standing by its products for so long shows the brand has strong faith in them.

If you are a frequent traveler, or a mobile worker who lives and dies by having constant access to a laptop, this is the best high-capacity battery pack I’ve tested to date. It’s definitely too big to fit in your pocket, so it’s overkill if you just need to top up a phone or tablet occasionally, but this is the ReelPro 200W, a big battery backup that you can depend on, and it costs far less than the Anker Prime, our previous laptop charger of choice.

ReelCharge ReelPro Charger and Power Bank

#6298. I’m a Tape Measure Guy. But This Laser Measuring Tool is Testing My Loyalty.

Measuring long walls, gauging ceiling heights, and handling the awkward math are where the Mileseey S50C shines.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Look, I’m a tape measure guy. Always have been. Always will be. That red Milwaukee 25-footer rides on my hip like Wyatt Earp’s six-shooter, ready to draw when I need fast dimensions across a 2x4 or sheet of plywood. I ask a lot of it, and it always delivers. That is, until I ask it to stretch across a long wall and maintain its rigidity.

But I got my hands on Mileseey’s S50C Laser Measure and it has me reconsidering how often I reach for my trusty tape—especially when my foe is notably larger than normal and physically out of my league. No one ever said I had to fight fair, so lately I find myself reaching for a more technologically advanced weapon of choice. And in that moment before I grab, I always have the same thought: Why am I working so hard?

What’s won me over about the S50C is how easily it takes over the measurements I least enjoy making with a tape. Long distances. Wall-to-wall dimensions. Floor-to-ceiling heights. The sort of thing that usually has me looking around for another person to whom I need to say “Hey, could you hold this for a second?” Aim, press the button, read the measurement. Nobody has to put down what they’re doing and walk over.

The S50C has been impressively accurate and simple to operate. It’s also handy as heck, which matters to me more than a long list of functions. A tool can have enough computing power to figure out a Mars landing, but if taking basic measurements becomes a small administrative project, I’m going straight back to the tape. With this one, I’ve found myself grabbing it as soon as a measurement starts feeling like it’s going to give me a fight, which is exactly how any new tool tends to earn a home in my usual routine.

The S50C also goes way beyond telling you how far away the opposite wall is. You can easily toggle through its measurement modes on the touch screen display to select area, volume, and wall area calculations, along with more specialized functions for awkward dimensions. For something like a basement renovation, that means you can gather room dimensions and calculate floor area without balancing a notebook on your knee or pulling up the calculator app on your phone. For painting, wall-area calculations give you a useful starting point for estimating coverage. You still have to account for multiple coats, product coverage, and waste—I mean, this device isn’t going to manage your entire renovation. But it can take a welcome chunk of arithmetic off your plate.

The trick is choosing the proper mode and taking the measurements it requests. It isn’t one magical button that automatically understands your basement. You supply the dimensions by placing the green laser dot on the opposing wall or ceiling, press the button, and record the measurement. The S50C handles the rest of the calculations.

The S50C has a built-in camera with up to 8x zoom—but it’s for helping you aim at distant targets. A 2.4-inch AMOLED touch screen displays the targeting view, measurements, and menus. That gives the camera a practical reason to exist. Finding a little laser dot at a distance—especially outdoors measuring distances for a fence installation—can become its own project and a huge source of frustration. The camera is there to help you see where you’re aiming, which is great for me and my ever-flagging eyesight.

Mileseey lists a maximum measuring range of 670 feet. I’ve yet to verify that distance without putting the laser on my neighbor’s home five houses away from me, but it does give you some semblance of the work this device is designed to accommodate. It also charges through USB-C and carries an IP65 dust- and water-resistance rating.

There are plenty of measurements for which I’ll keep pulling my tape. Most, come to think of it. Marking a board for a miter saw cut, checking a short dimension, laying something out directly on a workpiece. That familiar steel blade is like an extension of my hand most times.

But the S50C is worth grabbing when distance, access, or a shortage of available hands suddenly turns that tape measure into a nuisance. Its more advanced functions expand the possibilities, I suppose, but its quick convenience is what brings me back in those moments of need. On that note, if you think your measuring needs are more basic in nature, Mileseey’s S50 PrecisionX model is an ideal alternative to all of those extra features of the S50C.

I really didn’t expect to become attached to a laser measure, let alone one with so many bells and whistles. But then my tape buckled halfway across my ceiling, and the S50C gadget was sitting right there waiting.

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

Recently, TPG launched its  inaugural State of Loyalty report, a "data-backed look at consumer loyalty, industry trends, the best loyalty program benefits and how far your points, miles and dollars go these days."

Inside our comprehensive report, there are some interesting data points to look at, like which hotel loyalty points have increased or decreased in value over the year, the average points and cash price for hotels across the major loyalty brands, and our takeaways about what it all means.

It's a nice deep-dive into the world of loyalty — and a great weekend read with a strong coffee in hand.

Here's the other hotel news you need to know this week.

Aman has been on a significant expansion streak of late. Now, the luxury hotel brand has its eyes set on Puerto Rico with the announcement of Amantaru in Cabo Rojo. Though no opening date is available, we do know the hillside resort near the ocean will feature a hotel and residences, a wellness center, bars and restaurants and more in the Escencia development on the Southwestern coast.

Wyndham is making a big play in the luxury hotel space with a new partnership with HotelREZ Hotels & Resorts. The partnership will bring more than 40 independent luxury hotels into Wyndham's Registry Collection Hotels Brand by early 2026. For fans of Wyndham Rewards, this means exciting (dare I say unexpected?) locations to earn and burn points, like The TownHouse Mykonos in Greece, TreeHouse Villas Koh Yao in Thailand and Galgorm Resort in Northern Ireland.

Viceroy Park Avenue is now accepting reservations from Feb. 1, 2027, starting at $850 per night.

What's old is new again in St. Augustine, Florida, where the nearly 140-year-old Casa Monica Resort & Spa has emerged from a makeover with a new name: Grand Bohemian Casa Monica. The 137-room hotel, the first to join Marriott's Autograph Collection in 2010, now features Moroccan- and Spanish-inspired interiors, jewel tones, intricate tilework and original art. Guests can also enjoy the revamped Soltana Pool Lounge, complete with a new Moroccan-inspired bar, Mediterranean bites and cocktails made for sipping in the Florida sunshine.

There are few things I like in life more than hotel merch. It's a fun way for those of us who are travel-obsessed to inject a little hotel love into our everyday lives at home. For example, my Corgi's dog bed is from The Beverly Hills Hotel and my favorite hat was a gift from the Four Seasons Resort Maldives at Landaa Giraavaru.

Now, another brand I love, Raffles, has launched an online shop: The Little Shop by Raffles. Opening up just in time for the holidays (hey mom, you reading this?!), fans of the brand can now order everything from luxury linens to pajama sets and outfits, suitcases, fragrances and more.

“For more than a century, Raffles has inspired a sense of discovery and an instinct for the extraordinary, Claudia Kozma Kaplan, Raffles chief brand officer, said in a statement. "The Little Shop is an invitation to bring that world home through a curated collection of distinctive pieces, created by Raffles and in collaboration with a selection of houses we deeply admire."

#6295. For Over a Decade, They’ve Been the Face of the World’s Most Entrancing Treasure Hunt. Have They Finally Solved Oak Island’s Mystery?

There's gold in the water on Oak Island—but a maze of old tunnels is hiding where it’s coming from.

“Hundreds of thousands of dollars and the wits of the cleverest American engineers and college professors have been vainly spent in trying to solve the mystery of the Money Pits of Oak island and its sheltered haven, Mahone bay, Nova Scotia.”

Those words appeared in the pages of Popular Mechanics 100 years ago, in the March 1926 story “Hunting Hidden Treasures.” In the century that followed, the amount of money and wits expended on the mystery of Oak Island has only grown.

Since 2014, the public faces of the Oak Island mystery have been Rick and Marty Lagina, the stars of HISTORY’s long-running series The Curse of Oak Island. Across more than 250 episodes, audiences have followed along with the brothers’ success and setbacks, their obsession and their frustrations. When they began, via an investment in Oak Island Tours in 2006, they were pursuing a quixotic dream inspired by an old magazine article, joining a pantheon of prospectors that included Hollywood stars like Errol Flynn and John Wayne, and at least one U.S. President (Franklin D. Roosevelt, who kept tabs on the developments on Oak Island throughout his life).

Now, heading into their fourteenth season (debuting on November 10 on the History Channel), the siblings from Michigan are striking a more retrospective tone, reflecting on their role in this centuries-long quest for answers and the colleagues they’ve lost along the way (the season premiere pays homage to the late Dan Blankenship, a longtime partner of the Laginas who spent more than 50 years searching Oak Island before his 2019 passing). Now, there’s a question that’s become just as pressing for the two men as the Oak Island mystery itself: “After all these years, what was it all for?”

Ahead of the new season, Rick and Marty Lagina sat down with Pop Mech to reflect on fourteen seasons of television, how treasure-seeking has changed over the centuries, and what keeps them, and audiences, returning to Oak Island and its mysterious Money Pit year after year.

Although the marketing for Season 14 has leaned heavily on a new discovery through which the Laginas’ “lifelong quest has finally paid off,” the brothers kept the details of the coming episodes close to the vest. (Pop Mech was able to preview only the season premiere.) Otherwise, they were as candid and at times as self-effacing as they’ve been throughout fourteen seasons of television.

In fact, Rick is quick to dispel what he feels is the biggest misconception fans of the show often have. “We’re portrayed on some level as experts in every field, and we’re not,” he told us. “That’s why we have such a large tent of people helping us, because we’re not experts in every field, every arena.”

“It’s a very complex mystery,” he adds, “and we need everybody under the tent, if you will.”

That tent doesn’t just include the various experts who appeared on the program over the last decade, but also the centuries of treasure hunters who came before them. “Rick holds those prior searchers in this huge, high regard,” Marty says of his brother, “and thinks about them all the time.”

If one believes the account published in The Yarmouth Herald in 1863, that list of prior searchers stretches all the way back to 1795. That’s when a young farmer named Daniel McGinnis arrived on Oak Island via canoe, propelled by a piece of folklore which claimed that Captain Kidd had buried millions of dollars worth of treasure on the island. As he searched, he came across a depression in the ground that seemed deliberate, and called together a small team to dig on the site. As they excavated to a depth of 30 feet, they found remnants of a previous presence at the site (some accounts say flagstones, others oak platforms), and that led them to think they’d discovered the location of the buried treasure—or what’s long been referred to as the “Money Pit.”

In the early 1800s, the Onslow Company reportedly paid a visit to the same site, and they dug deeper into the Money Pit than McGinnis ever dared to go, roughly 80 to 90 feet deep. The Onslow Company found further indications that the pit was deliberately dug to store something, though their evidence was far more destructive. Their dig set off a booby trap that caused the Money Pit to flood with seawater up to the 33-foot level. The Onslow Company was unable to bail out the excavation site at the time. To make matters worse, Marty would note, later attempts only exacerbated the problem.

“There was almost certainly a flood tunnel that caused the initial booby trap,” he told us, “And people will come up to you and they’ll say, well, why don’t you shut off the water this way or shut off the water that way. The problem is there’s been so much pumping over the years by other people that the water is coming in from other places.”

Marty, who possesses an extensive engineering background in both petroleum and renewable energy, is both enamored with and exasperated by what’s been left behind by the treasure hunters who preceded him.

“From an engineering standpoint, I’m always astonished, absolutely astonished and in rapt admiration for what those people were able to do with picks and shovels,” Marty says of those earlier excavators. “I mean, you can’t believe it. If you were out there, and you saw these hand hewn timbers come up from 180 feet down. They had nothing. They had horses, you know? I mean, it’s just really amazing.”

Impressive as that work was for its time, it left modern-day diggers with consequences of their own.

“One of our scientific consultants, Ian Spooner, is a PhD geologist. He calls it Chutes & Ladders,” Marty says, before quickly adding, “He actually calls it Snakes and Ladders, because that’s the Canadian thing.”

“We have so many interconnected passages now that have been made by other people that we have to decipher all that,” he laments, “And every time a timber comes out, I mean, almost every time, you have to say, is this an original worker’s timber or is this a searcher’s timber? And we have to run the scientific analysis on that.”

In the show’s ninth season, water samples from the site turned up trace amounts of gold, a discovery that showed just how badly booby traps and centuries of earlier digging had muddied the trail.

“If you followed [the show], you know there’s gold in the water, which has kept us coming back for years,” Marty continued, “Now it’s there, it’s real, it’s coming from a source. And if the water was just moving geologically, like I’m used to in my prior business, we could trace it back, but the problem is it’s all interconnected, so it’s difficult.”

Have past attempts to solve the mystery actually further obscured Oak Island’s secrets? Did stories stoking the hunger for treasure actually, if unintentionally, contribute to the partial destruction of the Nova Scotia island?

If so, it’s a guilt that Pop Mech partially shares.

At one point in our conversation, Marty cuts in to jokingly ask, “By the way, can I do a quick commercial for Popular Mechanics?” to which this author, never afraid of a little self-promotion, gleefully assented. “Growing up, I loved that magazine. Absolutely loved that magazine,” he says, “And Rick will attest, we kind of had a hard time getting our hands on actual magazines. But I mean, I would read those from cover to cover.”

“There is one connection to Popular Mechanics too, aside from our interest in the magazine,” Rick chimed in to add, “There was an article in Popular Mechanics about Oak Island.”

As it turns out, there was more than one. But if Rick recalled an Oak Island story from one of the magazines he and Marty read cover to cover, it was likely the one published at the exact mid-point between 1926’s “Hunting Hidden Treasures” and today.

Fifty years ago, the September 1976 issue of Popular Mechanics ran with the cover story “7 Great Quests of Man,” and the mystery of Oak Island’s treasure was discussed alongside such cryptic quandaries (and just plain cryptids) as Bigfoot, the Loch Ness Monster, ancient aliens, and Noah’s Ark.

But if such outlandish company makes the Oak Island mystery feel like a fantasy, the work the Laginas have done over fourteen seasons has pulled things back into the realm of reality. While a literal pot of gold at the end of this proverbial rainbow would be a satisfying conclusion, Rick says that the true value of these excavations extends beyond the potential payday.

“When you talk about story, the science and technology has pushed the timeline of what happened on Oak island, or at least when something started to happen on Oak Island, to me, has been pushed back, literally, into the latter part of the 13th century,” he noted, “We have core samples from wells, we have carbon dates from old walls, we have archaeo-astronomical alignments. I don’t see any other explanation that some of these structures, including Nolan’s Cross, given the alignments contained within them, were of that time frame. So what happened long, long ago, well before Europeans were supposed to be on this continent, to me, that’s a story in and of itself.”

Perhaps, in that sense, the treasure has served as the profit motive, the lure that funded centuries of expeditions, which may finally be uncovering the site’s true history.

“Marty has always said that the mystery of Oak Island has endured because of treasure, because of that component, and he’s absolutely right,” Rick concluded. “But at this point, I think the treasure and the story are somewhat aligned in terms of importance, and I hope that we can push forward on both agendas.”

The new season of The Curse of Oak Island premieres on the History Channel November 10 at 9/8c.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group.
