Annual passes to major U.S. theme parks like Walt Disney World, Universal Orlando Resort, SeaWorld and Legoland come with a long list of benefits. You can visit as often as you like; you get discounts on extras like parking, merchandise and dining; and your pass often comes with access to special events throughout the year.

Theme park annual passes also come with a hefty price tag that can climb upward of $1,000. Because of this, it can be easy to assume an annual pass is only worth the cost if you live near one of these parks and can visit every week.

As an out-of-state resident who has held an annual pass to Universal Orlando Resort since 2020, I can assure you that assumption is incorrect. But you don't have to take my word for it.

I calculated the break-even point for 10 theme parks across the country to help you decide whether it's an option worth looking into. For consistency, I based these calculations on each park's top-tier pass and the lowest one-day ticket prices, using park-to-park tickets at resorts with multiple parks, since annual passes include park-to-park access.

Because these calculations are based on one-day tickets, you would still need to determine whether you could save money with an annual pass by considering the ticket cost on the date(s) of your visit (most parks have variable pricing), how many trips you take each year and the number of days you visit per trip.

**About 6 once you factor in the cost of free parking and the Express passes

Disney World offers several annual passes, but only one, the Disney Incredi-Pass, is available to out-of-state residents. The Disney Incredi-Pass has no blockout dates and includes complimentary theme park parking.

If you were to visit only on the cheapest days of the year, you would need to visit nine times each year to realize the value of a Disney World annual pass as a non-Florida resident. When you factor in shopping and dining discounts and free parking, you can probably break even after eight visits. But if you were to visit on the more expensive days, you could break even in closer to six days.

Related: Bluey, Buzz and Grogu: Opening dates for new Disney World and Disneyland attractions in 2026

Remember, though, this comparison is based on the one-day ticket price. If you plan to spend eight days at Disney World broken up between one or two visits per year, you could potentially do better to buy a multiday park hopper ticket versus an annual pass. Because Disney uses variable ticket pricing and tickets get less expensive as you add more days, you have to do the math to find out which is best for you.

Don't worry, the math on most other parks isn't quite as involved.

Disneyland's top-tier pass is called the Inspire Key. At $1,899 per year, this pass has blackout dates during the weeks of Christmas and New Year's Eve, and it includes free standard parking and unlimited Disney PhotoPass downloads.

The Inspire Key pass can pay for itself after 11 visits, since the lowest park hopper tickets start at $179.

Related: How Disneyland's newest ride proves that 'progress is impossible without change'

As with Disney World, the number of visits required to break even would decrease if you visited on more expensive days, and you could still save money by purchasing multiday tickets.

Universal Orlando has several annual pass options, but the 2-Park Premier Pass is the easiest to use and has the most benefits. You get park-to-park admission between Universal Studios Florida and Universal Islands of Adventure, complimentary skip-the-line Express passes after 4 p.m., complimentary valet and prime parking, one free ticket to Halloween Horror Nights, early park admission and several valuable discounts.

If you were to visit during the holidays when one-day park-to-park tickets climb as high as $255, you can break even after four days. It's also worth doing the calculations with the included Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $99. When you factor that in, you can break even after five visits.

Related: Epic Universe tips: 11 ways to spend less time in line and have more fun

A six-day park-to-park ticket that also includes access to Universal Epic Universe is only $550.99 per person, so if you only plan to visit once per year for six days, you would save significantly by purchasing a multiday ticket versus an annual pass.

Universal Studios Hollywood only has one park, making the math here easier to calculate. The park's Platinum Annual Pass has no blockout dates and includes free general parking most of the year, one Halloween Horror Nights ticket and Express skip-the-line access after 3 p.m.

You'd technically have to visit 6.0025 times to break even, but if you include the free parking and after-3 p.m. Express passes, we can safely say you break even after six visits.

Related: Thrills for all ages: 6 best rides at Universal Studios Hollywood

Similar to Universal Orlando, you can break even sooner if you factor in the cost of a Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $77 per person. When you factor that in, plus those other perks, you can break even after approximately five one-day visits.

This is where things get a little bit fun (in my opinion, anyway). Legoland's Premium Annual Pass includes visits to more than 20 Merlin attractions across the country, including Legoland, Peppa Pig Park, Sea Life Aquarium, Madame Tussauds wax museum and more. A lot of these parks are in theme park hubs like Florida, California and Texas, so you likely aren't too far from one or multiple locations.

In this case, you don't need to plan multiple visits to a single park to see the value in an annual pass. You can visit multiple locations around the country with no blockout dates, free parking and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets (one ticket per quarter), which make the math very appealing.

If you assign a $69 value to the "Bring-A-Friend" tickets, four per year would equal $276, just $23 less than the total annual pass cost. So, if you were to visit one of the 20+ parks nationwide four times per year (once per quarter) and bring a friend or family member with you, you'd save money with an annual pass before even factoring in free parking and other discounts.

This is another instance where you can access multiple parks with a single annual pass. SeaWorld Orlando's Platinum Pass includes unlimited admission to 11 parks across the country with no blockout dates. These include all SeaWorld and Busch Gardens parks, as well as their affiliated water parks. You also get eight free guest tickets, free photos and free preferred parking.

A few notes here. You can't use all eight free guest tickets at the same time and they are limited to select parks. SeaWorld allows you to use a certain number of tickets during different calendar windows throughout the year. But if you were to visit these parks eight times per year and bring a friend, you would save more than $600 by purchasing an annual pass.

It's also worth noting that SeaWorld San Diego's Platinum Pass is only $201 on sale, and its lowest one-day ticket costs $64.99, so you'd break even after just four visits. While it provides the passholder access to the same 11 parks, its guest passes can only be used at the California parks.

Opened in July 2026, Universal Kids Resort is the newest park on this list. The park recently started selling annual passes, with the Gold Annual Pass being its top-tier offering. The Gold pass has no blockout dates and includes regular self-parking.

Assuming you visit on five separate days and only visit on the least expensive days, you would break even after five visits. But because the Gold Pass also includes free parking and other discounts, you could potentially break even in four one-day visits. Because the park also sells discounted multiday tickets, the above math only makes sense if you were to visit on five nonconsecutive days.

You don't need to live in Florida or California to have access to award-winning theme parks. Holiday World in Santa Claus, Indiana, consistently wins awards for its cleanliness, water park and thrilling coasters. Holiday World's Platinum Pass has no blockout dates, early entry for select attractions and discounted "Bring-a-Friend" tickets.

Holiday World already offers free parking, sunscreen and soft drinks, so you won't get additional discounts there. You would break even after four one-day visits, assuming you purchase the lowest-cost tickets.

Dollywood's top-of-the-line pass is a Diamond Season Pass (a very fitting name for our bright and shining queen Dolly Parton, if you ask me). With it, you get unlimited visits, complimentary parking, Time Saver skip-the-line access for the first hour of each day, a 20% discount on shopping and dining, and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets.

Dollywood handles its "Bring-a-Friend" tickets differently. You can use them one at a time or all four at once. If you brought four friends with you during your first visit after buying your annual pass, you would have more than covered the cost of your pass. In fact, you could save about $110 by purchasing an annual pass instead of five one-day tickets (you and four friends). Any future visits that year are just a bonus. Just one of the million reasons to love Dollywood.

Silver Dollar City and Dollywood are owned by the same parent company (Herschend Family Entertainment), but their annual passes work quite differently. Silver Dollar City's Diamond Pass includes unlimited visits to the park and White Water water park, eight free "Bring A Friend" tickets (to be used during specific redemption windows at Silver Dollar City or White Water), a bonus "Bring-a-Friend" ticket you can use on any day and $29.99 tickets for friends and family.

Even though you can't use all of your "Bring-a-Friend" tickets at one time, you only need to visit with a guest twice to break even with an annual pass before even digging into the savings you would find from in-park discounts.

In addition to the advertised benefits, there is a level of convenience that comes with being a passholder. You can pop in for a few hours without feeling like you wasted money on a full-day ticket, and you feel like a more valuable guest when you visit. I often get things like priority parade seating, fun freebies and passholder-only discounts of up to 70% off merchandise.

No amount of math matters unless you know you will actually use and enjoy the benefits of being a passholder. Use these calculations as a jumping-off point to decide if you are ready to be a passholder.

#6215. How to Spend a Rainy Day in New York City

A rainy day in New York City is no new phenomenon, but that doesn’t make its occurrence any less disappointing. According to reporting from News 12, Central Park only reported nine completely dry weekends out of the past 40 weekends of 2026, putting a real—forgive me—damper on park hangs and beach days. In case you count yourself among the masses with foiled plans, we at Condé Nast Traveler have you covered. Our editors have weathered their fair share of cold and dreary days in the city and learned to love the rain. After all, it’s the best excuse to dry off by the crackling fireplace of a plush hotel lobby, or conversely, to take a dip into the steaming Russian Turkish baths to cure the sinking cold. Instead of willing the clouds to part, bear your galoshes and head to our editors’ favorite things to do in New York City on a rainy day.

That travel editors love a hotel lobby is about as unsurprising as a dad joke, but there’s nothing like a mini staycation to salvage a lost weekend. Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is partial to The Hotel Chelsea. The neighborhood institution has moved far past its roach-ridden days when Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe were Just Kids, and the experience of their lobby is the apotheosis of that evolution. There’s a lot of modern polish, sure, but all the charming verdigris has been kept intact. There’s the art from the hotel’s most (in)famous guests splashed over the walls, the wrought iron chandeliers bathing the space in romantic lighting, and the aforementioned fireplace tying a bow around the mood. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that the hotel’s Lobby Bar is just right next door. If Chelsea feels like a slog to commute to, there are plenty of great options scattered across the map, from the Ace Hotel Brooklyn which has plenty of public workspaces, or Times Square’s Algonquin Hotel, which saw the genesis of The New Yorker just 100 years ago.

The easiest remedy for rainy day restlessness is to stretch your legs at one of the city’s finest museums, though even the impressive 2.2 million-square-foot expanse of the Met becomes easily dwarfed when you’re crammed in by a surge of fellow museum-goers who had the exact same idea. Instead, spend your day exploring NYC’s smaller scholarly corners. Editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez heads to East Williamsburg art organization Amant whenever she feels like she’s cooped inside her apartment, watching the hours just slip away. To start, there’s no need to worry about ponying up big ticket prices as entry is always free. “Peruse the titles at Kis Café and Bookstore, then head to gallery spaces 932 Grand and 315 Maujer; across the street, you’ll find multimedia installations in Géza,” says Alvarez, “The exhibit Sentient Earth currently spans all three galleries, bringing together 28 artists to examine the ways we’ve impacted the planet (and what—if it gained sentience—its response to us might be). Do explore Amant's event programming of screenings and panels, which you can find here.” Other small but mighty options include the Financial District’s public poetry library Poets House, which overlooks the Hudson and Bushwick’s Bone Museum, which also houses resident tuxedo cat Bone Jovi.

Film critic Anthony Lane once posited, “as a rough rule, cinema can be sundered into two halves: six-o’clock films and nine-o’clock films,” and a rainy day is certainly the occasion for the six-o’clock variety and all its ritual: rallying a group to go with, booking the early dinner reservation, whiling away at a nearby bar after to unpack what you’ve just seen. Commerce director Madison Flager likes the Lincoln Center AMC, home to the largest IMAX screen in the country, clocking in at 75.6 feet tall by 101 feet wide, which is roughly the size of a 10-story building. News editor Hannah Towey, on the other hand, dodges the rain at the Metrograph, a boutique two-screen theater keeping the spirit of Prohibition-era New York alive and well. Whichever way you lean, you can always count on NYC’s trusty movie theaters to show you something new.

The less-than-stellar weather shouldn’t keep you from embarking on a treasure hunt, and doing your due diligence enclosed inside one of the city’s coolest vintage stores is a surefire way to uncover a few gems. Alvarez recommends the Flatiron District’s Surrender Dorothy, where the racks are piled with the well-loved and pristine, collector’s items and forgotten blasts from the past, avant-garde art pieces, and buy-it-for-life workwear. It’s dopamine dressing at its best. You could also try your luck at one of the city’s larger franchises like Beacon’s Closet, or, if you’re willing to face the elements, dive into a flea market.

One of the best spots to people-watch in the city, come rain or shine, is the baths. And having a place to hide from the chill and unforgiving precipitation is a welcome bonus. Commerce writer Jessica Sulima touts the East Village’s Russian Turkish Baths as the perfect place to drop by. Melt away whatever’s ailing you in the 215 °F Russian Sauna, and if you need any help doing so, get the platza oak leaf ritual where spa employees forcefully smack your pores open with bushels of oak leaves in the sauna. If you’re looking for something a little more communal, Flager likes to warm up at Othership, which sets itself apart with its guided wellness experiences that combine breath work, aromatherapy, visualizations, somatic movement, live music, and group “shares.”

Nothing brings a bar together like its pool table, but if you’ve spent more time watching the queue of quarters waiting for your turn than the game itself, head to a dedicated pool hall instead, where there’s a better chance of scoring a table all your own and watching the real pros practice their hand. Union Square’s Amsterdam Billiards has been a staple ever since I came to the city five years ago. The 11,000-square-foot hall decked with its array of Brunswick tables might seem intimidating at first, but take it from a real amateur: they may be serious about their snooker here, but they’re not snobby. Pool aside, patrons keep occupied with the hall’s other offerings like table tennis, beer pong, and darts. If you’re serious about upping your game, you can even book one-hour lessons with their in-house pros.

Jazz is one of the country’s greatest art forms, and New York is the genre’s most inspiring muse and resourceful studio. The city cemented its status in the 1920s Harlem Renaissance when legendary venues like the Cotton Club and Small’s Paradise put Duke Ellington, Fats Waller, and Billie Holiday in the national consciousness. Jazz in the city has traveled beyond its uptown crucible, and there’s great clubs peppered throughout the boroughs. Some of our favorites include Ornithology Jazz Club, which also has a killer vegan menu; Funny Bar, which comes from the same team as Baby’s All Right; and Greenwich Village’s Smalls Jazz Club, which keeps things true to form and no-frills.

New York’s historic theatre scene is far from confined to Broadway’s flashing lights. Some of the most exciting, intimate, and interactive productions in the city are playing Off-Broadway. Big names like Andrew Lloyd Webber have found a second wind in shows like Masquerade, a roving retelling of Phantom of the Opera, and fresh concepts like Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody are attracting their own audiences with their lower budget, DIY charm. Shows like these are a trove of talent, and odds are you can find one where you won’t have to pay an arm and a leg for entry at venues like La MaMa or Signature Theatre.

Associate social media manager Bridget Knowles swears by the people's princess of a dive bar as a haven from the harsh weather: “Interjecting here with what I’m sure we’re all thinking. I mean, sheesh. This is unspoken. A great dive bar is an oasis in New York City on a rainy day: a grunge mecca, a throw-some-hours-away swan song. My kind of place. A healthy dose of grime on an already lyrically imposing, moody day is great for the soul. Even if you’re off the Miller High Life (ah, it hurt to type, but pun intended) one of the greatest pastimes in life, according to me, is to simply load up touch tunes and shoot at a table a bit. Make some friends, watch something insane playing on a corner TV. You know, commiserate. Get your hands on some of the best in the city here.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6214. 9 All-Inclusive Resorts in Cancún That Go Way Beyond an Open Bar

I first arrived in Cancún, Mexico, more than 20 years ago. I had big hair, pencil-thin eyebrows, and limited expectations for an all-inclusive vacation: A swim-up bar serving frozen margaritas was about all I needed. Since then, my priorities have shifted, and thankfully, Cancún’s all-inclusive resorts have grown up alongside me.

After two decades of return visits made easier by an abundance of nonstop US flights, I’ve become more discerning about what deserves a place in that up-front price. I’ve also discovered that Cancún’s enduring spring break reputation tells an incomplete story about what's on offer. Choose the right resort, and you can have a butler draw your evening bath, a private pool overlooking the Caribbean, and à la carte restaurants you’ll look forward to all afternoon, whether you prefer the Hotel Zone’s long sweep of white sand, the relative quiet of Playa Mujeres, or a boat ride out to Isla Mujeres.

The frozen margaritas are still here. But now, there’s much more worth checking in for. Read on for the best all-inclusive resorts in Cancún worth planning a vacation around.

Mexican art gives this Playa Mujeres resort its personality. Rubén Soto’s concrete mural depicts native wildlife amid geometric patterns, while suites carry the aesthetic through warm woods and marble rather than tropical clichés. At Atelier, which welcomes ages 16+, you might have lunch overlooking the water at El Suspiro, then enjoy a pre-dinner mezcal cocktail at Bar de la Calle. Back in your suite, a rolling minibar holds wine and gourmet snacks, and room service answers around the clock. Most dining and premium spirits are included, though María Dolores by Edgar Núñez warrants a separate reservation—and budget—for its contemporary Mexican menu. Book an Inspira suite, and a butler can arrange your dinner reservations while you spend the afternoon at the rooftop infinity pool.

At Le Blanc, the pampering begins before you’ve unpacked—and your butler can handle that, too. Once you’re settled, the day’s agenda might amount to a poolside cocktail, a soak in the spa’s hydrotherapy pools, and deciding what to wear to dinner. This adults-only Hotel Zone retreat pairs pale interiors and Caribbean frontage with an unusually generous all-inclusive package: À la carte dining, premium drinks, 24-hour room service, and access to the spa’s hydrotherapy circuit are all included. Dinner might mean a French tasting menu at the esteemed Lumière or Italian cooking at Blanc Italia. Massages cost extra, but the daily chance to steam, soak, and unwind in the spa does not.

Two beaches are better than one, especially when they come with a lighthouse and Caribbean views in nearly every direction. Perched on the tip of Punta Cancún, Hyatt Ziva makes the most of its peninsula setting, with room for both family playtime and grown-up downtime. Little ones can race down waterslides and splash beneath fountains, while teenagers claim their own turf over billiards and foosball in the teens' lounge. For those whose idea of vacation involves neither, Turquoize (a tower within the resort) offers an adults-only escape with ocean-facing suites, butlers just a WhatsApp message away, and a rooftop infinity pool blissfully removed from the splash zone.

Behind Paradisus’s five glass-topped pyramids, one of Cancún’s most recognizable silhouettes, vines cascade through a soaring atrium, fountains burble below, and newly redesigned rooms turn beds toward Caribbean sunrises or Nichupté Lagoon sunsets. A 2026 renovation refreshed this Cancún landmark without sacrificing its theatrical streak. Days might involve salsa lessons, pickleball, or children gleefully getting drenched beneath splash-park tipping buckets. Included meals feature freshly pressed tortillas at Taqueria Blue Agave and ceviche at Agua Marina, and bars pour Patrón and Grey Goose without a surcharge. For a quieter stay, The Reserve upgrade tier adds an adults-only pool, restaurant, and concierge service.

Here, the first cocktail arrives before you do, served aboard the open-bar catamaran that carries you from Cancún to this adult-only retreat on Isla Mujeres. Joining Hyatt’s Unbound Collection in November 2026, Impression lives up to its name, with terraces cascading toward a sheltered beach and rooftop infinity pools that give you every reason to admire the water without venturing down to it. Each of the 125 suites comes with dedicated butler service and all-inclusive coverage, including gourmet à la carte dining. At Spezia, decadent Italian cooking offers a reason to dress for dinner, though your butler can arrange a quieter evening in, should you desire.

Not all Cancún resorts are sprawling tropical compounds. At Secrets The Vine, a sleek adults-only tower brings a more cosmopolitan beach experience, with teak furnishings, Italian porcelain floors, and balconies suspended over that improbable Caribbean blue. As the name suggests, afternoons and evenings are devoted to the grape. Sommelier-led tastings gather guests around a handcrafted wooden table at the Vine Bar; evenings bring Mexican and international pours, and between glasses, a white-sand beach and three infinity pools tempt you outside. While many wines and premium spirits are included, special bottles from the cellar carry additional charges but are well worth it.

Dinner without one eye on a restless toddler is a luxury Finest Playa Mujeres has thought to provide. At Imagine Lounge, staff look after potty-trained children ages three and older for up to 90 minutes while parents eat nearby. The practical details are equally reassuring: homemade baby purées, bottle warmers, and family suites with a separate bedroom for the children. Meals, drinks, and 24-hour room service are included, so parents can order dinner after the little ones are asleep. One Spa even offers treatments for younger guests, though those appointments cost extra.

At Almare’s swim-up bar, the rum is blended with coconut or mango; at Botanik, the coffee is Mexican and locally roasted. Those touches give this 109-room, adults-only retreat on Isla Mujeres a sense of place. Get better acquainted through a tikin xic cooking experience devoted to the island’s signature fish dish, or take a kayak out from the beach—all complimentary. There’s a pool by the shore and an infinity pool on the rooftop, where dinner at Seasalt comes with Caribbean views and Mexican-European cooking. The resort also arranges guided visits to Punta Sur’s temple ruins for a fee, where you’ll hear stories of the Maya goddess Ixchel.

Excellence Playa Mujeres is a place to spread out—even the entry-level suites are upwards of 800 square feet, with whirlpool tubs and furnished terraces. Book a rooftop suite, and you can spend the afternoon between your plunge pool and daybed, with lunch delivered whenever you’re ready. Venture downstairs, though, and there's so much more: winding pools lead past swim-up terraces, beach waiters keep the margaritas coming, and dinner could mean Indian curries at Basmati or a lingering French meal at Chez Isabelle. Club suites at this adults-only Playa Mujeres retreat add private pools and beach areas and one Miilé Spa hydrotherapy session per person, per stay.

What is the best all-inclusive resort in Cancún?

For an adult-only stay, Le Blanc Spa Resort Cancún gets my vote. Butler service and French tasting menus make it feel suitably indulgent, and the rate includes access to the spa’s hydrotherapy circuit. With children, I’d choose Finest Playa Mujeres, where separate kids' bedrooms and supervised care during mealtimes give parents a holiday too.

Is it worth getting an all-inclusive package in Cancún?

Yes, especially if you plan to spend most of your vacation at the resort. At the right property, your rate covers dinners you actually look forward to, premium drinks, and activities you’d otherwise pay for separately. If you plan to spend each day exploring and eating around town, a traditional hotel may make more sense. Before booking your all-inclusive, be sure to check the exclusions—you might find you'll have to pay extra for spa treatments, special bottles of wine, and some restaurant experiences.

What’s the cheapest month to go to Cancún?

September is generally one of the cheapest months for Cancún hotels, after summer vacation crowds leave. The trade-off is wetter weather and the possibility of tropical storms during hurricane season. For a better balance of price and weather, consider late October through the week before Thanksgiving.

How we choose the best all-inclusive resorts in Cancún

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6212. What The TSA Liquids Rule Really Means At US Checkpoints In 2026

Elliott Cowand Jr | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) restriction on liquids, aerosols, and gels, widely known as the 3-1-1 rule in the United States, was not an arbitrary policy. Because legacy X-ray machines could not safely differentiate harmless beverages or toiletries from volatile liquid explosive components, it was implemented by the TSA in August 2006.

The decision followed a counterterrorism operation in the United Kingdom where intelligence thwarted a plot by terrorists to board transatlantic flights and detonate explosives disguised inside soda cans. Since then, advanced Computed Tomography (CT) scanners have improved the screening experience, even as regulations remain the same.

The machine's software can automatically calculate liquid density and identify hazardous substances packed deep inside luggage. CT allows TSA officers to rotate a bag's image a full 360 degrees, dissecting complex internal layers. Today, some airports in the UK and Europe now allow liquids up to two liters. However, the US network has yet to lift the 3-1-1 restriction because advanced scanners have not yet reached nationwide deployment.

The TSA will not lift the 3.4-ounce (100 ml) restriction nationwide until CT scanners are deployed at 100% of airports. To prevent security gaps and avoid confusing travelers moving between upgraded and non-upgraded domestic airports, the TSA is keeping the rule as the national standard. Once every airport in the country is equipped with the same machines, a new liquid policy is expected to follow.

Contrary to speculation among some Americans that it was lifted, the TSA liquids limit remains unchanged today. This misconception stemmed from the introduction of new screening technology, specifically CT scanners. Even with the rollout, travelers are still limited to a single clear, quart-sized plastic bag per person to hold three volume-compliant liquid containers.

Beyond being a mnemonic, the 3-1-1 rule continues to be the guiding principle that dictates the total amount that is allowed. Despite the rule's inconvenience and unpopularity, any modification depends on technological advances that allow reliable fluid identification. The restriction has evolved since its inception.

After the complete ban in 2006, the rule transitioned to the small-bottle and quart-bag limit on September 26, 2006. The change reflected a shift from a three-ounce limit to 3.4 ounces to align with the international standard of 100 milliliters. As of late 2026, over 1,100 million-dollar CT units have been deployed across 300 major domestic airports.

However, the remaining third of the network, comprising hundreds of smaller regional lanes, still depends entirely on legacy 2D X-ray infrastructure. Meanwhile, one public statement from a government official in 2025 triggered rumors about the potential lifting of the rule.

On July 8, 2025, the Department of Homeland Security ended the routine passenger shoe-removal requirement, according to CBS News. The sudden, total elimination of this 20-year-old protocol sparked widespread confusion among the flying public. As the signature post-9/11 hassle vanished overnight, it primed passengers to believe that a complete dismantling of all historical checkpoint rules was imminent.

This climate of high expectations set a trap for widespread public confusion just eight days later. On July 16, 2025, then-Secretary Kristi Noem spoke at a conference hosted by The Hill and explicitly singled out the standing policy. By musing that container volume increases would be "the next big announcement," she inadvertently caused millions of travelers to coordinate internal review with immediate policy changes.

Numerous outlets rapidly repeated her optimistic outlook, envisioning one-minute checkpoint walkthroughs directly to the aircraft gate. However, Noem provided no real details or concrete deployment timelines for a 3-1-1 rule overhaul. Former TSA Administrator John Pistole later confirmed that the agency had quietly evaluated liquid-restriction rollbacks for years.

The general public was led to believe that the technology had been put in place to support Noem's sweeping statement. Yet, more than a year later, the strict 3-1-1 mandate remains unchanged and fully enforceable at every US security checkpoint. Analysts say the core issue driving traveler confusion is that dropping the shoe mandate required no new equipment.

The 100ml rule is finally being scrapped after last year's false start.

The TSA prioritizes security enhancements over passenger convenience, as Peter Duffy, the agency's federal security director for Alaska, clarified in a July statement, that CT implementation significantly augments threat-detection capabilities. A checkpoint CT scanner operates on the same technological principles as a medical CT unit, using multiple X-ray perspectives of luggage on a conveyor belt to construct a three-dimensional model.

That 3D output lets automated threat-detection algorithms flag potential hazards while agents rotate and inspect the imagery. These scanners have been in deployment for several years. AFAR reported that the TSA began field tests of new scanners at a small number of airports in 2018. Meanwhile, CT units first became operational at Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) in November 2017, according to View from the Wing.

While sources disagree on the first deployment dates, both outline nearly a decade of operational development behind a technology that many passengers encountered for the first time this year. For travelers, the main advantage of CT is keeping laptops and liquids inside their luggage, as AFAR remarked. However, the new CT scanners are limited to luggage that can actually fit through the machine.

A TSA spokesperson was quoted by the Hill, saying the new units cannot accommodate certain large carry-on bags. AFAR noted that while CT scanners are currently being integrated into many PreCheck lanes, flyers with bags that do not fit will be asked to go to secondary screening stations. Screening procedures also remain inconsistent within individual airport terminals.

AFAR advised passengers to follow local rules because many facilities operate a mix of conventional two-dimensional X-ray and advanced CT lanes. In either case, the 3-1-1 restriction still remains fully enforceable, matching the protocol of standard lanes. Consequently, the primary operational variable for air travelers remains the statistical likelihood of encountering a CT-equipped checkpoint during their transit.

Water bottles outrank every weapon TSA finds. Here are the five items most often surrendered at US checkpoints.

The fundamental, insurmountable obstacle to full-scale deployment of PT scanning technology at US airports is the massive scale of the national network. The TSA is tasked with securing approximately 2,000 screening lanes across 430 airports nationwide. A comprehensive, nationwide technology overhaul requires billions in capital.

Until the entire country has a uniform network of equipment, it must maintain legacy policy to enforce the same standard from coast to coast. By July, the agency successfully hit a baseline of 1,162 advanced CT units across 296 domestic airports. On August 24, the TSA officially launched its 'Horizon 25 Strategy.' This decade-long modernization roadmap explicitly re-prioritizes the agency's goals.

The core pillars of the plan focus on integrating three technologies simultaneously to overhaul lanes: next-generation CT scanners, upgraded Advanced Imaging Technology (body scanners, and Credential Authentication Technology units. The 3D CT scanner gantries are massive, heavy machines that require a completely redesigned footprint.

Many older terminal checkpoints lack the physical square footage or floor-load capacity to house them without extensive remodeling. Total network deployment requires the TSA to cover roughly 2,000 screening lanes across 430 federalized airports. According to current DHS budget projections, the target timeline to reach Full Operational Capability for these property screening systems has been formally pushed out to fiscal year 2034.

Current funding earmarks roughly $192 million per year for the procurement and deployment of these Checkpoint Property Screening Systems. Because each machine requires significant capital to buy, test, and maintain, this localized funding rate prevents the TSA from purchasing the thousands of units needed for immediate rollout. While the US rollout remains a multi-decade project, the UK has moved much faster.

TSA is considering letting PreCheck travelers carry full water bottles through security as next-generation screening technology expands nationwide.

The rollout across the UK and the European Union has moved at a drastically different pace than in the US, but both regions have faced unique logistical and regulatory roadblocks. In January, London Heathrow Airport (LHR) completed a comprehensive £1 billion security modernization program.

LHR replaced every passenger checkpoint lane across all four active terminals with advanced CT scanners and officially scrapped the 100ml liquid limit. A select group of major UK airports has fully completed the transition alongside Heathrow. As of late 2026, Gatwick, Edinburgh, Birmingham, Bristol, and Belfast also allow the 2-liter limit.

Conversely, major gateways like Manchester, London Stansted, and Luton missed their infrastructure deadlines and still enforce the legacy policy. The UK Department for Transport initially aimed to eliminate the 100ml rule nationwide by 2024, but the reality has become a fragmented 'patchwork' map.

The European Commission originally cleared the way for EU member states to drop liquid limits on an airport-by-airport basis as they installed certified next-generation C3 scanners. However, across the English Channel, the European Union hit a regulatory roadblock. Conflicting progress among the US, UK, and EU has created a major pitfall for international travelers known as the 'Return-Flight Trap.' Security rules follow your departure airport, not your airline or passport.

#6211. What Travelers Should Know About the Galápagos Floods—and the Ongoing Impact of El Ñino

On October 30 and 31, 2026, torrential rainfall on the Galápagos's Santa Cruz island caused waterways to overflow, flooding neighborhoods, damaging homes, and disrupting essential infrastructure. The local government declared an emergency, with over 2,000 people affected by the damage. This places the Galápagos among several beloved tourism destinations that are already grappling with the effects of El Ñino.

The news has also left many travelers wondering: Is it safe to travel to the Galápagos right now? And how should those with upcoming cruises and hotel stays proceed?

Rodrigo Jácome, who runs La K-leta Guest House and a small coffee farm on Santa Cruz, which is the archipelago's main inhabited island and a central hub for tourism, says the flooding has not damaged key tourism infrastructure—though it devastated other local livelihoods. “The flooding affected residential neighborhoods that are not particularly close to the main hotel areas,” says Jácome, who lost most of his coffee harvest in the rains. For those with upcoming travel, and locals who rely on travelers to make a living, however, “tourism operations resumed within days.”

Authorities have reopened most visitor sites in the Galápagos National Park, and transportation has resumed, though conditions remain subject to change. Below, we report on all of the impacted areas across the Galápagos, which tours may be rerouted, and how to stay up on the news as future weather develops, according to those on the ground. Plus, local tour operators share advice on planning accordingly for trips in the months ahead.

Santa Cruz is where you'll find many hotels, restaurants, tour operators, and transportation connections, and the area that experienced the most significant damage. Santa Cruz serves as a major base for day trips and cruises to other islands. Most visitors arriving by air fly in via neighboring Baltra, where the airport is located.

Puerto Ayora, the island's main town, and the highland parish of Bellavista, were among the affected areas. Floodwaters damaged homes and roads, disrupted water and electricity services, and forced families to evacuate. The flooding also affected transportation infrastructure connecting Santa Cruz to Baltra Airport, the main gateway for visitors arriving by air to Santa Cruz. The road reopened on November 5 and reconstruction work is being carried out in parallel, allowing travelers to continue arriving to the island as planned.

Although the emergency was concentrated in Santa Cruz, other islands also experienced heavy rainfall and localized flooding. Whitman Cox, a Galápagos National Park naturalist guide based in San Cristóbal, which is known for its sea lion colonies, volcanic landscapes, and popular snorkeling and diving sites, says there was no such damage in San Cristobal, but access to some of the beaches around the island has been restricted as weather conditions change.

Travelers should therefore check conditions for all destinations on their itinerary, across the archipelago, rather than assuming all islands have been affected equally. Constant communication with tour guides, your hotel, or cruise line is the best way to get up-to-date information.

While the Galápagos National Park has progressively reopened, the Los Humedales sector in Isabela (above) remains closed.

As of November 9, flights to Baltra and San Cristóbal were operating on their regular schedules, according to local reporting. Tourism activities have also continued, although some visitor sites remain temporarily closed.

The Galápagos National Park has progressively reopened areas following safety assessments: As of November 9, Playa El Garrapatero in Santa Cruz was accessible again, while popular visitor sites Las Grietas, El Chato, and El Puntudo remained restricted. In San Cristóbal, La Lobería and Punta Carola had reopened, while surfing spots Puerto Chino and Playa Baquerizo remained closed. The Los Humedales sector in Isabela also remained closed. From November 9-18, Tortuga Bay, a beach in Santa Cruz, will be closed as a preventative measure due to tide changes.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office updated its Ecuador travel advisory on November 1 to include the flooding on Santa Cruz. It advises travelers to follow local authorities' instructions, avoid flooded areas, and confirm travel arrangements with airlines and tour operators.

Cox emphasizes that travelers shouldn't panic—El Niño is a natural weather cycle. “People can still come. We shouldn't frighten them," says Cox. His main guidance is to be patient. “They may encounter transportation difficulties between certain points, which could take additional time.” He adds that the park has done its best in the interest of safety by closing the above sites as a precautionary measure.

The flooding comes as Ecuador experiences an El Niño event, a climate phenomenon characterized by unusually warm ocean temperatures across the equatorial Pacific, which can alter atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. In Ecuador, El Niño is often associated with heavier rainfall, particularly along the coast and in the Galápagos. However, its effects vary by region and over time.

According to the National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMHI), the El Niño event remained active and was strengthening for the upcoming months with weather reports suggesting that heavy rainfall may last until February 2027.

The potential implications for travelers include heavy rain, temporary road closures, changes to boat excursions, and restricted access to natural visitor sites. Weather conditions can also affect marine activities and inter-island transportation.

However, this is not the first time El Niño has impacted the islands, and tour guides understand how to prepare. “It is a cyclical part of nature that we have seen every 10-15 years,” says Charles Wittmer, president of the Association of Boat Operators in the Galápagos, ADATUR. “Nature is unpredictable and if anything, this is a chance to see the adaptations of animals to changing weather conditions,” he says. “Remember: this is a natural laboratory of evolution.” On the wildlife front, Wittmer mentions that Galápagos penguins and cormorants adapt to warming ocean waters. And there's a plus: These shifts in marine ecosystem activity may increase the variety of species spotted while snorkeling.

If you have an upcoming trip, local tourism specialists recommend staying informed and remaining flexible. It’s best to ask about excursion alternatives when booking a tour in the islands, should weather create the need to pivot.

Before departure, confirm your flights and accommodation directly with your airline and tour operator. Ask whether your planned excursions are operating as anticipated and whether alternative activities are available if certain visitor sites are closed. Ask your tour guide for updates daily.

It's also a good idea to purchase travel insurance that covers weather-related disruptions, medical emergencies, and unexpected accommodation or transportation expenses. Travelers can monitor official updates from INAMHI and the Galápagos National Park social media and from their website with forecasts, and plan smart by allowing extra flexibility in travel connections and excursions. Remember to also pack lightweight rain protection and waterproof bags for electronics and important documents.

Like Cox, Wittmer emphasizes that nature is out of our control. “People should bring clothing and be ready for heavier rainfall and be flexible in their expectations.”

Though travelers come to the Galápagos for the nature, local guides are the greatest resource in appreciating this place—and navigating it in uncertain times.

Whether staying in local communities, visiting for a few hours on cruise excursions, or simply passing through in transit, travelers contribute to the livelihoods of local businesses and workers, many of whom are also dealing with the consequences of the flooding, simply by visiting. As Jácome puts it, “Tourism is needed now more than ever to help rebuild the communities that lost everything.”

Consider booking locally owned accommodation, hiring licensed local guides, eating at independent restaurants, and purchasing goods from small businesses.

As always, travelers should also be mindful that affected neighborhoods are not tourist attractions. Avoid visiting damaged homes or taking photographs of residents dealing with the aftermath of the flooding without their permission.

If you are traveling to Galápagos right now, consider packing water purification tablets, basic first-aid supplies, and hygiene kits to done to affected families (your guide or hotel can assist with routing these to the right place). You can also check with local emergency centers or your tour operator upon arrival to donate pet food or clean clothes directly to the most impacted neighborhoods.

If you want to contribute to recovery efforts from afar, several organizations and initiatives have mobilized support:

Fundación Charles Darwin: The foundation is part of an emergency fundraising initiative, with proceeds directed to the Santa Cruz emergency response committee (COE) to support urgent community needs.

San Francisco de Quito University: The University has established a SOS Galapagos fund, collecting donations on their campus in Quito. They also have a donations link.

Fundación Torraja: This local organization is administering a Community Kitchen and providing meals and donations directly to families who lost their belongings in the floods.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

At The Points Guy, we’re always looking for simple ways to save money and earn more rewards. One of the easiest yet often overlooked tools is Chase Offers.

With just a few clicks, you can unlock targeted discounts and cash-back deals at brands you already use. These range from streaming services and restaurants to travel and retail purchases.

Even better, Chase Offers can often be combined with your card’s usual earning rates and shopping portals, helping you get more value from everyday spending.

Here’s how the program works and how to maximize it.

Chase Offers is a program available on eligible Chase debit and credit cards that gives cardholders access to targeted deals, similar to Amex Offers. These offers typically provide cash back or a percentage back as a statement credit when you make a qualifying purchase.

Like similar programs from other issuers, offers are personalized. That means the deals you see may differ from what someone else receives. You may also see different offers across your own Chase cards.

Most Chase-issued consumer and business credit and debit cards are eligible for Chase Offers if the primary cardholder has a U.S. address listed as their primary residence or place of business.

To see if Chase Offers is available for your card, check your Chase mobile app or log in at Chase's website.

For Chase credit cards, primary cardholders and authorized officers can view and add offers. Authorized users and employees can't add offers themselves, but they can redeem offers that have already been added to the account.

Some of the most popular eligible cards include:

Chase Offers are also available on many cobranded Chase credit cards, such as the (see rates and fees) and select United Airlines and Marriott Bonvoy cards.

Each card may offer different deals, so it's worth checking all your accounts if you hold more than one Chase card.

You can find available offers on the Chase website and on the Chase app. To view your available offers on the website, log in to your account and find "Chase Offers" on the right-hand panel.

Alternatively, you can click on "Benefits & travel" on the top panel and select "Chase Offers", as shown below. Note that the offers shown below may not be available to you.

To view your Chase Offers on the Chase mobile app, log in to your account and then scroll down toward the middle of the main account dashboard. You should see a section titled “Chase Offers” showing some of your current offers.

Either the website or app option will bring you to the offers currently available for you to browse.

Offerings change daily and typically feature various types of goods and services. You may see deals for:

Offers typically range from about 5% to 30% back or provide a fixed statement credit after meeting a spending requirement. For example, you might receive a $20 statement credit after spending $100 with a specific merchant.

Chase Offers can be an easy way to save on purchases you’re already making, which is something TPG staffers have seen firsthand across a range of everyday spending.

TPG travel writer Rachel Craft, for example, recently used an offer on her for 15% back at home improvement stores. She bundled supplies for a few projects she already had planned into a single purchase and received $33 back. Meanwhile, TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson earned an $85 statement credit on a DISH Network purchase using his World of Hyatt card.

TPG editor-in-chief Nick Ewen has also had success with Chase Offers. He recently earned $15.81 back on Trans-Siberian Orchestra tickets purchased through SeatGeek with his Chase Freedom Flex. Since the purchase also fell within one of the card's Q3 rotating quarterly bonus categories, he earned 5% cash back on top of his Chase Offer savings (on up to $1,500 in combined purchases each quarter, activation required).

And in an even bigger example of how these savings can add up, Nick earned a $125 statement credit through a Chase Offer on an IHG hotel stay booked through The Edit by Chase Travel℠, using his . By combining that offer with the card's The Edit and select hotels credits, he saved a total of $625 on the stay.

While individual savings may vary, these examples highlight how these targeted offers can add up, especially on purchases you already planned to make.

While you don’t have to enroll your card to start using the Chase Offers program, you do have to add each individual offer to your credit card. Adding them is easy — all you have to do is navigate to Chase Offers either online or through the Chase Mobile app and click “Add to card” on any available offer that interests you.

Alternatively, if you have a subscription to a service like MaxRewards Gold, your offers should be automatically activated for all linked cards.

Then, use your card at the specific merchant, and you should see a statement credit applied to your account within 30 days after your qualifying transaction posts, unless the offer terms state otherwise.

Once you arrive on the Chase Offers landing page, adding an offer to your account is very simple.

If you have multiple eligible Chase cards, you’ll see a “Choose your account” drop-down near the top of the screen. Note that if you have multiple sign-ins with Chase, such as one for your personal cards and one for business credit cards, you will only see cards associated with the account for which you’re currently signed in.

Again, note that the offers you see here may not be available for you.

Click on any offer to add it to your card. Then, use your card at the specific merchant and wait for your statement credit to post.

Once you find an offer you would like to use in the app, the process is similar to the website process.

You can click on “See all available deals” to see the rest of your offers. You’ll see a “Choose your account” drop-down near the top of the screen if you have multiple eligible Chase cards.

Click on any offers to add them to your card, use your card at the participating merchant and wait for your statement credit to post.

When you add an offer for a specific card, you must use that same card to redeem the offer. For example, if you add a Chase Offer to your , you must use that card to redeem that offer successfully.

Be sure to read the terms and conditions for each offer carefully. You only have a certain amount of time to use each offer, and many come with maximum earning limits. As long as you make your purchase by the expiration date, you should receive the credit even if the transaction posts after the expiration date.

Chase Offers are rewarded as a statement credit, even if you have a card that earns Ultimate Rewards points on regular spending.

One of the common threads among all Chase Offers is this condition: Payment must be made directly with the merchant. While you can still use services like mobile wallets and PayPal with Chase Offers, you can’t use third-party providers to make purchases.

Finally, Chase Offers are only available on eligible U.S.-issued Chase credit cards tied to U.S.-based accounts. However, some offers may still be valid at international merchants, particularly global brands like hotel chains, as long as the transaction is processed by the eligible merchant and charged to your enrolled card.

Since new offers are constantly added, it’s a good idea to go through your Chase Offers at least biweekly to review and add new offers. It doesn’t cost anything to add an offer and then not use it, so you can be pretty lenient with which offers you add.

If there’s even a tiny possibility that you’ll use an offer, you might as well add it to your card. If you use it, great; if not, it’s not a problem.

Chase Offers become significantly more valuable when you stack them with other rewards opportunities. This means combining an offer with a shopping portal and a credit card bonus category to earn multiple layers of rewards on the same purchase.

For example, imagine you’re booking a $200 stay at a Hyatt property. You could:

In this scenario, you’d earn 1,000 points through the portal, $10 cash back from your Freedom Flex and a $20 statement credit from the Chase Offer.

Instead of earning rewards from just one source, you’ve effectively tripled up on the same purchase.

Chase Offers are best used for purchases you were already planning to make. Like any coupon or sale, saving 10% on something you didn’t need isn’t actually saving money. But when used strategically, especially in combination with shopping portals and bonus categories, they can meaningfully boost your overall return.

Chase Offers is one of the easiest ways to save money on purchases you already plan to make. While the discounts may not always be large, they require minimal effort and can add up quickly.

By checking your offers regularly and combining them with bonus categories and shopping portals, you can turn everyday spending into meaningful savings over time.

#6207. 14,388 Miles: Airbus A350-1000ULR Test Flight Officially Breaks The Guinness World Record

Airbus has officially broken the Guinness World Record for the longest nonstop flight by a commercial airliner, with its Airbus A350-1000ULR covering an extraordinary 14,388 miles (23,155 km) in 24 hours and 24 minutes. The achievement, announced earlier today, ends a record held for more than two decades by Boeing with its Boeing 777-200LR Worldliner.

The flight took place between Melbourne Airport (MEL) and Toulouse-Blagnac Airport (TLS) on July 27–28 as part of the A350-1000ULR's development program for Qantas' Project Sunrise. Remarkably, the official announcement of the record came exactly 21 years after Boeing's record-setting aircraft departed Hong Kong on November 9, 2005. The achievement represents an important milestone ahead of Qantas' planned introduction of nonstop Sydney–London services in October 2027.

Operating as AIB35LR, the Airbus A350-1000ULR departed Melbourne at 5:27 PM local time on July 27, arriving in Toulouse at 9:51 AM the following morning. The aircraft flew eastwards, initially flying over Sydney before crossing the Pacific toward Los Angeles, traversing North America and the Atlantic, and passing over London. The extraordinary routing crossed three continents and two oceans, treating those onboard to two sunsets and two sunrises.

The flight carried just 13 people, including three Airbus test pilots, two Qantas pilots, engineers and an International Aeronautical Federation representative. The extended flight-test program focused particularly on fuel management and cabin environmental systems. Airbus also evaluated its redesigned crew-rest compartments, while pilots operated overlapping four-hour shifts, staggered every two hours.

Today's Guinness certification follows independent validation of aircraft data by the International Aeronautical Federation and Flightradar24. Interestingly, Airbus originally reported the flight distance as 14,338 miles (23,076 km), approximately 50 miles (79 km) shorter than the officially certified figure. Airbus Commercial Aircraft CEO Lars Wagner described the achievement as confirmation of the aircraft's ultra-long-range capabilities, adding:

"This achievement reflects the pioneering and innovative spirit that is part of our DNA at Airbus. Flying 12,503 nautical miles non-stop, we have fully proven the aircraft's capability to fulfill its mission. And the world record was the icing on the cake!”

To achieve the record, Airbus had to surpass a truly extraordinary journey. On November 9, 2005, Boeing's distinctive blue-and-white 777-200LR demonstrator, N6066Z, nicknamed Baby Blue 2, departed Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) on a momentous journey.

Rather than following the conventional westbound route to London, Captain Suzanna Darcy-Hennemann and her crew headed east across the Pacific. The aircraft crossed North America and the Atlantic before reaching Heathrow, setting a remarkable record of 13,423 miles (21,601 km) in 22 hours and 42 minutes.

The Worldliner carried 35 people, including Boeing executives, engineers, airline representatives and journalists. Its fuel tanks contained approximately 164 tonnes of fuel, with the weight of passengers and baggage carefully controlled. A specially fitted interior even featured a reception area and business class seating. Remarkably, the aircraft still had approximately two hours of fuel remaining upon arrival. Baby Blue 2 subsequently entered commercial service with Pakistan International Airlines as AP-BGZ.

Two decades later, Airbus has finally surpassed Boeing's achievement. The A350-1000ULR benefits from advances in composite structures, aerodynamics and engine efficiency, alongside a new rear center fuel tank holding approximately 5,521 gallons (20,900 liters). The modification extends the A350-1000's range by approximately 1,000 nautical miles (1,151 miles, 1,852 km).

The flight from Hong Kong to London, the 'wrong way round', remains the longest-ever flight by a commercial aircraft.

The record comes as the Australian flag carrier edges closer to introducing the world's longest scheduled passenger flights. The airline expects its first A350-1000ULR delivery in April 2027, with nonstop Sydney–London services launching in October under flight numbers QF1 and QF2. The existing Singapore-stop services will continue as QF5 and QF6. Sydney–New York will follow in mid-2028, with Qantas expecting the new nonstop journey to take approximately 18 hours.

Qantas has ordered 12 A350-1000ULRs, each configured with 238 seats, including 98 premium seats and a dedicated Wellbeing Zone. The commercial strategy centers on attracting higher-yield passengers while removing the inconvenience of stopovers. Qantas forecasts approximately A$400 million ($265 million) in additional annual earnings once Project Sunrise reaches scale, supported by new nonstop flying, network optimization and freight opportunities. Its broader fleet strategy also includes 12 standard A350-1000s.

Significant operational preparations remain underway. Qantas is preparing more than 360 pilots and 1,200 cabin crew for the new fleet, while simulator training has already begun in Sydney. Aircraft certification, crew preparation and further deliveries will determine how quickly the airline can expand its network. With five A350-1000ULRs expected by November 2027, the Guinness World Record marks a remarkable engineering accomplishment, but the more consequential achievement will be translating that capability into regular commercial operations.

#6206. Qantas Reaches Deal to Sell 44 Boeing 737s

Qantas has agreed to sell 44 Boeing 737-800s to British aviation aftermarket specialist AerFin as the Australian carrier prepares to retire most of its 737 fleet.

The deal includes the aircraft’s 88 CFM56-7B engines. AerFin said Wednesday it expects to receive the first jet before the end of 2026, with the rest transferring over the next seven years as Qantas retires them.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson said the agreement gives the airline “flexibility to adjust the timing as new aircraft arrive,” in a news release.

Qantas operates nearly 80 Boeing 737-800s, according to data from planespotters.net. The carrier ordered 28 Airbus A321XLRs in 2022 to begin replacing the Boeing jets and later ordered another 20. Seven A321XLRs have joined the fleet, with 41 still on order.

AerFin, which supplies parts and engines to airlines and maintenance providers, said the acquisition is the largest in its history. The company said the deal would help it supply aircraft and engine parts to customers worldwide.

#6205. Combative LaGuardia ATC Berates Southwest Pilot Over Taxiway Mistake

The pilots of a Southwest Airlines flight departing New York LaGuardia (LGA) made a mistake. What’s wild to me is how unprofessionally the air traffic controller handled that mistake, though, and the clear joy he got from being able to chew out the pilots…

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an incident that happened shortly after 7PM local time on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at New York LaGuardia Airport.

A Southwest Boeing 737-800 was getting ready to depart to Dallas Love Field (DAL), and was just getting permission to taxi to the runway, which is when the issues started:

Air traffic controller: “Southwest 4541, runway 13, give way to an E170 off the left, taxi via L, B, G, hold short of runway 22.”Southwest pilot: “Taxi runway 13 via L, B, G, hold short of runway 22, give way to E170 off our left, Southwest 4541.”

The Southwest plane then started taxiing, but immediately cut off the Embraer E170 it was supposed to give way to on the taxiway. That was probably a dumb error (more on that in a bit), but that’s when the air traffic controller really got excited:

Air traffic controller: “Southwest 4541.”Southwest pilot: “Southwest 4541, go ahead.”Air traffic controller: “Did you give way to the 175 we told you about?”Southwest pilot: “Uh, sorry, we were looking at a different one. We’ll still be on B. Are we clear?”Air traffic controller: “Southwest 4541, hold there. Show me the 175 that you were looking out for.”Southwest pilot: “We’re looking at the Delta colors to the left, Southwest 4541.”Air traffic controller: “So that’s the one we told you to give way to and you cut them off, right?”Southwest pilot: “Affirmative, Southwest 4541. Where would you like us to go?”Air traffic controller: “Southwest 4541, possible pilot deviation, advise ready to copy a phone number.”

The Southwest pilot then copied down the number, and then the air traffic controller broadcast on frequency that “Southwest looks like just decided to do whatever they want.”

There are two issues here — the mistake on the part of the Southwest pilots, and how the air traffic controller responded.

Obviously the Southwest pilots screwed up here, as they did cut off the Embraer. As much as Southwest pilots are known for their speedy taxis, I’d be willing to bet this wasn’t intentional, because if you try to fight a NYC-area air traffic controller, you’ll lose every time. 😉

My guess is that the pilots were genuinely confused by the word order of the instructions, and didn’t fully process the instructions until it was too late (which isn’t to excuse it, but just to try to make sense of how this happened).

The instructions were to taxi to “runway 13, give way to an E170 off the left, taxi via L, B, G, hold short of runway 22.” Based purely on those instructions, it wasn’t entirely clear where the Embraer would be, since the instruction to give way was given after the runway assignment.

It seems like a clearer way to describe that would be to give the taxi instructions, and then explicitly say where the plane is that they should be giving way to. So something like “runway 13, taxi via L, B, G, hold short of runway 22, give way to the Delta colors E170 off on your left on A.”

But the real issue was the laser focus that the controller had on just talking down to these pilots and proving a point. He literally stopped traffic so that he could win an argument. By all means give the pilots a number for a possible pilot deviation, and discuss this stuff off frequency. But to stop traffic, argue with the pilots, give them a number, and then throw in another insulting comment, is just uncalled for and incredibly unprofessional.

Compare this to an incident at Boston Logan (BOS) a few weeks back, which I’d argue was more serious. An Etihad Boeing 787 entered a runway without permission and caused a go around. Shocking as it might be to some New York area controllers, the Boston controller didn’t take it as an opportunity to insult someone on frequency, and stop traffic. Instead, he handled it professionally, kept planes moving, and then they got a number for a pilot deviation. That’s how it should be handled.

The pilots of a Southwest Boeing 737 chose the wrong airport to make a mistake at, as it quickly turned into the highlight of the air traffic controller’s day. The air traffic controller stopped traffic so that he could school pilots and give them a number for a possible pilot deviation, rather than keeping planes moving and then discussing this off frequency.

What do you make of this LaGuardia ATC interaction?

#6203. Atmos Rewards Summit Card 3x Points On Foreign Purchases: Any Catch?

The $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) is the premium personal credit card of Atmos Rewards, which is the combined loyalty program of Alaska & Hawaiian.

There are lots of reasons to get this card, from a huge welcome bonus, to a great return on spending, to valuable perks just for being a cardmember, like free points sharing and waived partner award booking fees. It’s a card I’ve already applied for.

In this post, I’d like to talk about what might just be the most interesting aspect to spending on the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, which borders on seeming too good to be true. Specifically, I’m talking about how the card earns 3x points on all foreign purchases, with no caps, which is a pretty unheard of bonus category.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card offers 3x points on eligible foreign transactions, with no caps. This applies to both the primary cardmember and to any authorized users (authorized users can be added to the card at no extra cost). Specifically, eligible foreign purchases include:

In the interest of being thorough, let me copy and paste the portion of the terms addressing this:

3 Points for eligible Foreign Transactions: Earn 3 points for every $1 spent on eligible foreign transaction Net Purchases (1) made in a foreign currency, or (2) made in U.S. dollars if the transaction is made or processed outside of the United States and US Territories. Bank of America is not responsible for how foreign transactions are billed to the card.

Let me emphasize that the card has no foreign transaction fees, so not only are you not paying those fees, but you’re being rewarded very handsomely. The exchange rates used by the card are also totally fair, and competitive.

Personally, I value Atmos Rewards points at 1.5 cents each, so I’d consider that to be a 4.5% return on all foreign purchases, which is unrivaled. If you have an eligible Bank of America account, you can even get a 10% relationship bonus, meaning you could net 3.3x points per dollar spent.

While there are some cards that might be slightly more rewarding for specific categories of foreign spending — like dining, airfare, or hotels — there’s not another card that’s broadly this rewarding for all foreign spending.

Keep in mind that this is only the start of the rewards you get for spending on the card:

Admittedly this is a very specific situation, but if you were to spend $60,000 abroad, you’d earn 180,000 Atmos Rewards points, 30,000 Atmos Rewards status points (not including the 10,000 status points boost the card offers annually), and a 100,000-point Global Companion Award.

If you want to take it a step further, those 40,000 Atmos Rewards status points are enough to earn Atmos Rewards Gold status, which gets you oneworld Sapphire, offering perks like priority services and lounge access. That’s a pretty incredible setup, eh?

As you’d expect, there are a lot of questions about the Atmos Rewards Summit Card 3x points on foreign spending:

“I’ve looked but I couldn’t find what the terms are for the 3x points on foreign purchases. Is there an annual limit? Does it need to be combined with domestic spend?”

“Let me get this straight – any transaction outside the US will be in the 3x category? Is this capped? As someone living in Europe, that could make this card extremely valuable for me…”

Officially, there are no limits on how much you can spend abroad. Of course to get this card, you need to be eligible for credit cards in the United States, which requires having an address in the country, among other things.

As I look at the terms, there’s nothing there stating any limits as to how much you can spend abroad, both in absolute and relative (to domestic spending) terms. In practice, there are plenty of Americans living abroad who use US credit cards (given how much more lucrative they are than most foreign cards) without any issues.

So I don’t think there’s a catch here, but I will say this (and I’m not trying to fear monger, but am just trying to address the only potential concern) — banks can shut down your credit cards at will, and decide they no longer want to do business with you.

In the past, I’ve read reports where credit card issuers have shut down accounts because too big of a percentage of spending was consistently abroad. That’s far from consistent, though, and I’ve also heard of people using their card living abroad for a decade without an issue.

My point is to say that based on how things currently stand, I think this benefit is as good as it sounds, and I wouldn’t expect any major changes (though who knows, maybe at some point down the road we’ll see a cap on how much foreign spending can earn bonus points).

Many people may wonder if this is sustainable in the long run, so let me point out a few things:

My point is simply to say that this doesn’t strike me anywhere near the top of the list of unsustainable credit card benefits, though we’ll see how this plays out.

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card offers 3x points on foreign spending, with no foreign transaction fees and no caps. This is an unheard of bonus category, and makes this by far the best card for foreign spending.

What makes this even better is that beyond the 3x points, you also earn one status point for every $2 spent, and if you spend $60,000 in an anniversary year, you can receive a 100,000-point Global Companion Award. This return on spending is every bit as great as it sounds, and this is the card to have in your wallet if you travel abroad a lot.

What do you make of the Atmos Rewards Summit Card 3x points on foreign purchases?

One important nuance is that although many regions around the world impose interchange fee caps, those caps generally do not apply to U.S.-issued cards. (Fees still tend to be lower outside of the U.S., however.) It is entirely possible that 3x (or 3.3x) on foreign purchases will turn out to be an unsustainable perk because it does not align with the underlying unit economics of a foreign purchase. However, the same could be said of 5x on airline purchases (Platinum Card) or 4x on hotels (CSR). In general cards offer generous bonus categories and accept that, for certain customers, they may not recover the full costs of doing so. As someone living in Europe, I am certainly maximizing this very unique and rewarding bonus category.

#6202. Allegiant Says MAX 7 Seat Cost ‘Loses Pace’

Allegiant prefers the economics of the Boeing 737 MAX 8 over the smaller MAX 7 as its plans for premium seating change how it evaluates the two aircraft.

The MAX 7 originally accounted for the majority of Allegiant’s Boeing commitment. In January 2022, the airline announced an order for 50 aircraft, split between 30 MAX 7s and 20 high-density MAX 8-200s, with options for another 50 jets.

The agreement, signed in December 2021, was Allegiant’s first direct Boeing order and marked a shift for a carrier that had largely built its business around buying used aircraft. At the time of the announcement, Allegiant operated 108 Airbus A319s and A320s.

Boeing said the new jets would reduce fuel consumption by about 20% compared with the older Airbus aircraft.

Speaking during the carrier’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, President and Chief Financial Officer Robert Neal said the MAX 7 initially offered an attractive balance between the cost of operating each flight and the cost per seat.

“When we did the order, we really liked the MAX 7 because we were looking at both the MAX 8 and MAX 7 at very high density,” Neal said. “And so you’ve got a really nice trip cost seat cost mix with the MAX 7.”

That calculation has changed as Allegiant expands its extra-legroom Allegiant Extra product and prepares to introduce Allegiant First.

“But over time, as you’ve seen us roll out incremental premium offerings at the moment through Allegiant Extra and eventually with Allegiant First, the seat cost just sort of loses pace with the MAX 8,” Neal said. “And so we prefer the cost economics of the MAX 8 at this point.”

Allegiant began shifting its order toward the larger variant in September 2023. An amended agreement retained the 50 firm aircraft but increased the number of MAX 8-200s, reduced the number of MAX 7s and expanded the option pool to 80 aircraft.

The MAX 7 faced years of certification delays, including work to redesign its engine anti-ice system. The FAA approved the variant on Aug. 3, after requiring changes to that system, flight-control software, and cockpit alerts.

The ultra-low-cost carrier added to its MAX 8 commitments last month, exercising six options for delivery in 2028. That brought its firm Boeing order to 56 aircraft, including 22 delivered through Oct. 23, with 74 options remaining.
