Among major hotel loyalty programs, Marriott Bonvoy offers some of the most attainable lifetime elite status tiers. I already have lifetime Gold Elite status with Marriott Bonvoy and will secure lifetime Platinum Elite status in three years.

If you're wondering if it's within reach for you, here's what you should know about Marriott lifetime status.

Marriott Bonvoy lets its members earn three tiers of lifetime elite status as follows:

Marriott also historically let members earn lifetime Titanium Elite status, but the program stopped offering it Dec. 31, 2018. Additionally, keep in mind that some Marriott brands don't offer a full qualifying night per eligible night stayed; for example, City Express, Four Points Flex and Protea Hotels award half an elite night credit per qualifying night, while StudioRes doesn't award any elite night credits.

The years of elite status don't need to be consecutive, and years spent at higher elite tiers count toward the requirements for lower lifetime tiers. Marriott status you get as a credit card perk counts toward the calculation of years in a specific elite status tier.

In addition to elite night credits earned from qualifying stays (which include qualifying award stays), elite night credits from credit cards and the five elite night credits you can select as an Annual Choice Benefit also count toward lifetime status.

Related: The complete guide to earning Marriott elite status with credit cards

Members with lifetime Marriott elite status enjoy the same benefits as members who earn these statuses annually, including waived points expiration. Plus, upon earning lifetime Platinum Elite status, you'll also get a complimentary gift and access to a webpage that looks back at your lifetime journey.

However, lifetime Platinum Elite status doesn't automatically qualify you for Annual Choice Benefits. You'll still need to earn 50 or 75 elite night credits in a calendar year to unlock these benefits.

And while lifetime members get the perks of the status they've earned, there's no guarantee that Marriott won't change the benefits of a particular status tier. So, if you earn lifetime Platinum Elite status, you'll get the current benefits of Platinum Elite instead of the benefits available at the time you secured lifetime status.

Marriott has made it easy to check your lifetime status progress. Go to the Marriott website, log in to your account, click your name in the upper-right corner and select "Overview." Then, click "Nights this year" on the left side of the page.

On the right side of the panel, you'll see your lifetime statistics.

This panel shows your lifetime nights, lifetime years with each status and how far you are from earning the next lifetime status tier.

Earning lifetime Marriott elite status can be relatively easy if you frequently stay with Marriott Bonvoy, hold a Marriott credit card that provides elite status and elite night credits, or both.

I'm looking forward to securing lifetime Platinum Elite status in three years. Although Marriott could change the benefits associated with each status tier, I'm excited about eventually enjoying Platinum Elite perks without requalifying each year.

#6200. My 9 Favorite Hotel Toiletry Brands, From Aesop To Le Labo, And More

Luxury hotel brands try to differentiate themselves in all kinds of ways. One (arguably) minor way they do so is by partnering with other luxury brands on their toiletry and skincare lines. While I’m not suggesting that you should pick a hotel brand because of the toiletries that they offer, I think I’m not alone in preferring some brands to others.

In this post, I’d like to share my favorite hotel toiletry brands, and then I’m curious to hear what brands OMAAT readers prefer. To be clear, my rankings are based purely on my perception of products and brands, from the packaging, to the scent, to how it feels using them, to memories I associate with them. I’m not claiming any authority with my opinion, so please don’t ask me to defend my preferences!

Still, I’m sure I’m not alone in getting more excited about some toiletry brands than others. With that out of the way, below are some of my favorite hotel toiletry brands (let me also emphasize that not every single property belonging to these groups has the brand standard toiletries).

Le Labo generally supplies toiletries for EDITION and Park Hyatt hotels, as well as select Fairmont properties, and it’s probably my single favorite toiletry brand. I love how there are different scents, and how they’re often customized for individual hotels (with the branding on the bottles even reflecting that). I enjoy the scents, and also appreciate that they seem to be fairly mild.

Bamford toiletries are generally available at ultra-luxury hotel group Capella, and sister brand Patina. I absolutely love Bamford, and find the product scents to be pleasant, and I also like the simplicity of the branding. For airline geeks, Bamford is also nowadays the premium toiletry partner of Cathay Pacific, so don’t be surprised if you see these products in Cathay Pacific lounges, and onboard the carrier’s flights.

Within the past few years, Ritz-Carlton has started partnering with Diptyque on toiletries. What an absolutely massive upgrade this is, compared to the previous Asprey Purple Rain collection, which I personally found to be completely unremarkable. I find Diptyque to have a very pleasant scent without being overpowering. It’s something I otherwise associate with Qatar Airways, as it’s the only major airline to partner with the brand. Speaking of changes in recent years in the luxury Marriott portfolio, St. Regis has moved to SACHAJUAN, which I find to be unmemorable.

A few years ago, Waldorf Astoria made the switch from Salvatore Ferragamo toiletries to Aesop toiletries. I’d consider that to be a significant upgrade. I love the scent of Aesop, and it can’t help but always remind me of Cathay Pacific back in the day (which, as noted above, has now switched to Bamford).

I love BVLGARI toiletries, including the packaging, scent, and feeling of using them. The catch is that while many hotels have BVLGARI toiletries, there’s not much consistency as to which brands have them. Yes, as you’d expect, BVLGARI hotels have these products, but that’s a small hotel group, with under 10 properties. On top of that, you’ll find BVLGARI toiletries at select properties of Four Seasons, Rosewood, and more.

Acqua Di Parma is another one of my favorite hotel toiletry brands, in terms of packaging and scent. The catch is that there’s not a major hotel group that consistently stocks these products, though they’re common enough among hotel groups that I feel good about including it on the list. For example, while not brand standard, the St. Regis Venice uses Acqua Di Parma products.

Molton Brown makes great products (I particularly like the soap). While no major hotel group consistently has Molton Brown products, I find that they’re pretty common at luxury hotels, including at many Marriott Luxury Collection properties.

I think Byredo is worth mentioning, as you’ll find the Bal d’Afrique product line at many InterContinental properties, and the Le Chemin product line at many Luxury Collection properties. While I don’t like this quite as much as some of the brands mentioned above, I appreciate that it’s often available at more mid-range properties, where you won’t typically find brands like Aesop and Le Labo.

Admittedly this is a bit lower end than the other options, but I wanted to also throw in a toiletry brand from a more mid-range hotel brand. For upscale hotels, I’d say that MALIN+GOETZ, available at Le Meridien properties, is probably my favorite line.

The above are nine of my favorite hotel toiletry lines. As you can see, some are pretty consistently available at select hotel brands, while others are frequently offered, though not consistently at any brand. I don’t claim that my opinions are right, but the above are the toiletry brands I’m typically most excited to see at hotels.

What are your favorite hotel toiletry brands?

#6198. KLM Plans 1,000 More Job Cuts

KLM expects to eliminate approximately 1,000 positions through productivity improvements as part of a restructuring announced Thursday.

The Dutch carrier said it would seek to limit the impact through natural attrition, voluntary arrangements and transfers. Other changes include moving about 800 ground services positions to outside providers and transferring 2,000 positions to Air France-KLM, including 1,500 at customer contact center Cygnific.

“But KLM’s future is not guaranteed,” CEO Marjan Rintel said in a statement, citing global instability, high fuel prices, and pressure on the industry.

KLM is targeting a structural productivity increase of at least 8% by 2028, alongside restrained wage growth. It said an additional €1 billion in annual earnings improvement is needed to fund investments.

The changes also affect its European fleet. KLM will replace planned Airbus A320s with Embraer E195-E2s, giving regional subsidiary Cityhopper a larger role. The A321neo will remain, while Boeing 737s and Embraer E190s will be phased out.

The announcement came as KLM reported a third-quarter operating profit of €458 million, up from €352 million a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, operating profit reached €526 million on revenue of €10.9 billion.

Despite the improvement, KLM said profitability remains insufficient to support its investment needs. Higher fuel costs and Middle East flight cancellations weighed on its passenger business, while Transavia faced competition and operational challenges.

“We need to increase it to more than 8% to secure a financially healthy future for KLM,” Chief Financial Officer Bas Brouns said of the airline’s profit margin.

With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Through 11:59PM ET on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is tiered, as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status.

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses. With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 200,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 400,000 points at a cost of $2,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 200,000 points, pre-bonus.

When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through November 10, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

#6196. Introduction: An Orient Express Adventure Via Africa

Welcome to my next trip report series, covering a trip that I recently wrapped up, which will include reviews of flights and a cruise. This will be a relatively short series, since the trip didn’t last that long, and had a specific purpose. However, as usual, I tried to take an unconventional routing to get to and from the destination, so I could review new experiences.

You can expect reviews of Air Algerie and Royal Air Maroc business class, as well as a review of Orient Express Sailing Yachts, which is Orient Express’ new cruising venture. In this post I’d like to share a basic outline of the trip, and then I’ll have individual review installments in the near future.

The primary reason for this trip was simple, and it was to take a cruise with Orient Express Sailing Yachts. It’s a fascinating time for the luxury cruising industry, and in particular, the increasing number of new lines associated with existing luxury hospitality brands.

Prior to this year, I hadn’t taken a cruise with any cruise line since I was a child, so I’ve been curious to check this all out. At the beginning of the year, I reviewed Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, which was surprisingly lovely, and a very nice reintroduction to cruising.

Then over the summer, I reviewed Four Seasons Yachts, which was definitely upmarket, but had some growing pains.

The newest entrant into this market is Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and arguably it takes luxury cruising to a new level, so you can expect a full review of the experience. Full disclosure — Ford was invited on the sailing (so traveled as a guest of Orient Express) and I tagged along. I’ll still review the experience objectively, of course, but I’ll say upfront that Orient Express simply nailed it, and this matched the feedback Ford has received from clients who have sailed with the company.

Anyway, we sailed with Orient Express Sailing Yachts on a four night journey that started in Marseille, France, and ended in Malaga, Spain, so we needed to position to and from there.

I’m of course always looking for an interesting airline angle when I travel long haul, since my goal is always to try as many new airline products as possible. So rather than flying to Marseille and from Malaga on the “typical” airlines (Air France, British Airways, Lufthansa, etc.), I tried to see if I could instead check some airlines off my list that I’ve been wanting to try. I accomplished that, and below is what my routing looked like.

While I sent Ford direct, I booked a four segment routing for myself, spread across three different tickets.

I had heard a lot about Air Algerie over the years (and not in a good way!), so I decided I finally had to give the carrier a try. Air Algerie typically has very high business class fares, despite the carrier’s lackluster product.

However, I found one decent fare on the carrier’s only route from North America, from Montreal (YUL) to Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, that doesn’t start where I’d like to start, and it doesn’t end where I’d like to end, but that has never stopped me if the price is right. 😉

This included a flight in Air Algerie’s Airbus A330-900neo business class across the Atlantic, and then a connecting flight in Avion Express’ Airbus A320neo business class for the short hop in Africa (this was a wet leased flight operated on behalf of Air Algerie). So I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day) 10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

From there, I of course had to get from Tunis to Marseille (MRS), so I had booked Tunisair’s A320 business class for $270, with the following schedule:

10/04 TU902 Tunis to Marseille departing 1:05PM arriving 3:40PM

Unfortunately I ended up being downgraded shortly before departure due to an aircraft swap. That’s because the flight was swapped to a wet leased Fly2Sky Airbus A320, and I guess they don’t offer business class on those planes. I’m still waiting on any sort of a refund.

Suffice it to say that the outbound wasn’t that smooth, between Air Algerie just royally sucking, and Tunisair downgrading me. I’m happy I had the experience, though!

I should also mention that I had to position to Montreal, so I did that in Air Canada Rouge economy, and flew the following for 11,500 avianca lifemiles plus $54 in taxes & fees:

10/04 AC1651 Miami to Montreal departing 7:55AM arriving 11:28AM

The return portion of our trip was a little more straightforward. Our priority was to get home the same day as our cruise arrived, since we wanted to minimize time away from our kids, and had a family event the next day. So we booked the one routing that would best get us home the same day, which was on Royal Air Maroc, from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN) to Miami (MIA), with the first flight in Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class, and the second flight in Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 787-8 business class.

I booked one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM 10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

On this trip, we just had a single hotel night ahead of our cruise in Marseille (in order to build in a buffer), and we decided to stay at the Hôtel Dieu Intercontinental Marseille. I booked this using an IHG free night award, and it cost 60,000 points before applying the award, so I just had to redeem the difference in points.

I had intended to review the hotel, but I have to apologize, it just didn’t end up working out (since I pride myself in thoroughly reviewing hotels). To be honest, I was dead tired from the journey over, and then we had some drama to deal with back at home most of the afternoon. Then the next morning I prioritized sleeping in, as I was just getting over a cold, rather than getting up at 5AM so I could photograph all parts of the hotel.

So I’m sorry about that. My conclusion is that the hotel has a central location, and from the outside you’d think it’s super charming, but the interior feels mismatched and rather uninspiring and generic.

We had an absolutely amazing time cruising with Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and I was blown away by the experience. What I was less impressed by was my flights to and from Europe, which I routed via Africa in both directions. Air Algerie was downright terrible, while Royal Air Maroc was just unnecessarily bad.

JetBlue Airways is set to debut its latest transcontinental service as the airline begins flying from San Diego International Airport (SAN) to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) on November 19. The airline's expansion of its transcontinental footprint will see the launch of a daily service between Southern California and South Florida.

The flight will operate with a block time of almost six hours. The daily service will be operated onboard the airline's Airbus A321ceo and marks the return of the airline, which previously served the route periodically between June 2016 and January 2025.

The corridor between San Diego and Fort Lauderdale is tight, with three competitors all operating multiple weekly flights across the year. Alaska Airlines provides nonstop flights on the route, while Southwest Airlines adds a seasonal service between November and January.

JetBlue's resumption on the route marks the third to begin out of Fort Lauderdale, adding to the new flights to Indianapolis International Airport (IND) and Columbus (CMH).

As already mentioned, JetBlue will fly the route daily with the schedule below, departing in the early morning from Fort Lauderdale, with aircraft pushing back at 7:00 AM, for a mid-morning arrival into San Diego. Return flights depart late morning for an early evening arrival into Florida.

JetBlue has expanded aggressively at Fort Lauderdale since Spirit Airlines' collapse in May. The airline is now the largest airline at the South Florida airport, and the airport has even been suggested to be a highly likely location for the airline's third BlueHouse lounge.

From Fort Lauderdale, JetBlue has a network of 62 total destinations, with the most popular routes from the airport being to New York (JFK), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), New York (LGA), Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), and San Juan (SJU).

As already mentioned, JetBlue has operated the route from San Diego to Fort Lauderdale before, having operated it up until January 2025. During the eight and a half years the airline operated the service, it had an average load factor of 82.5%, according to data from the US Department of Transportation. In the final months before the route was axed, 85% of passengers traveled on the route point to point, whereas a further 15% connected onto another JetBlue flight.

JetBlue is doubling down at FLL just as Spirit Airlines is forced to pull back.

This coming winter season, JetBlue's major routes from Fort Lauderdale are to New York JFK and Los Angeles LAX, which, from November through the summer of 2027, will see in excess of 1,900 flights up until May. Other leading destinations from Fort Lauderdale across the 187 days are detailed in the table below, per data from Cirium:

San Diego ranks 58th on this list, with a total of 286 departures over the same period, with an average of one daily flight to Fort Lauderdale. Fort Lauderdale became JetBlue's third destination from San Diego, adding to its existing services from New York JFK and Boston.

#6194. Teamsters Sue Horizon Air Over Pilot Rest Rules

The Teamsters have sued Horizon Air, alleging the Alaska Air Group subsidiary violated federal labor law by changing how it handles pilots who report fatigue.

The Teamsters Airline Division and Local 1224 filed the lawsuit Oct. 23 in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. The union alleges Horizon requires pilots who report fatigue at their home base to travel to another city as passengers before taking the rest provided under their contract.

The union alleges the practice violates the Railway Labor Act and is asking the court to order Horizon to stop it and restore the negotiated rest protections.

“Management cannot pick and choose which parts of our contract it wants to follow,” said Sean Lenney, a Horizon pilot and member of Local 1224, in a news release.

The Teamsters also said Thursday that 99% of pilots who voted backed a no-confidence measure against Carlos Zendejas, Horizon’s senior vice president of operations. The union’s Horizon Air Pilots Executive Council called for his removal following the vote.

Horizon and its pilots have been negotiating a new collective bargaining agreement for more than three and a half years, according to the union. Pilots held informational pickets in Seattle and Boise, Idaho, on Oct. 15 over issues including pay, staffing, and training.

If you’ve been frustrated by soaring airfare, now may be your best chance to book flights without the sticker shock.

American Airlines just launched one of its biggest AAdvantage award sales of the year. And you'll want to act quickly: It’s only scheduled to be live for 72 hours.

American has put more than 1 million main cabin seats on sale for the winter months.

If holiday fares were out of your budget this year, this could be a chance to redeem miles for a long weekend getaway in the Caribbean in January — or to hit the ski slopes over President’s Day weekend in February.

American’s winter AAdvantage award sale covers flights from Jan. 11 through Feb. 28, 2027.

The deals are slated to run through 12:59 a.m. EST on Nov. 12.

These aren’t the cheapest AAdvantage award redemptions we’ve ever seen (a similar award sale last year offered award prices even lower than this year’s).

And some of these redemptions are in the range of what I typically look for in the quieter winter months.

The good news here is that these cheaper award prices are widely available. And that’s significant in a year where fares (and award prices) have surged.

As an AAdvantage member myself, I'd feel pretty good about booking at any of these price points.

You won’t find these discounted award prices on every flight, date or route. Instead, American simply says it’s discounting more than 1 million main cabin seats across its network.

Fortunately, there aren't blackout dates — which means you don't need to fly at 10 p.m. on a Tuesday to take advantage of this deal. There are options on Fridays, Sundays, peak long weekend travel days and during other popular times.

These deals apply to economy bookings; American is not offering up these discounts on premium economy, first class or business class.

However, these cheaper award redemptions could be a way to get a spot on the plane and then watch for a targeted upgraded offer to a premium seat.

You can find domestic bookings within the 48 contiguous U.S. states for as low as 8,000 miles one-way.

That includes longer transcontinental flights.

For instance, here’s a January flight from Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

There are also short-haul international redemptions to warm-weather island destinations at that rate, too — like this February flight from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) to Turks and Caicos.

As a Raleigh-based flyer, I could book this Martin Luther King, Jr. weekend flight from North Carolina to Zurich, Switzerland, for 22,500 miles one-way.

There are a ton of AAdvantage redemptions to Europe at that price point, with options for both nonstop and connecting itineraries, depending on your final destination.

I also found pretty open award availability for 25,000 miles one-way.

Here are some examples: LAX to Tokyo’s Haneda Airport (HND), and another to Sydney, Australia.

Passengers in Chicagoland are the biggest winners.

American's award sale includes discounted AAdvantage redemptions starting even lower than the rest of the country, at 7,000 miles one-way.

These AAdvantage deals for the winter months aren’t the cheapest award discounts American has ever offered. But they’re pretty solid — and widely available — for the upcoming winter months.

And for consumers plagued by high prices this year, that could be reason enough to lock in a winter getaway.

Just be sure to book by Wednesday night to take advantage of these deals.

#6190. Which Airlines Fly To The Most Countries? One Carrier Has A Huge Lead

I don’t want to bury the lede — in posts, I often reference how Turkish Airlines flies to more countries than any other airline in the world. However, how many countries does the airline actually fly to, and how far ahead of competitors is Turkish Airlines? I thought that would be interesting to explore…

Turkish Airlines has the record for flying to more countries than any other airline in the world. That has been the case for a long time, and in late 2024, the Star Alliance carrier made it official, with a Guinness World Record in the category of “most countries flown to by an airline.” The airline has flown to more countries than any other airline since 2012, and has a sizable lead over competitors.

Just how many countries does Turkish Airlines fly to? This is where it always gets tricky as to what you count. If you count active flights operating at the moment, the airline flies to 117 countries. However:

As you’d expect, when you’re an airline serving virtually every corner of the globe, there will always be some suspended services due to geopolitical factors, etc. What’s cool is that Turkish Airlines is also far from done with its expansion, as the airline still has big growth plans. It’ll be fascinating to see just how many countries the airline eventually serves.

What’s perhaps most impressive about Turkish Airlines’ record for serving the most countries is just how far ahead of competitors the airline is. Turkish Airlines is 30+ countries ahead of the next airline when it comes to countries served.

Does anyone want to take a guess as to which airlines are next on the list? Here are a few general thoughts that come to mind:

With that in mind, which airlines serve the most countries, aside from Turkish Airlines? According to flightconnections.com, here are some observations:

As you can see, that means Qatar Airways serves the most countries after Turkish Airlines, while Air France, British Airways, and Ethiopian Airlines, are currently tied for third place.

Meanwhile it’s impressive that Emirates serves so many countries when you consider that the airline just flies wide body jets. If you combined the networks of Emirates and flydubai (both are owned by the government, but the airlines are run separately), then the combined airline would have close to as many destinations as Turkish Airlines.

Let me of course also acknowledge that the number of countries served and number of destinations served is very different, and US carriers would do much better by the latter metric. And if the question is the number of premium destinations served, then there’s only one right answer. 😉

When you put it all together, below is the chart with the 13 most “global” airlines, in terms of countries served (I had to include KLM as well, since it ties Air Canada and Delta, even if it doesn’t lead the way among European carriers).

Turkish Airlines sets the world record for serving the most countries in the world. The airline actively flies to 117 countries, but including suspended routes, serves 130+ countries. That puts the airline way ahead of the next carriers by this metric, which include Qatar Airways at 86 countries, followed by a tie between Air France, British Airways, and Ethiopian Airlines, at 80 countries.

Are you surprised by the airlines serving the most countries?

#6189. PSA Pilots Secure Contract Extension Through 2030

PSA Airlines’ pilot union leaders have approved an agreement that extends the regional carrier’s pilot contract by two years and locks in three rounds of pay increases.

The Air Line Pilots Association announced the agreement Wednesday. It extends the existing contract through April 1, 2030. The previous extension, ratified in 2022, had set an amendable date of April 1, 2028.

Current pay rates will remain in place until June 1, 2027, when the first increases take effect. Additional raises are scheduled for June 1 in each of the following two years. The deal also changes scheduling and work rules. ALPA’s announcement did not specify the size of the raises or detail the scheduling changes.

“When we asked our pilots what mattered most, the answer was clear: Protect our pay. This agreement does that,” said Capt. Chris Sabia, who chairs the union’s PSA Master Executive Council, in a news release.

ALPA represents approximately 2,260 pilots at PSA, which is a wholly-owned regional subsidiary of American Airlines.

#6187. Livery of the Week: JetBlue’s Florida Panthers Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Since the beginning of its operations in 2000, New York-based airline JetBlue has always considered South Florida as one of its primary markets, with a presence at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood Airport that has grown during the past 25 years to include up to 25 aircraft based overnight at the airport and over 2,000 people supporting its operations in Broward County.

As a sign of its commitment to the South Florida community, JetBlue has announced a multi-year extension for an expanded partnership with the Florida Panthers, the NHL’s southernmost franchise that captured back-to-back Stanley Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. The partnership will see JetBlue present a newly redesigned Champions Club at the Amerant Bank Arena in Sunrise, Florida, home of the Panthers, and to celebrate the announcement, the airline unveiled a special Panthers-themed livery for one of its Airbus A320 aircraft.

The new livery draws its inspiration from the Panthers’ jersey, therefore sporting the iconic Panthers’ red across the entire fuselage, with the outline of a golden panther all across the central part of the fuselage, right next to JetBlue’s logo. The Panthers’ shield logo is on the aircraft tail in navy and gold.

Bold red letters spelling FLORIDA appear on the bottom of the aircraft, where there’s also a leaping cat, the team’s logo. More symbols of the Panthers and the State of Florida appear in other parts of the fuselage: a simplified Florida flag appears near the front of the aircraft together with a palm tree and a hockey stick, which represent the secondary logo for the team.

“South Florida has been part of JetBlue’s story since our very first flight more than two decades ago, and we’re continuing to build on that history in a big way as Broward County’s largest airline,” said Marty St. George, JetBlue’s president, in a press release. “The Panthers know a thing or two about winning in South Florida, and we’re bringing that same energy as we expand our network, elevate the customer experience and deepen our commitment to the community. ‘Go Cats Go’ is a fun way to celebrate our shared passion for South Florida and team up with a franchise that knows how to make some noise.”

The aircraft chosen to display this special livery is an Airbus A320, registered as N784JB, delivered to the airline on Feb. 11, 2011.

The original name of the aircraft was “Blue And Infinity And Beyond,” which has been changed to “Go Cats Go” following the repainting in this new livery.

#6186. Confused Air France Pilots Make Wrong Turn After Takeoff From LAX, Leading To Close Call

An Air France Airbus A350 departing from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) made a wrong turn after takeoff, sending the plane dangerously close to the path of an American Airlines Airbus A321. The way the pilots responded to this isn’t exactly great, though one thing is for sure — there seems to be a recurring problem involving runway 24L departures from the airport, whatever the cause may be.

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the audio and a visualization of an incident that happened shortly after 12AM on Saturday, November 7, 2026. It involves Air France flight AF28, which was operating to Papeete, French Polynesia (PPT).

LAX has four parallel runways, and the Air France A350 was cleared for takeoff on runway 24L, on the north side of the field. The Air France pilots were instructed to initially fly to the DLREY fix, instructions which they correctly read back.

Once through the DLREY fix, they were instructed to climb via their assigned SID (that they had received with clearance), but then the pilots suddenly made a turn to the left. The issue is that an American A321 had been cleared for takeoff on runway 25R just moments earlier, and that’s to the south of runway 24L.

So when the Air France pilots started turning to the left, they went directly into the path of the American plane. Fortunately the air traffic controller quickly caught this, but it created a traffic alert, and the planes had less than a mile of separation.

Mistakes happen, but what’s strange here is how this was handled after the initial incident. The air traffic controller asked the Air France pilots why they made a turn. The Air France pilot responded “standby,” which is fair enough. Pilots are supposed to be focused first on aviating, then on navigating, and then on communicating.

Moments later, the air traffic controller followed up and asked what departure the pilots had been instructed to fly. Once again, the pilot responded “standby one.” I do think the air traffic controller should’ve been a bit more patient here when a pilot is asking him to hold on for a second. At the same, the Air France pilots seemingly just kept stalling, and seemed to be unable to answer the question.

Of course we don’t know what was going on in the cockpit (it’s possible they were dealing with something else), but the controller wasn’t asking a complicated question. The pilots ended up getting a phone number for a possible pilot deviation.

It’s truly a mystery what caused the pilots to make that left turn, especially since they were flying to Tahiti, which is basically a straight westbound departure (and in the middle of the night, it’s not like you typically need to vector to the east when departing LAX).

Regardless of how good a system looks on paper, you of course have to consider human factors, and how systems are actually perceived. For reasons that are somewhat of a mystery, there seem to be repeated issues with planes departing from runway 24L at LAX making a turn to the left, and turning into the path of planes departing from runway 25R.

Just a couple of weeks ago, I covered how a TAP Air Portugal Airbus A330neo departing runway 24L at LAX made an unauthorized left turn immediately after takeoff, putting itself in the path of another jet.

Heck, just a couple of months ago, an Air France Boeing 777 departing runway 24L at LAX made an almost identical mistake, and turned left right after takeoff, when it wasn’t supposed to.

That’s only the tip of the iceberg in terms of the number of these incidents we’ve seen. I’m not sure what exactly is going on here, and if it’s a case of pilots programming their computers for a departure from runway 25R, only to get assigned runway 24L, or what.

But either way, it seems something should be done here. As redundant as it might sound when you’re sending pilots to a specific fix (which already tells them which direction they should go), it almost seems like air traffic control needs to add in a warning about not making a left turn without authorization. I mean, it sounds silly, but…

An Air France Airbus A350 departing LAX made an unauthorized left turn after takeoff, sending it right into the path of a departing American Airbus A321. The pilots really seemed to struggle with answering air traffic control’s basic questions, though I don’t know what was actually going on in the cockpit.

What’s so strange is how there seem to be repeated issues with departures from runway 24L, as we’ve now seen this “unauthorized left turn” situation from this exact runway several times in recent weeks alone.

What do you make of this LAX runway 24L issue?

Among my friends and family, I see couples manage their finances and credit cards in many different ways. But across all the couples I know, I've found that two people can work together to earn more rewards and enjoy more benefits than they could individually.

So, here are some credit card strategies you should consider if you're part of a couple.

Couples who manage their finances separately will generally want separate credit card accounts. However, even if you manage your finances separately, you may want one or two cards you both use for shared expenses.

Likewise, even if you generally manage your finances jointly, having a few separate cards can be nice for purchasing surprise gifts.

You'll be approved or denied for a card based on your credit score and history, independent of your partner's credit score and history. But depending on your age and circumstances, you may also be able to include income from your partner that you can reasonably access when applying for a new card.

Some banks offer joint credit card accounts, which you apply for together and are jointly responsible for the bills. But joint accounts are relatively rare, so this article instead considers the more common situation in which one person opens an account and then adds their partner as an authorized user.

Primary account holders can make their partner (or anyone else) an authorized user on their account. Authorized users can make purchases on the account, but the primary cardholder is responsible for all the charges (including those made by authorized users).

Related: Here’s how my husband and I maximize each dollar we spend on household expenses

One of the biggest advantages couples have over solo travelers is access to more welcome offers. Specifically, each member of a couple could earn the welcome bonus on the same card if they each apply separately.

This can be particularly useful if you're earning welcome offers for a specific trip. You could use one person's welcome offer for hotel bookings and the other person's for flights. Or, you could each use your welcome offer to book an award flight for the same trip.

But while both partners can potentially earn welcome offers on the same card, it's still important to coordinate application timing and avoid taking on more minimum spending than you can comfortably manage. Plus, each individual must keep in mind issuer application restrictions, such as Chase's 5/24 rule, when deciding which cards to apply for and when to apply for them.

Related: Cards currently offering welcome bonuses of 100,000 points or more

If you and your partner each want to apply for a new card, you must decide whether to get the same cards or different cards.

The biggest reasons to get the same cards are an exceptional welcome offer or perks you'll each want.

For example, each member of a couple might want their own Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card if they frequently travel separately and value airport lounge access, especially since lounge access for authorized users now costs extra.

And I love that my husband and I each have our own , as this lets us use our anniversary night certificates for consecutive nights to make a two-night stay.

However, it often makes sense for couples to have complementary cards. By applying for different cards that complement what's in your partner's wallet, you can unlock better bonus-category coverage, different travel perks and access to different transferable rewards currencies.

This can be particularly useful if one person in a couple travels more frequently, as they may want to carry more cards with travel benefits, such as lounge access and airline or hotel elite status.

Be sure to weigh the combined annual fees against the benefits you'll actually use. And keep in mind that some cards let you share benefits with other travelers. For example, many airline credit cards offer a checked baggage benefit that extends to other travelers on your same reservation.

Related: Better together: The ultimate guide to the best credit card combinations

In some cases, you may want to add your partner as an authorized user on a card. This can be an easy choice when there's no fee. But it can also make sense to pay an authorized-user fee in some situations.

For example, many couples have one primary and pay $195 per additional Platinum card for each other family member (see rates and fees). By doing so, these family members can enjoy many of the Platinum Card's perks, including lounge access and select hotel elite statuses (enrollment is required for select benefits).

However, keep in mind that some benefits don't extend to authorized users. For example, purchases on additional Platinum Cards count toward many of the Platinum Card's statement credit benefits, such as up to $200 in airline incidental fee statement credits per calendar year (enrollment required). But additional Platinum Cards don't get their own statement credits.

So, while it might make sense for one partner to hold a premium travel card and add the other as an authorized user, it can make sense for both partners to independently hold cards that offer valuable benefits you'll use.

For example, my husband and I both hold several hotel credit cards, such as the (see rates and fees) and (see rates and fees), since their annual free night certificates and other perks provide ample value.

Adding your partner as an authorized user may also help them build credit if the issuer reports the account to credit bureaus and the account is managed responsibly. However, missed payments or high credit utilization could hurt their credit instead.

Related: 7 credit cards with the best authorized user benefits

Whether you and your partner earn the same currencies on your credit cards or different currencies, and whether you combine your finances or not, it makes sense to coordinate how you earn and redeem rewards.

Consider what types of rewards you should both be earning based on the trips you want to take. For example, if you have your sights set on visiting a far-flung international destination, spending on a Southwest credit card likely isn't the best choice. Instead, earning hotel points in a program with properties in your desired destination, airline miles with a program that serves that destination or transferable rewards is a better bet.

The benefit of both partners earning the same transferable currency is that you can each transfer to the airline or hotel program of your choice once you're ready to redeem. But there's also value in diversifying your earnings in case flight availability appears in a program that only some transferable currencies can access.

Before deciding which rewards to earn, consider how you'll redeem them together. Some credit card issuers let you move rewards between eligible household accounts, while some airline and hotel loyalty programs allow members to pool points or transfer them to each other. Even when you can't combine rewards, you may be able to use your points or miles to book travel for your partner.

Related: These 14 apps and websites make award redemptions easier to find

Couples have plenty of opportunities to earn more rewards and enjoy more credit card benefits by coordinating their credit card strategies. Whether you and your partner decide to get the same cards, hold complementary cards or add each other as authorized users, the best approach depends on your spending habits and travel goals.

My husband and I have found that having our own credit card accounts while coordinating which rewards we earn and redeem works well for us. But you don't need a wallet full of cards to benefit from a two-player strategy. Even a few carefully chosen cards can help you earn more rewards and enjoy more perks together.

Related: How to earn and use an IHG annual lounge membership

#6184. Boeing Cuts 5% Of Commercial Airplanes Workforce As Production Ramp-Up Slows

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

American plane manufacturer Boeing has announced that it will reduce its workforce by around 5%. Affecting those working in the division of Boeing Commercial Airplanes (BCA), the decision comes as the US plane maker confirmed that it plans to slow down its factory production rate increases as a result of factory and supply chain challenges.

This 5% reduction across the commercial division is forecasted to affect around 2,500 workers, and the headcount reduction will be achieved through involuntary layoffs and natural attrition.

Boeing, one of the world's largest aircraft manufacturers, will shave around 5% of its workforce beginning in December. The 2,500 positions will see formal layoff notifications starting next month. Chief Executive Officer of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Stephanie Pope, shared a memo to employees, as shared by CNBC:

"Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position. Unfortunately, that means we need to align our staffing levels to our revised business plans."

The decision continues to stem from challenges in the assembly lines and component delivery flows. This has meant that the plane maker must recalibrate to its current supply chain abilities instead of aggressive output targets. This will affect the Boeing 737 MAX and 787 Dreamliner assembly lines.

Simple Flying reached out to Boeing for comment on the layoffs on Monday; however, a company spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

As Boeing looks to stabilize its assembly line and component delivery flows, the Boeing 737 MAX line has had its target timeline of 47 planes per month pushed out until mid to late 2027. This will see fewer planes being delivered but easing the delivery projection bottlenecks that were expected to be seen for wing assembly operations in Renton.

Output increases on the widebody 787 Dreamliner have also been reduced to allow a slower timeline for suppliers to achieve the factory's stability. Despite these changes, Boeing continues to hold a backlog of more than 6,300 airplanes, which is valued in excess of $610 billion.

The ongoing operating losses and supply chain friction continue to weigh on Boeing and its BCA division's short-term recovery. Adjusting the production schedule has ultimately put the plane maker in an overstaffed position, which has led to the decision to lay off 2,500 workers.

Boeing is facing arguably its most impactful crossroads to date, with an imminent workers strike coming, will the 737 MAX production be affected?

Kelly Ortberg, Boeing CEO, spoke to investors last month and outlined that the company will not increase production on the MAX until the second half of 2027, with wing production having been slower than expected. This sees the lifting of the 737 MAX production timeline from 47 to 52 jets per month, pushed out until the second half of 2027.

Ortberg noted in October that while Boeing continues to make progress, there is still 'a lot more work to do', and this is expected to take until the middle of next year. For investors, the overall MAX output has been seen as central to revenue and profit growth after a long period of ongoing financial losses and safety problems (including the deadly MAX crashes in 2018 and 2019). The 737 and 787 outputs will remain at 47 and eight jets per month, with ongoing disruption hampering the 767 and 777 programs as well. Targets as detailed below:

Low-rate, steady production of a couple per month tied with commercial freighter and KC-46 tanker demand

As noted on the Boeing website, the Boeing Commercial Airplanes division employs a total of 50,494 workers, with the 5% employee cuts resulting in approximately 2,500 jobs. No layoffs are expected in November, with the beginning of job cuts expected in December.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

This is the first time a boing employee is hearing this. I’d like to know where you’re getting your information from.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is currently offering a multi-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn three free night awards. The bonus is broken down as follows:

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each, given all the great ways there are to redeem them. While the maximum value of this offer is 150,000 points, I wouldn’t value the bonus quite that high, given the limited flexibility (you need to redeem the free night award within a year, you’re capped at properties costing 50,000 points, etc.).

However, if it were worth 150,000 points, I’d consider that to have a value of $1,050, and that doesn’t factor in the potential airline statement credits.

If you’re applying for the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, the general Chase application restrictions apply. There aren’t too many direct, consistent rules, but considerations include Chase’s 5/24 rule (which isn’t always enforced), being able to get up to two Chase cards every 30 days, etc.

Beyond that, since both American Express and Chase issue cards for Marriott, there are some pretty complicated restrictions regarding eligibility for this card, so see this post for more details.

To summarize the very basics, you can’t get the welcome bonus on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card if:

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card has a $95 annual fee. You can add authorized users at no extra cost. That’s an incredibly reasonable annual fee, given the amount of annual fee inflation we’ve seen over the years on other cards.

The Bonvoy Boundless Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s an excellent card for purchases abroad. That means you can earn rewards on your foreign spending, without having to pay any fees that will offset those rewards. In particular, it’s a good card to use for foreign Marriott spending.

While I wouldn’t recommend using the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card for your everyday spending, there are potentially some situations where it could make sense. Let’s go over the rewards structure of the card, including the bonus categories and other incentives to spend.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 6x Bonvoy points for spending at Marriott-family hotels globally. For many people, this will be a worthwhile bonus.

Since I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, that’s the equivalent of a 4.2% return on hotel spending. While there are other great cards for hotel spending, some people will want to use this as their card for Marriott spending.

Keep in mind this is on top of the standard points that you can earn for Marriott Bonvoy hotel stays. At most brands, Bonvoy members earn 10x points per dollar spent, and that’s before elite bonuses, which range from 10-75%. So as a Bonvoy Silver member paying with the card (the minimum status you get with this card), you’re looking at earning 17x points per dollar spent at most brands, minimum.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 3x Bonvoy points on dining, gas station, and grocery store purchases globally. This only applies to the first $6,000 spent on combined purchases in those categories annually, and after that, you’ll earn 2x Bonvoy points on those purchases.

Since I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, the 3x points is like the equivalent of a 2.1% return on eligible gas, grocery, and dining spending. While there are still more rewarding cards for spending in the categories of dining, gas stations, and groceries, this is about as good of a rewards structure as you’ll see on a Bonvoy credit card.

The Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 2x Bonvoy points on all other eligible purchases. I don’t consider 2x points per dollar spent to be especially compelling since I value that at a return of 1.4 cents per dollar of spending, and there are better cards for everyday spending.

How would I approach the value of Marriott points? As mentioned above, based on my valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each. I’m not going to suggest that Bonvoy points are my favorite points currency — they’re not — but the reality is that Marriott has a huge global portfolio, and many of the properties are quite decent.

Generally you’ll find that Bonvoy award stays cost anywhere from 10,000 to 200,000 points per night, though some hotels do fall outside of that range. You can maximize value by taking advantage of the fifth night free benefit, which is open to elite members.

This is an extreme example of value, but take Hotel Cala di Volpe, a Marriott Luxury Collection hotel in Sardinia, which is the brand’s most expensive property in summer. I just pulled up a five night redemption (including a fifth night free) for 776,000 Bonvoy points. By my valuation, that’s like $5,432 worth of points.

Meanwhile the cash rate at the hotel is 4,161 EUR ($4,639) per night, so those same five nights would cost you $23,195. Talk about huge savings!

One unique thing about Bonvoy points is they can also fairly efficiently be converted into airline miles. You can transfer your rewards to dozens of different airline programs, and a vast majority allow a 3:1 transfer ratio. On top of that, you get a bonus of 5,000 airline miles for every 60,000 Bonvoy points you transfer. In other words, with most programs you can convert 60,000 Bonvoy points into 25,000 airline miles, which is potentially a decent value.

For more details, see my guide to redeeming Bonvoy points.

One of the primary reasons to consider getting the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is how the card can help you earn elite status in the Bonvoy program. Status starts to get valuable around the Bonvoy Platinum tier, when you become eligible for perks like complimentary breakfast and valuable room upgrades.

One of my favorite perks of having the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is that you get 15 elite nights toward status annually just for having the card.

Note that several co-branded Marriott credit cards offer this, and you can only receive the benefit once per year on a personal card. In other words, if you have three Marriott personal cards, then you wouldn’t get 45 elite nights.

However, you could earn 15 elite nights from this personal card and 15 elite nights from a business card, so that you’d earn 30 elite nights in a year. The ideal setup would be to have a personal card in conjunction with the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more).

This makes it more attainable to earn Platinum status, which requires 50 elite nights. If you had the Bonvoy Boundless Card, you’d only need 35 more elite nights, and if you also had the business card you’d only need 20 more elite nights.

Note that if you really want to maximize elite nights with personal credit cards, the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) offers 25 elite nights per year, which is the most elite nights you’ll get with any Marriott credit card.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers one elite night for every $5,000 spent on the card. Any elite nights earned this way will be credited to your account within eight weeks of the last day of the calendar month in which you qualify.

Personally, I think spending $5,000 to earn one elite night is a lot, but everyone’s situation will differ, and for some people, this could make sense if you’re otherwise close to earning status. This is the only Marriott credit card that offers bonus elite nights for spending.

Perhaps this is a bit redundant, but just for having the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card you receive Silver elite status in the Bonvoy program. Now, don’t get too excited, as this doesn’t exactly come with that many benefits.

Marriott Silver elite status ordinarily requires 10 elite nights, and comes with perks like 10% bonus points on hotel stays, priority late check-out, and free Wi-Fi. So it’s better than nothing, but that’s about all I can say.

If you have the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, you can earn Marriott Gold elite status if you spend $35,000 on the card in a calendar year. This status ordinarily requires 25 elite nights. Bonvoy Gold elite status gets you benefits like 25% bonus points on hotel stays, 2PM late check-out, a room upgrade subject to availability, and more.

In addition to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card spending bonus categories and ability to earn elite status, there are some other major perks to having the card. This is where the card’s annual fee becomes really easy to justify, in my opinion.

The real perk that makes the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card worthwhile is that you get a free night award every year on your account anniversary, valid for a one-night hotel stay at a property costing up to 35,000 points.

It’s also possible to top off Marriott free night awards with up to 25,000 additional points to redeem at more expensive properties. This means you could redeem a free night award plus 25,000 points to stay at a hotel costing 60,000 points per night.

This is an exceptional deal, and I think this card is worth having. Marriott is the world’s largest hotel chain, so regardless of your preferred hotel program, just about everyone may find themselves in a situation where this could come in handy.

I consistently redeem this certificate at hotels costing $250+ per night. Based on my valuation of 0.7 cents per point, I’d consider the free night award to be worth around $245, more than double the annual fee… that’s awesome!

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers auto rental collision damage waiver coverage. Decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card.

Coverage is provided for theft and collision damage for most cars in the United States and abroad. Do note that within the United States, coverage is secondary to your personal insurance, though. Of course you’ll always want to check the guide to benefits for all the details.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers a variety of protection when traveling. Among these features are:

Make sure you check your cardmember agreement and guide to benefits for all of the details, since there are terms to be aware of.

Personally, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card isn’t a card that I would be using for my everyday spending. However, I think the card is worth having, given that it offers a free night certificate on your account anniversary every year, which should more than justify the annual fee.

If you’re going for status, the 15 elite nights toward status annually is incredibly valuable as well, and makes it easier to earn Platinum status.

I think there’s absolutely merit to picking up the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, though I’d say that the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) might be the best alternative to consider. While the card is issued by American Express and has a steep $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees), there are lots of reasons to consider this card, including:

Obviously this card won’t be for everyone, and the fee is steep. However, I do think the perks add up, and if you’re involved quite a bit in the Bonvoy ecosystem, it’s easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re not actually that committed to the Marriott Bonvoy ecosystem, there are lots of other great cards to consider. In particular, these are cards with relatively reasonable annual fees and great rewards structures, and they’re very well rounded:

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is a great card with a reasonable annual fee, and offers an annual free night award and 15 elite nights toward status annually. This is an especially good time to apply, given the welcome offer that’s currently available.

For those looking to earn Bonvoy points, this is also one of Marriott’s better credit cards for being rewarded, between the points and additional elite nights. However, this still isn’t the card I’d be used for my everyday spending. Instead, this is a card you get for the perks it offers, as it can make sense to hold onto this card even with minimal spending.

If you want to learn more about the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, follow this link.

#6181. Can You Redeem Airline Miles For Others? Yes, With Some Caveats

While I love redeeming miles & points for an amazing first or business class flight, one thing that brings me even more joy is being able to do that for friends & family. Along those lines, in this post I’d like to talk about which airline loyalty programs allow you to redeem your points for others. In a separate post, I addressed the topic of whether you can redeem hotel points for others.

While there are some areas where airline loyalty programs are stingy, the ability to redeem miles for others isn’t among those. Generally speaking, airline loyalty programs will let you redeem your miles for anyone you’d like (I’ll note some exceptions below, but unless otherwise noted, that’s what you should expect).

You can almost always do this directly through your frequent flyer program account, by just entering the name of the traveler during the booking process.

Now, it’s important to emphasize that this is for situations where you truly want to gift your rewards to others. Bartering airline miles violates the policies of virtually any airline loyalty program, and your account could be suspended and ticket could be forfeited if you’re caught doing this (and airline auditing departments are quite savvy).

So if you are going to redeem your airline miles for others, make sure you do so in good faith, without expecting anything in return.

To make things as easy as possible, I’d recommend that the person redeeming miles be the one to make the booking, rather than the person being redeemed for. Admittedly the policies do vary by airline:

If you’re making your reservation online, you can always just share your account number and password with someone to make a booking, though that does potentially pose a risk if you can’t fully trust the person (in which case you probably also shouldn’t share miles with them, come and think of it).

I won’t break that down by airline, since there are so many different policies, they sometimes change, and phone agents also often interpret them differently. However, the best way to go about this is to have the person with the miles make the booking. Just make sure you have the full, correct passport or travel document details for the traveler, so that the name matches the ID that will be presented at the time of travel.

There are hundreds of airline loyalty programs out there, and a vast majority of them will allow you to redeem your miles for anyone you’d like. There are some exceptions, though, as some airlines either limit the number of people you can redeem your miles for, or limit the types of people you can redeem your miles for (for example, direct family members).

Most of the programs restricting who you can redeem for are based in Asia. Let me note some of the most common programs with restrictions below. I’d like to emphasize, though, that this list is by no means exhaustive, so if I’ve missed any major programs, please do let me know.

Let me also mention that this is all about the program you book through, rather than the airline you travel with. For example, while All Nippon Airways Mileage Club has restrictions, you could book an award on All Nippon Airways through a partner program without being subjected to these rules.

There are airlines with just a few airplanes that have loyalty programs, so I’ll be focusing on “major” airlines, which I’ll define as airlines with 50+ planes. With that in mind, below are some of the major programs with restrictions:

With some programs that have these restrictions, you simply have to state what the relationship is between the person redeeming and the traveler. In other situations, you may have to provide proof of that relationship.

In some situations this gets tricky, like if we’re talking about same sex relationships that are recognized in some countries, but not others. For example, Korean Air SkyPass will accept same sex relationships as family if they’re recognized in a foreign country (and there’s documentation to prove it). However, since the South Korean government doesn’t legally recognize same sex relationships, a couple in the country wouldn’t be considered family for these purposes, unless they have a legally recognized relationship abroad.

With a vast majority of airline loyalty programs, you’re free to redeem your miles for friends & family without many restrictions. The best practice is to have the person redeeming the miles out of their account make the reservation.

There are a limited number of airline loyalty programs that limit who you can redeem your miles for. In some cases you’re limited to redeeming miles for direct family members, while in some cases you just have to specify redemption nominees, limiting the overall number of people you can redeem for.

What has your experience been with redeeming airline miles for others?

#6180. Southwest 737 Flew 44 Times Before Wind Damage Was Found

A Southwest Boeing 737 MAX 8 flew 44 times before maintenance crews discovered tail damage that investigators traced to a thunderstorm more than a week earlier. In a final report released Thursday, the National Transportation Safety Board said the damage went undetected through a scheduled maintenance check and caused a standby rudder control unit to operate abnormally.

The damage came to light after Southwest flight 746 experienced unexpected rudder movements on May 25, 2024, while flying from Phoenix to Oakland, California. All 175 passengers and six crew members were uninjured. The aircraft, registered N8825Q, sustained substantial damage.

The NTSB traced the damage to the night of May 16, when the jet was parked in New Orleans, and thunderstorms brought gusts of up to 73 knots, or about 84 mph. Investigators said the wind likely moved the rudder enough to damage ribs inside the vertical stabilizer where the standby rudder control unit was mounted.

At the time, Boeing’s 737 maintenance manual called for a special inspection after an extreme wind event but gave no wind speed at which the check was required. The manual listed signs such as an aircraft moving over its wheel chocks or leaving tire skid marks.

Southwest also lacked a process to notify maintenance control when a parked aircraft had been exposed to extreme winds. The jet flew the next morning without the inspection.

Over the next week, the aircraft completed 38 flights with no reported rudder or yaw damper problems. It then underwent scheduled maintenance in Houston on May 23, including a test of the standby hydraulic system. The procedure required a mechanic at the tail to verify that the rudder moved in response to pedal inputs.

Hangar video showed the rudder moving to the right but failing to move to the left. Investigators said no one was at the tail to verify the movement. Southwest’s maintenance records showed the test was signed off as passed, and the aircraft returned to service. The NTSB could not determine whether the test worsened the existing damage.

On the fourth flight the next day, a crew disconnected the yaw damper after reporting that it was overcorrecting in turbulence. The yaw damper uses the rudder to counter side-to-side motion.

The jet flew one more leg with the system listed as inoperative. It then passed a functional test, and the yaw damper was returned to service before Flight 746.

On the Oakland flight, the captain noticed momentary stiffness in the rudder pedals while turning onto the runway. Shortly after reaching 34,000 feet, he felt what he described as “a small amount of Dutch roll.” Both pilots felt the pedals move, and the oscillations recurred after the crew descended to 32,000 feet.

Flight data showed one episode of rudder and pedal oscillations lasting about 20 seconds, with no significant change in heading or bank angle. Investigators found that the abnormal movement appeared in the data from the first flight after the Houston maintenance check, before crews reported it. They observed it only when the yaw damper was engaged.

Southwest removed the aircraft from service after it landed in Oakland. The airline later inspected the rudder control unit mounting areas across its 737 MAX fleet and found no similar damage. It also added individual mechanic sign-offs to the hydraulic test and set up a process to alert maintenance control after extreme winds. Boeing revised its maintenance manual to require the special inspection at a wind threshold of 65 knots, or 75 mph.
