#6179. How To Combine World Of Hyatt Points Between Accounts For Free

The major hotel loyalty programs all have different policies when it comes to combining points between accounts belonging to different members. I’ve already covered the options and policies for Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at the policy of World of Hyatt.

The good news is that World of Hyatt recently introduced a new way to transfer points to others for free, and I’d argue the program now has among the most generous policies in the industry. Long story short, you can transfer or receive up to 525,000 points per year, and this can all be done online, and at no cost. In this post, I’d like to look more closely at the mechanics of Hyatt points transfers.

World of Hyatt offers a generous feature to allow members to transfer points to others at no cost. Let’s first cover the basic rules for Hyatt points transfers:

It’s worth noting that this system is much better than it used to be. Back in the day combining Hyatt points required completing a form and took days, and you could only combine points in order to have sufficient points for a specific redemption. That policy no longer applies.

The process of transferring World of Hyatt points between members online is straightforward. To start, you can either follow this link, or go to your account overview page, and go to the section that reads “Gift your points more seamlessly.”

On the next page, you’ll want to go to the “Gift points or eligible awards” section, and then click “Gift your points.”

There you’ll first want to select how many points you want to transfer, using the slider.

Then on the next page, you’ll need to enter the account information for the account you want to move points to.

Then you’ll just need to confirm the details, and that’s it! Regarding transfer times, reports suggest transfers take anywhere from a few minutes to several days. It does seem like the more points you transfer, the more likely that it takes days for the transfer to go through. So if you are moving a large chunk of points, don’t be surprised if it takes some time.

What are the benefits to being able to combine points between World of Hyatt accounts? On the most basic level, it allows you to combine points so you have enough for an award stay. In other words, if you have two accounts with 15,000 points each, you can combine the points so you have enough for a one night stay at a hotel costing 30,000 points.

Furthermore, if you’re traveling as multiple people and one person has elite status, there’s value to booking the stay out of their account, so that you could take advantage of World of Hyatt Globalist or World of Hyatt Explorist benefits, for example.

However, thanks to the Guest of Honor program, it’s actually pretty easy to give elite perks to friends and family nowadays. For that matter, even Suite Upgrade Awards and Club Access Awards are transferable nowadays.

Lastly, combining points is also considered “activity” for the purposes of keeping your account alive, so it would reset the expiration of points.

World of Hyatt has a great system for letting members combine and share points. World of Hyatt members can transfer up to 525,000 points per year to other members, with limited restrictions. This is possible online, and typically points transfers happen pretty quickly.

There’s lots of value to this, and I’d say Hyatt’s policy is comparable to Hilton Honors for being the best in the industry.

If you’ve ever combined World of Hyatt points, what was your experience like?

#6177. Which Airlines Fly To The Most Destinations? Some May Surprise You

Recently, I wrote a post about the airlines that fly to the most countries. Turkish Airlines wins that title by a long shot, and has a 30+ country lead over the second most “global” airline.

In this post, I want to address a different but related topic — which airlines serve the most destinations? As you’d expect, this is a very different list. That’s because serving a lot of countries is much easier if you’re an airline that has a lot of service in Europe and Africa, given the number of countries there that are in close proximity. It’s one of the reason that US airlines don’t score that well when it comes to absolute number of countries served, despite otherwise being among the biggest carriers in the world.

However, the list of total number of destinations served is a different story…

I don’t think anyone will be surprised by the three airlines that serve the most destinations. As it currently stands:

This makes sense. In terms of fleets, the “big three” US carriers are among the biggest in the world. A majority of their networks are domestic, which is why the airlines don’t rank that high when it comes to total number of countries served, but they do great when it comes to the total number of destinations served. Note that the number of destinations also includes flights operated by their regional subsidiaries.

I don’t think the order above will surprise anyone. United is of course the most global US airline, and has a very impressive route network, including with ultra long haul flights. Meanwhile American is a massive domestic airline, and has a strong network in Latin America and the Caribbean, which is why it doesn’t appear that far behind United in terms of international destinations. And Delta, ummm, gets a revenue premium.

Just in the interest of being thorough, I’m sure some people are curious how many destinations Southwest serves, since it’s an absolutely massive airline in the United States, though doesn’t operate long haul flights. That number is less impressive — it’s a total of 120 destinations, including 104 domestic destinations and 16 international destinations. That’s because the airline is more about depth of service than breadth of service, and doesn’t have a regional subsidiary.

After US carriers, which airlines otherwise top the list of most destinations served? Most people wouldn’t be surprised to learn that Turkish takes that spot, serving 269 destinations, including 46 domestic destinations and 223 international destinations.

What about after that? Here are the next eight airlines (I think this is where some of the airlines may surprise people):

It’s interesting just how different the airlines on the list are. You have the “big three” Chinese carriers, the “big three” European carriers, and then you have Ryanair and Air Canada.

When you put it all together, below is the chart with the 12 airlines serving the most total destinations.

In the interest of being thorough, for those curious about Gulf carriers, Qatar Airways is in first place among them, serving 175 destinations, so it doesn’t quite make the list. Meanwhile Ethiopian Airlines, as Africa’s most global airline, serves 163 destinations

While Turkish Airlines flies to the most countries of any airline in the world, it doesn’t serve the most destinations. Instead that title goes to United, with the “big three” US carriers taking the three top spots. Then Turkish is in fourth place, and is followed by the “big three” Chinese carriers, the “big three” European carriers, and then also Ryanair and Air Canada.

Are you surprised by any of the airlines serving the most destinations?

#6176. Delta’s 1st A350-1000 Spotted In Full Livery Ahead Of June 2027 Debut

The first Airbus A350-1000 for Delta Air Lines has been spotted in full airline livery at Airbus' facility in Toulouse, France, providing the first public look at the widebody as it approaches completion. Aviation photography outlet Airways Magazine shared the sighting on November 9, with photographs credited to aircraft spotter Eurospot. The aircraft is the first of the A350-1000s Delta has ordered, and its appearance marks a significant milestone ahead of the airline’s planned June 2027 commercial debut.

Delta originally announced the order in January 2024, becoming the first US airline to commit to the largest version of Airbus’ A350 family. The aircraft will become the largest in Delta’s fleet, adding capacity, cargo capability, and a new premium cabin product to its long-haul operation. Although the aircraft has now received its exterior livery, further production and preparation work remains before delivery and entry into passenger service.

The aircraft was photographed at Airbus’ Toulouse manufacturing site, where the A350 family is assembled. The sighting was shared on X, seen below. The completed exterior gives the aircraft its recognizable Delta appearance, although a finished paint scheme does not mean it is ready for delivery.

The first A350-1000 is identified in aviation tracking reports as manufacturer serial number 841. The aircraft still needs to progress through the remaining production and testing stages before Airbus can hand it over to Delta. Engine installation, ground checks, and flight testing are among the steps required before delivery. Delta's official A350 media kit currently lists early 2027 as the start of deliveries, while industry reporting has pointed to June as the intended commercial launch period.

Delta has 20 aircraft on firm order, with the possibility of expanding the commitment through additional options. The airline expects the new variant to support long-haul international and hub-to-hub flying, where its larger capacity and extended range can be put to use.

The updated product will include a flat-bed seat more than six-and-a-half feet (1.98 meters) long, a pillow-top cushion, additional storage, wireless charging, and a 24-inch (60.96 centimeters) high-definition seatback screen. Delta also plans to provide Bluetooth connectivity, USB-C and universal power outlets, and an onboard self-service refreshment area for business-class passengers.

Premium upgrades extend beyond the front cabin as well. Delta says all A350-1000 seats will feature its largest seatback screens, memory foam cushions, and fast, free Wi-Fi. The aircraft will offer four cabin products: Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta Comfort, and Delta Main. Delta describes the aircraft as having a 50% premium seat mix, reflecting its strategy of allocating more capacity to higher-fare cabins.

The carrier is adding a new long-haul powerhouse that will bring more capacity, range, and premium travel options.

The A350-1000 is powered by Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines and has a published range of up to approximately 8,700 nautical miles (16,112 km), depending on configuration. Delta expects the aircraft to deliver more than 20% lower fuel burn per available seat mile compared with the aircraft it is intended to replace. Its larger fuselage also provides additional passenger and cargo capacity compared with the A350-900 already in Delta’s fleet. Simple Flying reported that the airline is expected to debut the new aircraft on routes to Seoul from Atlanta and Detroit.

Delta initially described the aircraft as a key part of its international expansion, rather than simply another option for replacing existing widebodies. Its additional range and premium-heavy layout could support high-demand transpacific services and longer routes that are difficult to operate profitably with smaller aircraft. However, Delta has not publicly confirmed the first destinations for the A350-1000, so specific route assignments remain speculative.

The order also fits into a wider fleet modernization effort. Delta continues to invest in A350-900s and A330neos while preparing to introduce the larger A350 variant. Airbus says the aircraft offers improved fuel efficiency and lower operating costs, giving the carrier more flexibility as it expands international capacity. Its January 2024 order announcement described the A350-1000 as the most capable aircraft in Delta’s future fleet.

#6175. United Unveils 14-Gate Concourse at Dulles

United and the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority unveiled Washington Dulles International Airport’s first new concourse in nearly two decades on Monday. Concourse E opens to passengers Nov. 10, giving United 14 new gates at a hub where its departures have risen 30% since 2022.

The 435,000-square-foot concourse connects directly to the airport’s AeroTrain and has jet bridges at every gate. It can handle both domestic and international flights. The airports authority said existing gates were already fully in use several times a day, with passengers crowding waiting areas and concessions during peak periods.

The concourse also houses United’s second-largest United Club. The nearly 40,000-square-foot lounge seats more than 600 people and increases the airline’s total lounge space at Dulles by about 70%. New concessions include local businesses such as Good Company Doughnuts & Café and Honor Brewing.

“Washington Dulles is a critical part of United’s global network and growth strategy,” United CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement. The carrier currently offers more than 250 daily flights from Dulles to 135 destinations.

United has added six international destinations from the airport this year. It plans to begin international Airbus A321XLR service from Dulles in December with flights to Amsterdam and Dublin, followed by new service to Toulouse, France, and Milan in 2027.

Concourse E is the first phase of the broader Dulles Global Gateway program, which United and the airports authority estimate will involve more than $20 billion in investment. Later work is expected to add gates, expand the main terminal, and build a new U.S. Customs facility. The program also calls for extending the AeroTrain so the airport can eventually retire its mobile lounges.

Target has a gift card deal running through Nov. 14 that gives you a $10 bonus Target gift card on $100 in eligible gift card purchases. If you have the right Target Circle offers, you may be able to stack even more savings.

I just combined three Target deals to earn $30 in Target gift cards and rewards on $200 in Disney e-gift cards I needed anyway. And I did it all from my couch in just a few minutes.

Related: Best credit cards for Target purchases

Until Nov. 14, you can get a $10 bonus Target gift card when you purchase $100 worth of other retailer gift cards available from Target — and yes, this works with e-gift cards, too.

A few of the big-name gift card options this works with include:

Note that this deal does not work with Target gift cards or Amex / Visa-type gift cards.

To get this deal, purchase $100 in eligible gift cards during this sale, and you'll also get a bonus $10 Target gift card emailed to you. In my tests, it works more than once, though likely not indefinitely. I received both the retailer e-gift card and the Target e-gift card within minutes of making the purchase.

In my Target Circle account, I had a deal for $10 in bonus Target Circle Rewards (essentially $10 in Target credit) after making two eligible $50 Target purchases by Nov. 18. Third-party retailer gift cards worked for this deal.

So, when I placed two back-to-back orders for $100 Disney e-gift cards that I can use to pay my Disney Vacation Club dues, I also earned $10 in bonus Target Circle credit on top of the two $10 Target gift cards I received for those orders.

You could stop with the first two steps — or even just the first step — and still have a solid deal.

But another Target Circle deal in my account is making this overall deal even better. That deal is for 25% off one children's toy or book. And one of the items on my daughter's Christmas list is a boxed book series that is sold by Target and is regularly $47.99.

With that 25% off Target Circle deal, the price drops to $35.99 before tax. I used the three $10 Target credits I already had from the gift card purchases and almost fully covered the cost of the gift.

Target even already had the two $10 e-gift cards and the $10 in Target Circle Rewards available at checkout for me to click to use, as shown below, making the whole process very simple.

TPG tip: Start your online purchases through a site such as Rakuten to earn bonus points or cash back on top of the deals you're getting directly through Target.

If you have a Target credit card, you should also get your typical 5% discount on these purchases.

And if you are sad this doesn't include Target gift cards, I'd stay tuned, as in the last few years Target has offered a one- or two-day sale of 10% off Target gift cards for Target Circle members, so it is certainly possible that will return, too.

#6171. Air France Takes Its 60th A220 as A318s Fly On

Air France took delivery of its 60th Airbus A220-300 on Friday, completing the order it placed in 2019 to replace its A318s, A319s and some A320s. The airline’s remaining A318s are still scheduled to fly through March 27, 2027.

The new A220, registered F-HOZJ and named Mimizan, arrived just over five years after Air France put the type into commercial service in October 2021. The airline says its 148-seat A220s now serve 50 destinations and have carried nearly 24 million passengers.

Air France had initially expected to have all 60 A220s in its fleet by 2025. The carrier has also pushed back the end of A318 flying. An August schedule update moved the last planned flights from Nov. 8 to March 27, according to AeroRoutes. The winter schedule includes A318 service from Paris Charles de Gaulle to destinations such as Barcelona, Dublin, and Rome.

Air France took delivery of its first A318 − the smallest A320 family variant − in October 2003 and went on to operate 18, the largest fleet of the type. Three remain active, according to fleet data from Planespotters.net.

The 60th delivery closes out the initial firm order, which also included 30 options and 30 purchase rights. Air France says its 61st A220 and subsequent deliveries will have Wi-Fi installed before entering commercial service. About 85% of the A220s already in service have the equipment, with the remaining installations due by February 2027.

#6169. Can You Redeem Hotel Points For Others? Yes, You Just Have To Know How

One of the nice things about miles & points is being able to share the gift of travel with friends and family. Now, ideally we’d always be able to go along on those journeys, but there are some situations where that’s not practical, for obvious reasons.

Many people wonder if it’s possible to share their points with others, so they can enjoy a hotel stay. This is a great question, so I’d like to take a look at the policy of each individual program. While hotel loyalty programs in some ways offer more flexibility than airline loyalty programs, this isn’t necessarily one of those areas, as you sometimes have to jump through some hoops. For what it’s worth, in a separate post, I’ve addressed whether you can redeem airline miles for others.

All major hotel loyalty programs have some sort of policy for allowing you to redeem your points for others. In some cases you can directly make a reservation for others, while in other cases you need to transfer your points to another member (at no cost).

Let’s break this down by program. Before we start, let me emphasize a couple of important points:

With that out of the way, let’s get into it…

Accor Live Limitless (ALL) is the one hotel loyalty program that doesn’t let you redeem points for others. However, that’s not necessarily a huge loss. Keep in mind that Accor’s program is revenue based, and every 1,000 Accor points gets you €20 toward a hotel stay folio. You can use this for your own rooms or the rooms of those traveling with you, but you can’t just gift them to a third party.

Choice Privileges allows members to redeem points for reward nights for immediate family members, including a spouse, partner, children parents, in-laws, brothers, and sisters.

You can book a reward night for someone else in one of two ways. If you book through your online profile, be sure to include the name of the guest who will be staying in the room in the “Special Request” field. Alternatively, if booking by phone, ask the reservations agent to include the name of the guest in the notes field of the reservation.

Global Hotel Alliance’s GHA Discovery program is one that I’ve become increasingly intrigued by in recent times, given that it’s associated with dozens of independent hotel groups. GHA Discovery doesn’t have points, but instead, has D$, or Discovery Dollars, as they’re called. Each D$ gets you a dollar off an eligible hotel stay.

What’s cool is that you can actually transfer your D$ to others. A transfer can be initiated through the GHA Discovery app, and you just have to enter the recipient’s membership number and last name. You can begin sharing D$ if you’ve been a member of the program for at least 90 days, and you can perform or receive up to two transfers daily, with a minimum of D$100 and a maximum of D$500 per transaction.

The best way to book a Hilton Honors stay for someone else is to simply transfer points to their Hilton Honors account. Hilton has a free points sharing feature, whereby you can transfer points to another Hilton Honors member. You can transfer no more than 500,000 points to another member, and can receive no more than two million points per calendar year from others. That’s the easiest and most foolproof way to go about this.

One alternative is that you could call Hilton Honors to make a reservation, and explain you want to redeem your points for others. They might be able to book the reservation so that the second guest is listed on the reservation, and it’s documented that this is a gift. However, this might not be quite as seamless as just transferring your points to someone else.

One other option people use is that they’ll make a booking in their own name, and then in the “Add guest names” field on the payment page on Hilton’s website or app, they’ll add the name of the guest in the “Additional guests” field. I’ll talk more about this below — while this might work, it’s not really the official method you should use.

IHG One Rewards’ official policy is that you can book a reward night (either with points or free night awards) for someone else by making a booking via IHG’s website, and then adding an additional name to the reservation. In other words, you’re basically just making a reservation for yourself, with a second guest listed.

There’s also a comments section when making an IHG booking, so I’d recommend writing in that section about your intention to gift an award to someone else.

Marriott Bonvoy allows you to redeem your points directly for others, with some restrictions:

Another option is that Marriott Bonvoy lets you combine points between accounts. You can transfer up to 100,000 points per calendar year, and you can receive up to 500,000 points per calendar year. That’s the biggest restriction, as 100,000 points won’t get you very far, at least for an extended luxury hotel stay. Still, this is a feature I find to be useful.

With World of Hyatt there are a couple of practical ways to redeem points for others. The first is that World of Hyatt lets you outright redeem points or free night certificates for others. This can simply be done by contacting World of Hyatt customer service by phone, and they can process this request, or alternatively, you can transfer reward certificates to someone else’s World of Hyatt account.

If you have World of Hyatt Globalist status, keep in mind that you can also earn Guest of Honor certificates. These allow you to essentially share your Globalist perks with a friend or family member, regardless of whether or not they’re traveling with you. You can apply this either to a stay booked with cash or points, and you can either book the Guest of Honor award out of your account, or you can transfer the Guest of Honor certificate to someone else.

You even get one elite night credit in your own account for each certificate that’s gifted to someone else, after it’s redeemed. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there, and it’s a great way to share hotel elite status perks with others.

The other thing to keep in mind is that Hyatt lets you combine points with anyone else at no cost, and this can be done online, through the Hyatt website or app. The person doesn’t have to be related to you, and doesn’t have to live at the same address as you.

The only limitations are that you can transfer up to 525,000 points per year, and can make no more than six points transfers per calendar year. This is probably the easiest option, since the person can just directly redeem out of their own account.

Wyndham Rewards allows members to redeem points for reward nights for friends and family, with no limitations.

This is super straightforward. You can book a stay using points in someone else’s name either directly through the Wyndham Rewards website, or by calling Wyndham Rewards member services. There are no hoops to jump through.

People will often point out “oh, the best way to make a hotel reservation for someone else is to just book it for yourself, and then add the actual guest as the second person on the reservation.” As people view it, the upside is that it lets you earn points, and also share elite perks with others. However, unless explicitly noted above, this isn’t how it’s supposed to work.

It goes without saying that technically you’re only supposed to be able to earn points and take advantage of elite perks if you are actually staying, as the elite member. That’s not to say that this method won’t work sometimes. However, there are some things to keep in mind:

I play by the rules, but there are also plenty of situations where Ford arrives at a hotel before I do (I often take a different and more circuitous routing to get places), and he almost never has issues checking in, and I never even have to go to the front desk.

I’m not making a judgment call here one way or another, but I would only even remotely consider doing this if you and the actual guest both know what you’re doing.

Just about all major hotel loyalty programs let you redeem points for others, though the process varies by program. In some cases you can transfer your points to others, while in other cases you can just redeem a reward for others.

Regardless of which method you choose, just keep in mind that you can’t barter hotel points, and also that your elite perks generally won’t transfer over to others (with the exception of World of Hyatt’s Guest of Honor feature).

If you’ve redeemed hotel points for others, what was your experience like?

Despite these policies, some hotels just do what they want and the corporate office just lets them: Had a situation at an IHG hotel in Ft. Lauderdale where I booked for my parents using a free night certificate. (HI Express & Suites Fort Lauderdale Airport West). I called IHG months in advance to have them list my parents as secondary guests, thinking I had given advance notice and confirmed what was needed. The MORNING OF the reservation, the hotel sends an email saying they don't accept awards booked for others. The email was sent so early that we missed it. When my parents finally arrived late that night after traveling, they were told the reservation would not be honored and that they'd have to pay for the room out of pocket. I escalated this to IHG, asking why this was different from the official policy. No one could show me any hotel policy in writing, despite acknowledging IHG's own corporate policy. IHG refused to do anything and refused to reimburse my parents for the issue. Left an extremely sour taste in my mouth (IHG is ****), and devalued going after hotel loyalty for me.

LHW not allowing awards for a spouse is a strange one, most big chains just need the guest name added and a heads up to the hotel. If you’re booking for parents, emailing the hotel their name and arrival time a few days ahead avoids awkward check-ins, some properties ask for a card for incidentals

"Hotels can also report you to corporate, and you could get in trouble if you’re found to be making a pattern of this" i suppose this is conceivable in theory but these guys can't be arsed to process my room upgrade; i cannot fathom them going through the effort to actually nail down what's going on here and figure out how to report it

Leading Hotels of the World does not allow making award bookings for others. This needs to change. Not even family members? Not even a spouse? Major disincentive for me.

Having elite status with an airline can make a significant difference in your travel experience. Shorter lines, faster service, complimentary upgrades, international lounge access and other benefits can easily make stressful trips more seamless. But these perks don't come without a cost, and United MileagePlus overhauled how members earn status in 2026.

This guide will evaluate United Airlines Premier status and break down the different status tiers, how to earn them and whether their perks are worth the effort for United flyers.

Related: Your guide to United MileagePlus

When you choose to fly United and add your MileagePlus number to your booking, in addition to earning miles, you also earn points toward Premier status. Depending on your status tier, elite perks range from complimentary first-class upgrades on most domestic flights (depending on availability) to earning bonus miles that can be redeemed for future travel.

United currently has two ways for members to climb the Premier status ladder:

PQPs are based on a combination of your spending on flights and on eligible United credit cards.

Starting in 2027, PQPs will become the sole elite status metric. As part of those changes, top-tier Premier 1K status will also become even tougher to earn.

The old metrics are still in place through the end of 2026, so we will cover both options.

Related: Why United's elite status changes are bad news for many flyers

Anyone can create a United MileagePlus account for free online. Once you take off on your elite status expedition, you’ll have four official elite status tiers to work toward:

There’s also an unpublished exclusive tier called Global Services, which can only be achieved by flying 4 million miles or receiving a personal invitation.

Here's an overview of what you'll need to earn each status tier before and after the changes.

One requirement that is not changing: You must take at least four flights operated by United or United Express in a calendar year to qualify for any status tier.

When you reach any elite status tier, it is valid for the remainder of the calendar year, the entirety of the following year, and the first month of the year after. For instance, if you reach status requirements anytime in 2026, you will hold the status through Jan. 31, 2028. So, the sooner you earn elite status, the longer you can enjoy the benefits.

Now, let's dive into how to earn PQPs (and, through the end of 2026, PQFs).

Related: Earn MileagePlus miles with United’s airline, hotel and credit card partners

The classic way to earn PQPs is via your spending on flights. The earning rate depends on which airline operates the flight and whether you book it with cash or miles. PQPs are awarded to the passenger, not the person who buys the ticket.

Earn 1 PQP for every 6 award miles on MileagePlus partner airlines, up to a maximum of 500 PQPs per flight in economy and premium economy and 1,000 PQPs per flight in first and business class.

You can also earn PQPs through spending on United's cobranded credit cards. None of these cards provide complimentary elite status, but you’ll earn PQPs on everyday purchases (up to a certain amount), and some cards offer PQPs as part of the welcome bonus.

The information for the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Although United is making it harder to earn status in 2027, it is also giving existing elite members a boost toward next year's status. If you hold elite status and an eligible United credit card (or open one by Dec. 31, 2026), you will receive 5% of the PQPs required for your current status level at the start of 2027:

Related: The ultimate guide to earning elite status with United cards

The perks of United loyalty get more and more appealing as you climb the Premier status ladder. You'll also earn more MileagePlus miles on United purchases as you gain status, though the number of miles you'll earn also depends on whether you hold a United credit card.

United's lowest elite tier confers benefits such as:

When you reach the Gold tier, you'll receive all the perks of Silver as well as:

At Platinum, you can enjoy all the benefits of Gold, plus:

Members who get all the way to the top are rewarded with the Platinum benefits listed above, in addition to:

On top of the various metrics for earning miles and status, United MileagePlus awards something called PlusPoints, a separate currency available only to Platinum and 1K members.

PlusPoints were originally used for seat upgrades, though these have become harder to get in recent years as demand has skyrocketed. That’s why United introduced several new ways to redeem your PlusPoints, including for bonus miles, PQPs, TravelBank cash and gifting Premier status to other MileagePlus members.

Related: When does airline elite status expire?

Elite status can certainly make travel more comfortable and convenient. If you regularly travel with United or its partner airlines and/or spend significantly on a cobranded credit card, you may find it relatively easy to earn Premier status. And it can be a savvy way to maximize your travel.

Plus, this means you’ll also be earning plenty of United miles, which you can redeem for United award flights — all while enjoying your elite status benefits.

However, it’s not worth pursuing status when you can’t enjoy the benefits you’ve worked hard to earn. Be sure to consider United’s route map, its presence at your home airport and how easy it is to get to your desired destinations. If United and its partner airlines don’t fly where you live or where you want to travel, you won’t get much use from Premier status. You may be better off pursuing status with a different program, such as Delta SkyMiles or American AAdvantage.

Finally, remember that Premier status does not provide domestic lounge access when traveling with United. If this benefit is important to you, consider applying for the , which provides United Club access and perks such as two free checked bags and Premier Access travel services.

Related: Complete guide to United’s fare classes

Earning elite status, especially a top-tier status like Premier 1K, is no easy feat and requires countless hours on planes and thousands of dollars spent. Understanding the cost and perks of United’s elite status is important to determine if it is right for you — especially since United is making status harder to earn in 2027.

#6167. United Adds Four Domestic Routes

United added four domestic routes to its 2027 schedule last week, a spokesperson confirmed to AirlineGeeks. Three of the new flights will depart from the carrier’s California hubs.

The airline will begin seasonal service from Los Angeles and San Francisco to Traverse City, Michigan, on June 19. Both routes will operate with Boeing 737-800s on Saturdays through Sept. 11, with additional flights on select Wednesdays. The additions will give Cherry Capital Airport nonstop service to all seven of United’s mainland hubs.

These additional routes were first flagged as part of last week’s Cirium Diio schedule update.

United will also fly year-round between San Francisco and Jacksonville, Florida, beginning March 29. The carrier will operate the route on Mondays and Fridays with a Boeing 737-800. Jacksonville Aviation Authority CEO Mark VanLoh said the Bay Area was “one of our largest unserved markets.”

San Francisco will become United’s sixth hub with nonstop service from Jacksonville.

The first of the four routes will start March 4, when United adds twice-daily flights between Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and Washington Dulles. The service restores a connection previously flown by Southern Airways Express. Southern’s Dulles flights ended in June when SkyWest began flying between Lancaster and Chicago O’Hare under the United Express banner as part of a federal Essential Air Service contract.

#6166. 5 Reasons Premium Economy Can Beat Business Class On Value

Ultimately, what is better value for money or 'worth it' is a matter of personal opinion and experience. No article can definitively inform readers that it's better to book one class of airfare over another. Travelers have dramatically different means, expectations, and need for sleep and rest. Some will view flying as a core part of their vacation and travel experience that has an enormous impact on their overall trip; others will view it as little more than a subway ride during which they will zone out and wait until it's over.

That said, there are some reasons why it may be more prudent to purchase a premium economy fare over a business class fare. It can also be noted that airlines deliberately construct premium economy to avoid this choice. The choice airlines seek to impose is encouraging economy passengers to upgrade to premium economy. Premium economy is set up to avoid passengers downgrading from business. Here are some reasons why premium economy may be a better choice for some passengers.

The most obvious factor in choosing premium economy over business is that it is much more affordable, and the price gap can be huge. Realistically, this is the only factor stopping the vast majority of passengers from flying in higher-class cabins. As a general rule of thumb, premium economy costs around 50–120% more than economy, while business costs around 100–200% of that and 2.5-4 times that of economy.

This is a very general rule of thumb, and there are massive variations throughout the industry. The price difference varies by airline, region, route, timing, demand, whether the airfare is one-way or return, and many other factors. Sometimes these factors can significantly narrow the price gap between premium and business, and at other times they open the gap massively.

The jump from premium to business can be two to three and a half times. During the jet age, flying carried considerable prestige and was something wealthier people did. Low-income people struggled to afford to fly, and when they did, it was a big deal for them. Today, flying has lost much of its prestige as a status symbol, with travelers focusing more on the destination than the class.

The trend in recent years has been towards premium economy, which is seen as 'good enough' for most passengers, including wealthier passengers. But this is an assessment that often changes with age. Older travelers can be set back days or even half their holiday if they miss a night's sleep. For them, fully reclining business seats can be the difference between a good holiday and not. For younger passengers, premium is often just fine.

As stated above, one of the main practical benefits of business class is the opportunity to get some sleep on a flat bed during overnight and longer-haul flights. This is generally more important for elderly passengers than younger passengers. It follows that some of the appeal of business class falls away for daytime and shorter flights.

On a daytime flight, passengers do not need to worry about losing a night's sleep and so spending the next few days recovering. The 'eight-hour rule' holds that on daytime flights shorter than eight hours, premium economy can offer enough comfort to rest without paying several times more for business class.

A passenger flying a daytime three-hour flight on Air New Zealand's widebody 787 fleet to Australia would typically not need business class to arrive feeling fresh. Air New Zealand's premium economy is well suited to these routes, without the need to upgrade. Yet another consideration is the direction of travel.

Generally, the eastbound flight is more important to sleep on, particularly when traveling between Asia and Europe or North America and Europe. This is due to jet lag and the impact of travel on the circadian rhythm. As a rule, it's better to put more effort into sleeping on a flight bound from London to Singapore than from Singapore to London.

One of the best arguments for purchasing premium economy for those who are willing to spend extra is that it can be a cheaper way to fly business class. This is a great way to get a discount on business class. Purchase an upgradable premium economy fare and then wait for promotions and special offers to upgrade to business.

Some airlines allow passengers to place bids for upgrading to business. Often, the original premium fare plus the subsequent upgrade bid are considerably lower than purchasing the business class fare outright. As a benchmark, passengers often save 20–40% of the business fare, although the variance is large; sometimes there are no savings at all. Depending on the airline and passengers' loyalty status, upgrades can be paid in cash or in loyalty miles.

This is a strategy mostly relevant to those who are willing to fly premium but will take the opportunity to upgrade given a sweet deal. It is not necessarily a good option for those committed to flying business. There is no guarantee offers will be forthcoming or that the airline will open a bidding window. Upgrading to business is only an option if there are empty seats that the airline wants to sell.

If the airline's algorithm finds that there are empty business class seats and that there will not be enough new bookings before the flight to sell them, then the system may seek to sell them by offering upgrades to already booked passengers. If the algorithm estimates that the business cabin will fully book out with full-fare paying passengers, then no offers are likely to materialize. Put another way, booking premium to upgrade to business is a risk.

The 8-hour flight rule explains when Premium Economy beats Business Class on price, comfort, sleep, and corporate travel value.

On some routes, airlines, and configurations, the quality gap can noticeably narrow. This is especially true when the business seat is a recliner instead of a flat bed. These are often found on domestic and short-haul international routes. One example is Qantas's domestically-configured A321XLR on its Brisbane to Manila route. These have 20 recliner seats with no seatback screens. One of the big attractions of business class is a flat bed for some shut-eye; when the seat is instead of a recliner, it is less appealing.

There are also routes where airlines offer exceptional premium economy options. Examples include Japan Airlines and EVA Air, both of which offer 42-inch (107 cm) seat pitch and 19-inch (48 cm) wide seats. These are found on specific aircraft, so it is always important to check the route, which aircraft it is, and what its configuration is. Japan Airlines also undercuts the appeal of business by offering Sakura Lounge access on eligible international premium economy itineraries (more below).

Qantas Domestic Business Class Vs. JAL Premium Economy

Comparing these two airlines, Qantas' Airbus A321XLR domestic business class recliner is much closer to a long-haul premium economy seat than it is to a conventional international business class seat, even though it is used on international trunk routes. In some respects, it can be argued that JAL's 777-300ER premium economy seat has the advantage. It offers a greater seat pitch, deeper recline, and a personal entertainment screen.

Another factor that may tip the balance in or out of the favor of premium economy is lounge access. After all, benefits of higher classes are not restricted to the airplane; they are also experienced at the airport. Complimentary lounge access with a premium economy ticket is rare, but it does happen. Two of the most notable exceptions are Japan Airlines (again) and its rival, ANA.

South America's LATAM also offers lounge access on international premium economy itineraries. LATAM states, "When traveling in the Premium Economy cabin, on international flights only, you will have access to the LATAM lounges located at Santiago, Bogotá, Guarulhos, Ezeiza, and Miami airports."

SAS offers it with select premium flights within Scandinavia. Note that access, even in these cases, may depend on the sub-class of premium economy ticket purchased. Japan Airlines allows Sakura Lounge access with qualifying premium economy bookings, but passengers cannot bring along a complimentary guest, and it is not necessarily available on partner-operated codeshares.

There are a few other airlines that may have some lounge access, such as Air Canada Rouge and Air Astana. There may be others, but it is uncommon. Always check the terms and conditions of the lounge access in advance, as it may not be available on some routes.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6165. Air Algerie Business Class Airbus A330neo Review: Utterly Awful

For the first long haul segment of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A330-900neo business class on the 6hr50min flight from Montreal (YUL) to Algiers (ALG). I had heard almost entirely negative things about Air Algerie, which intrigued me, naturally! Well, now that I’ve flown Air Algerie I can confirm that everything I heard was true, and then some.

I don’t want to be dramatic — obviously flying business class is better than economy — but honestly, just about everything sucked. On the plus side, the seats as such were fine, but that’s where the good news ends. The food was not good, and took an insanely long amount of time to be served. There were no amenity kits… or menus… or meal choice… or alcohol… or diet soda. If the crew were any more indifferent, they would’ve been invisible.

I wouldn’t fly Air Algerie again unless I absolutely had to, which… I can’t imagine that’ll ever be the case. Honestly, Air Algerie made me yearn for my recent flight on Turkmenistan Airlines, which was at least fun.

Air Algerie is a pretty isolated airline, which perhaps reflects Algeria overall — the country just isn’t interested in visitors, and getting a visa requires jumping through hoops.

So Air Algerie doesn’t have any useful partnerships when it comes to earning or redeeming miles. As a result, booking a cash ticket is just about the only option, unless you’re a frequent flyer with the airline. Air Algerie tends to have rather steep business class fares, despite its lackluster product.

However, I did manage to find a rather attractive one-way business class fare. I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

The first segment was operated by an Airbus A330-900neo, while the second segment was operated by an Airbus A320 that was wet leased from Avion Express.

I had flown into Montreal the same day from Miami (MIA) on Air Canada Rouge, so I had an extended layover. I was at the Air Algerie check-in counter before it opened at 12:30PM, and there was already quite the queue of passengers waiting. Unsurprisingly, and as is very common for North Africa flights, people had a ton of checked bags.

It took me around 30 minutes to get checked in, since there was one counter for business class, and there were half a dozen people in front of me. At first I was asked if I had a visa for Algeria, though I explained I was in transit, which seemed to catch the check-in agent off guard. Air Algerie is clearly targeted at the local community, and doesn’t see much international connecting traffic.

Security was a breeze, and Air Algerie sends its business class passengers to the National Bank Lounge, which is the contract lounge in the international portion of the terminal. I won’t do a full review, but it was actually a pretty pleasant facility, with plenty of seating, lots of natural light, and it wasn’t very crowded.

The food selection was pretty average, with a handful of hot options, plus cheese, cold cuts, etc. There was coffee, tea, wine, beer, and soft drinks. I made the mistake of saving my hunger and thirst for onboard the Air Algerie flight!

My Air Algerie flight was departing from gate A58, with boarding scheduled for 3:10PM, a full hour before departure. I was at the gate early enough to see the inbound aircraft arrive, and goodness, what a stunner it was!

The Montreal route is primarily served by an A330neo with the registration code 7T-VLB, which is in a special livery celebrating the country’s football team. Looking at the plane was honestly the best part of the flight experience, unfortunately.

The boarding area got very full before departure, with lots of passengers in wheelchairs, and lots of crowding around the gate. Boarding ended up starting at 3:20PM, with those needing extra time, as well as business class passengers, being invited to board first.

I can’t describe how excited I was to step onboard, as I always love trying new airlines! I wasn’t fully prepared for the level of indifference shown by every part of the experience, though.

Before I get into this review, I should mention that Air Algerie has recently started taking delivery of Airbus A330-900neos as part of its fleet modernization initiative. However, the airline isn’t just taking delivery of these planes factory fresh, but has also acquired a couple secondhand from Air Belgium, which went out of business in 2024.

Air Algerie maintained the Air Belgium interiors — they also have staggered seats, but it’s a slightly different configuration. I boarded through the second door on the left, and then turned left into the business class cabin.

Business class takes up the entire space between the first and second set of doors, and consists of 30 seats, spread across eight rows, in a 1-2-1 configuration. These seats are from the Stelia Aerospace Solstys line, so they’re typical last generation staggered business class seats. When it comes to the seat details, they have 44″ of pitch, 21″ of width, and convert into 77″ flat beds.

On the plus side, it’s really easy to photograph Air Algerie cabins, since crews are nowhere to be seen. 😉

If you’re traveling with someone, you may appreciate the sets of center seats in odd numbered rows, as these are “honeymoon” seats, which allow you to sit really close to your companion. Meanwhile in even numbered rows, the seats in the center section are further from one another and really close to the aisles, so those would be my least preferred seats in this configuration.

Along the windows, seats alternate between being closer to the aisle and closer to the windows. In odd numbered rows, seats are closer to the aisle. What I particularly don’t like about these staggered seats is just how exposed some of them are to the aisle, as you really have no separation.

In even numbered rows, seats are closer to the windows, and these are the best seats in the house, in terms of offering some separation from the aisle, and an easy view out the window.

I assigned myself seat 6A, the window seat on the left side in the third to last row.

These staggered seats have a console to the side of the seat, and on the side of that is a panel with seat controls, an entertainment controller, and a small armrest.

There’s an exposed storage area above the panel, where you can store things, or even hang the headphones. As you can see, the seat just wasn’t well maintained, and also wasn’t clean, as it also needed a good wiping down.

In terms of charging, the AC power outlet and USB-A outlet were located underneath the seat. There was no USB-C or wireless charging, unsurprisingly.

Looking at the front of the seat, the tray table is stored behind the seat in front, and can be extended by being lowered and then moved over. One of the nice things about these tray tables is that you can angle them away from you, so it’s possible to get up during the meal service.

The entertainment system is in a fixed position and is located above the ottoman. The monitor here was 16″ and was touchscreen, but wasn’t terribly high definition.

As much as there are many aspects of this seat I don’t love, I do like how big the footwell is, which is great for those of us with big feet. It’s not necessarily that comfortable when you’re laying sideways in terms of space for knees, but still, there was a great amount of space here.

One other interesting note is that there were no overhead bins in the center of the cabin, so the overhead bins along the windows got pretty full, since the A330neo doesn’t have huge bins. On top of that, there were no individual air nozzles above seats, sadly. That was a problem on this flight, given how warm the cabin was kept.

All-in-all, Air Algerie’s business class hard product is okay. The cabin maintenance could definitely use some help, but honestly, this is the least of Air Algerie’s problems.

The Air Algerie business class entertainment system on the A330neo is pretty awful. For one, there’s not even a map feature. I’m sorry, I’m not sure the last time I flew an airline with seat back entertainment that didn’t have a map feature. What’s going on there?

The system did have some movies, TV shows, and music, but it was a really lackluster selection.

In total, there were 100 movies and 36 TV shows, but it definitely felt like the number of “popular” options was limited.

The airline presumably went with the cheapest entertainment package available. For example, when it comes to sitcoms, there was one episode of “Fresh Off The Boat,” and it was the pilot episode from 2015. Yikes.

When it comes to Wi-Fi, that’s something that just isn’t offered by Air Algerie. Funny enough, these ex-Air Belgium A330neos have Wi-Fi installed, but the airline just chooses not to use the system. So expect that you’re going to disconnect when flying with Air Algerie.

When it comes to amenities in Air Algerie business class, they were also very limited. The highlight was the pillow and blanket, which were at the seat upon boarding, but not exactly very nicely presented.

Anyway, this was the highlight of the amenities, and while they were nothing amazing, they were at least decent.

Headphones were also passed out well after takeoff, though the quality of them was very poor. This was closer to what you’d expect in economy than business class.

There were no amenity kits, or anything else to speak of. I don’t remember the last overnight business class flight I’ve taken where I wasn’t offered an amenity kit?

Despite the very drawn out boarding process, the crew was nowhere to be seen for most of boarding. Finally at 4:10PM, right at departure time, they came around with pre-departure drinks. There was no “hello” or “welcome onboard,” but instead, just the tray being held out with orange juice or water. At least it was served in glassware… yay?

Boarding this Air Algerie A330neo took an incredibly long time. Every seat was taken (business class seemed to be occupied mostly by operational upgrades plus friends and family). There was just endless confusion, and the crew’s only involvement with things was to occasionally check on people they knew and have chats with them, while everyone else was ignored.

Boarding was also rough because it seemed like the APU was broken, so the cabin was incredibly hot. During boarding, I had asked the flight attendant if I could use the lavatory (I try to do that as a courtesy, even though it showed as unoccupied), and she responded “wait.” I checked with her again some time later, and she again said “wait.” I didn’t end up getting to go before departure… oh well!

Our departure time came and went, and about 20 minutes later I asked a flight attendant if we were delayed. She didn’t understand my question, but after rephrasing, her answer was “no.” The door ended up closing at 4:35PM, 25 minutes behind the scheduled departure time.

At that point the manual safety demonstration began, which was exclusively performed in French and Arabic, and not in English. In fairness, I was probably the only person onboard who didn’t have French or Arabic as my first language. I should also mention there were no safety checks during taxi — some people had their seats reclined, plenty of people still had their (glass) pre-departure beverages, and the guy across from me didn’t even have his seatbelt on.

We began our pushback at 4:40PM, and then at 4:50PM we began our taxi.

While taxiing (and turning a corner), the captain made his welcome onboard announcement at 4:55PM, telling us “this is captain, good morning, taking off shortly.” Okay, we’ll ignore the “morning” part (I’ll assume it just means he’s well rested!), but I assume at Air Algerie the captain is also the one taxiing, right? If so, that’s a lot of multitasking, especially when you’re actively turning.

But hey, credit where credit’s due, this guy was good at turning corners. When we got to runway 24R at 5PM and were cleared for takeoff, we didn’t slowly make the turn and then accelerate. Instead, we started accelerating pretty aggressively in our turn, and were going over 15 knots, while turning at a 90 degree angle. Seriously, check the Flightradar24 data.

We had a very powerful takeoff roll and the captain pulled up on the sidestick as if we were in a fighter jet. The views on the climb out were gorgeous — what a lovely afternoon!

We made a sharp turn after takeoff, and had some nice views of the airport thanks to that.

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. A little while later, we started to get a beautiful sunset view as well.

Dinner was served after takeoff in Air Algerie business class, but my gosh, what a bad and drawn out meal it was. I can deal with bad food or slow service, but bad food, bad drinks, and slow service? BLEH. The first thing to understand is that there were no menus or choices. You’re just served stuff, and it’s a “take it or leave it” situation.

Service began 50 minutes after takeoff, when warm towels were distributed.

Then around 15 minutes later, tablecloths were handed out. These felt more like large, flimsy napkins, than actual tablecloths, but whatever, no biggie.

Another 10 minutes later, the first course was served. The actual food was a little smoked salmon, some egg, some olives, etc. It didn’t taste good at all, but what was worse was the presentation. It’s as if they just threw a bunch of packaging on the tray, and put zero effort into how it’s presented.

I couldn’t help but do their job for them, and make it look a little nicer, because it’s just embarrassing. Oh, and bread is just served by hand out of the basket. Nice.

I kind of loved the Air Algerie branding on the cutlery, but that’s the same cutlery you have to use for the entire meal. For that matter, the cutlery was downright sticky when I removed it from the packaging, so clearly it just hadn’t been cleaned properly.

Drinks were brought out separately from the meal, but they might as well not have bothered. I didn’t realize that Air Algerie is a “dry” airline — it hadn’t even made my list of airlines that are dry. As it turns out, this is only a fairly recent development, as the airline switched to being dry a few years ago.

It’s not only that they don’t have alcohol, but they don’t even have any diet sodas. They have juice or full calorie soda. There was also a huge language barrier here:

“Drink?”“Do you have wine?”“Soda, juice.”“Do you have Diet Coke?”“Coke?”“No, Diet Coke.”“What?”“Coke Zero? Diet Pepsi? Pepsi Max?”*stares blankly*“I’ll have a water, please.”*serves me Sprite*

Another 15 minutes later the main course was served. Again, there was no option, and it seemed to be some sort of a swordfish, or something. As someone who typically loves fish (and orders it way too often on planes), I found this to be way overcooked, dry, and completely tasteless. If you’re not going to offer people a choice of meals, what a random thing to serve!

After an additional pause, the crew came around with cheese plates. I mean, they certainly serve quite a quantity of food, the issue is just that there are no choices, and none of it is actually good. They also don’t actually clear any plates. They just keep bringing more and more food, and if your tray is overflowing, so be it (for the below picture, I had placed the other stuff from the tray over on the side console).

Next up, two whole apples were served, which… I mean, I can’t blame them for the excessive amount of food, serving cheese, fruit, and dessert. But still, this very much feels like an afterthought. I also couldn’t help but wonder if those apples had been washed, given that we’re talking about an airline that serves bread by hand.

Lastly there was a little dessert tart trio. I tried to order a tea without caffeine, but that was a challenge:

“Coffee or tea?”“Do you have any tea without caffeine?”“Coffee or tea?”“Tea please, but no caffeine.”“Coffee?”“Tea, please.”

The entire meal service took close to three hours. Nothing about it was good. The food wasn’t good. The service was terrible. I mean, everything was just so poorly timed. There was never even the offer for more drinks (even just bottled water), and when I did ask, it took them 15 minutes and multiple reminders to actually get some more water.

I just don’t get it. As another example, they served the cheese plates, and then 10 minutes later they came around with more bread, after just about everyone had finished their cheese course. I’m exhausted writing about this. I need a drink.

The Air Algerie A330neo business class lavatory is located at the very front of the cabin. One lavatory really isn’t enough for a full business class cabin plus the crew, so there was often a wait. While there are two lavatories behind the cabin, they’re shared with economy passengers, so there’s usually a line.

The lavatories were fine. Toward the end of the flight they definitely weren’t clean, but to be honest, I’ve seen much worse lavatories on airlines in the region, so I’m hardly going to complain.

By the time the meal service was complete, we had well under four hours remaining to Algiers. So I reclined my seat into bed mode, and tried to get a bit of rest. The bed was okay, and again, compared to the rest of the experience, it was one of the better things.

The issue is how hard it was to actually get rest on this flight. The lights were fully on until after the meal service was complete, so at that point it was under four hours until our arrival in Algiers.

Then the cabin lights were once again fully turned on exactly two hours before arrival. So for those keeping track at home, on a 6hr50min flight, the lights were dimmed for around 1hr50min. I’m not sure I actually slept for a minute. The cabin was really warm, and with the lack of individual air nozzles, I just couldn’t get comfortable.

It absolutely boggles my mind why the crew has to start the pre-landing service a full two hours before landing, when the extent of the breakfast is a single tray with a small side of fruit, a small piece of cake, and a croissant. Seriously, this is what everyone is being woken up two hours before landing for?!

Credit where credit’s due, the drip coffee with milk was drinkable, and perhaps the culinary highlight of the flight. Getting a refill was beyond my abilities, but I sure did savor that one cup!

I understand that North African countries are often known for warm hospitality in a non-transactional setting, where there’s a genuine warmth and generosity to hospitality. Clearly that doesn’t apply in a transactional setting, though, and certainly not on Air Algerie.

I don’t want to say the crew was rude — that wouldn’t be fair, and I didn’t even communicate with them enough to draw that conclusion. They actually seemed to be very nice in how they chatted with their friends who were in the cabin.

As a customer, though, everything about the service was terrible. The crew had no warmth, no attentiveness, they were incredibly disorganized and slow, and the service flow just made no sense. If I were to train a crew on how to provide good service in business class, I’d have them experience this flight, and then have them do exactly the opposite. I think I’ve ragged on them enough.

You’ve gotta love how the refreshing towel has Air Algerie’s logo, and then says “Always caring for you.” If this is what care looks like, I’d love to see what not being cared for looks like!

I was excited when my Air Algerie flight was slowly coming to an end. At around 4:20AM Algiers time the seatbelt sign was turned on, and the crew prepared the cabin for landing. Now, that didn’t actually involve doing any security checks, but they made sure passengers were aware there would be no more service.

We ended up touching down at 4:50AM, and it must’ve been one of the smoothest touchdowns of my life, as you could barely feel it. From there, we had a short five minute taxi to a remote stand, where we pulled in at 4:55AM.

It’s very odd how an airport that has so many empty gates and that’s rather underutilized sends its “flagship” aircraft to remote stands, but whatever.

Upon deplaning, there wasn’t so much as a “goodbye” from the crew. There also wasn’t any priority deplaning for business class, or a separate business class bus. It was quite a long drive to the terminal, and we got there at 5:15AM, where my interesting transit experience started…

I highly recommend flying Air Algerie business class… if you want to be reminded how every other airline doesn’t actually suck that much, by comparison. Air Algerie’s A330neo business class hard product is okay, and is the least of the issues.

The problem is everything else, from the completely indifferent crew, to the unnecessarily drawn out service, to the lack of meal options, amenity kits, menus, diet soda, alcohol, etc., to the subpar entertainment and lack of Wi-Fi… the list goes on and on. And that says nothing of the bizarre elements of the flight, like no English safety demos, no safety checks before takeoff or landing, etc.

What’s sad is that I would’ve actually had a more favorable impression of the flight if they just said “this is a sleeper flight, and we have no inflight service.” Truly, no service would’ve been better than this. I’m happy I had the chance to fly Air Algerie, but you know, I think I’m good for the time being!

What do you make of Air Algerie’s business class?

Is a 15 knot 90 degree turn perhaps stretching the safety of the parts ya roll on? If that is what the cabin looks like, how is the engine/software/moving parts maintenance? The service was horrendous. The only thing missing was a cigar smoker in front of you!

Loved this review but they did manage to get you from A to B --safely. All that matters. Let's not forget your last trip with Royal Jordanian to HK...

Hypothetically speaking, how would you rate this flight if all else remained same but the seats had a door? 4.5 stars?

I am not very knowledgeable but there are sometimes reasons for a forceful takeoff. I do remember reading that on certain types of equipment, every now and then a takeoff should be full power. There also might have been weather or traffic issues that made this decision necesary.

#6163. Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card Review: Strong Bonus Categories, Weak Overall Value

Both American Express and Chase issue co-branded Marriott credit cards, meaning consumers have lots of options to choose from. This is my Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card review, as I’d like to take a look at whether this Marriott credit card is worth it.

Personally I don’t think that the Bonvoy Bevy Card is Marriott’s most compelling credit card option, and given how the offers on some cards are mutually exclusive, I think there’s a better strategy. However, everyone should decide for themselves, based on their own situation. Let’s look at the value proposition of the Bonvoy Bevy Card, including the welcome offer, annual fee, return on spending, and perks, so you can make your own decision.

Link: Learn more about the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

Before I get into the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card review, let me give you a high-level summary of the card’s main features and perks:

I also put together my list of the top pros and cons for the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card:

When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are major factors that people consider. After all, this determines how much value you can get upfront, and also how much this card will cost you in the long run. With that in mind, let’s take at the bonus and fee details for the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card currently has a welcome offer where you can earn 85,000 Bonvoy bonus points after spending $5,000 within the first six months. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Bonvoy points are worth 0.7 cents each, meaning I value the welcome offer at $595.

This is the standard welcome offer on the card, though we’ve definitely seen better bonuses in the past. For example, in the past I recall seeing a bonus of up to 125,000 points plus a $150 statement credit upon completing minimum spending. So it could be worth waiting to apply to see if a higher offer comes back around.

If applying for the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card, Amex’s general application restrictions apply, and on top of that, there are some additional restrictions for Marriott credit card eligibility.

The most important thing to understand is that you are eligible for this card, including the welcome offer, if you have the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more). However, you aren’t eligible for the welcome offer if you have the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more).

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card has a $250 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and you can add authorized users at no extra cost.

Among Marriott personal credit cards, this card has the second-highest annual fee (there are also no annual fee and $95 annual fee options), with the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) being the only card with a higher annual fee — it has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees).

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card is supposed to be the best credit card for actually earning points, so the card has a pretty decent rewards structure. The card offers the following return on spending, all with no foreign transaction fees:

Ultimately these are just about the best bonus categories you’ll see on a co-branded Marriott credit card. However:

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card offers a variety of perks for being a cardmember. Some perks are offered just for having the card, while other perks require spending or other activity. Let’s go over the details, in no particular order.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card offers 1,000 bonus points per paid eligible stay with Marriott, which is a perk that’s unique to this card. You need to pay for your stay with the card to be eligible, and only paid stays booked directly with Marriott qualify (so third party bookings and award stays don’t count). Bonus points will post within six weeks of an eligible stay.

For the very frequent Marriott guest, this has the potential to be pretty useful, especially if you make frequent, short stays. Based on my valuation of Bonvoy points, this is like an incremental return of roughly $7 per paid stay.

Unfortunately, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card doesn’t offer a free night award just for being a cardmember. Rather, you can earn a free night award valid at a property costing up to 50,000 points when you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

It’s also possible to top off Marriott free night awards with up to 25,000 additional points to redeem at more expensive properties. This means you could redeem a free night award plus 25,000 points to stay at a hotel costing 75,000 points per night.

This is a disappointing aspect of the card, as several other Marriott credit cards don’t require you to spend any amount to earn such a certificate.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card offers complimentary Marriott Bonvoy® Gold Elite status for as long as you’re a cardmember. This is better than nothing, but don’t get too excited. Marriott Gold status offers perks like:

Just for having the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card you receive 15 elite nights toward status annually. This can help you if you’re looking to earn a higher elite tier, like Marriott Bonvoy® Platinum Elite status, Titanium Elite status or Ambassador Elite status, and it can also help you with earning Choice Benefits (like Nightly Upgrade Awards).

It’s also worth noting that you can stack the 15 elite night credits on this card with elite night credits earned on a Marriott business credit card. That gets you a long way toward the Marriott Bonvoy Platinum Elite status requirement of 50 nights.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card offers some extra protections both when you’re traveling and making purchases with your card. These include:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Looking at the card in isolation, there’s a case to be made for getting the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card, especially if you’re a very frequent Marriott guest. If you put all your Marriott spending on the card, you’d earn 1,000 bonus points per stay, 6x points on Marriott spending, and you could earn a free night award after spending $15,000.

But even if you’re set on a Marriott credit card, there are better options, as I view it, especially given how some cards are (somewhat) mutually exclusive, at least when it comes to welcome offers.

If you ask me, the Bonvoy Bevy Card is the weakest card in the Marriott credit card portfolio in terms of value for the annual fee, and I think you’re much better off going for the higher annual fee card.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card (learn more) has a $650 annual fee, and offers:

As I see it, the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card’s annual fee easily pays for itself, between the dining credit, anniversary free night award, elite status, Priority Pass™ membership, and more.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card (learn more) has a lower annual fee of $95, but in my opinion it offers significantly more value than the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card. Its perks include:

The free night award alone makes this card worth it. You get this once every account anniversary year, and you can top off the free night with an additional 25,000 points. Even though the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card’s free night award is valid for rooms that cost up to 50,000 points, it’s not worth spending $15,000 on the card in a year just to earn it.

If you’re not actually that committed to the Marriott Bonvoy ecosystem, there are lots of other great cards to consider. In particular, these are cards with relatively reasonable annual fees and great rewards structures, and they’re very well rounded:

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card has a $250 annual fee, and offers some solid bonus categories, plus 1,000 Bonvoy bonus points per stay. The card also offers Bonvoy Gold Elite status, 15 elite nights annually for being a cardmember, and a free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

Ultimately, I’d say this is a pretty weak card, especially compared to the rest of Marriott’s card portfolio. It doesn’t offer statement credits or an automatic free night award to offset the annual fee, and you can’t even spend your way to a higher status level on this card. Personally, I’d much rather get the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card or Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card, as I think the cards represent a better overall value.

What do you make of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Card?
