#6162. PlanNet Sells The Dream Of A Travel Business—But 84% Of Its Representatives Earned No Commission In 2025

I’d never heard of PlanNet Marketing until a reader sent me its earnings numbers. I got started down a rabbit hole. They sell travel. Or, rather, they sell people on the idea of selling travel while signing up other people to sell travel. But for all of 2025, 83.96% of PlanNet representatives earned no commission or override at all. My first reaction was: this looks awfully like a pyramid scheme. It’s a multi-level marketing business selling access to a travel agency opportunity. And the more I read, the less comfortable I became with the way that opportunity is pitched to people who need money. Two companies, two ways to make money PlanNet was launched in 2015 by founder Donald Bradley. It works with InteleTravel, a host travel agency. These are separate businesses: . InteleTravel provides the travel agency operation. Advisors get booking tools, training and supplier access. They can sell actual trips and receive a share of the commission. PlanNet sells access to that opportunity. Its representatives earn money selling InteleTravel agency subscriptions and building networks of other representatives who sell them. InteleTravel reported $1.52 billion in 2025 travel sales and 140,000 independent contractors. A conventional host agency charges fees or keeps part of an advisor’s commission in exchange for infrastructure and support. But the salient feature of PlanNet is the multilevel compensation for selling agency access. You can be an InteleTravel advisor without joining the paid PlanNet representative program. However, InteleTravel’s sign-up page routes enrollment exclusively through PlanNet. Here’s the current U.S. pricing from InteleTravel’s benefits page and PlanNet’s current policies and compensation plan. Using monthly billing, doing both costs $59.90 a month, or $718.80 over twelve months, before joining fees or other business expenses. Program    Joining fee    Recurring fee InteleTravel advisor    $179.99    $39.95 monthly PlanNet representative    $19.95    $19.95 monthly; $191.52 annual option Here’s a video describing their commission structure: InteleTravel advertises paying advisors 70%–80% of supplier commissions. A hypothetical $4,000 commissionable booking at a 10% supplier commission produces $400 so an advisor receiving 70% gets $280. You can make a living with enough customers and bookings. What PlanNet Pays For PlanNet’s compensation plan pays for something different: Sell an InteleTravel agency subscription and receive $50. Personally sponsor a PlanNet representative who makes an agency sale and receive a $25 matching commission. A qualifying Gold Builder receives a $10 bonus on agency sales in their network, down to the next Gold Builder. Qualifying representatives receive $4 monthly per active agency subscription in their compensation matrix, potentially through nine levels. At least two active personal agency sales are required to qualify. Gold Builder requires nine active personal agency sales. Higher ranks and bonuses depend on building larger qualifying organizations. The plan also includes rings and a Rolex award. What triggers those payments is selling agency subscriptions. It’s not selling travel, it’s selling the ability to sell travel. Someone can keep paying for an agency, sell no travel, and still generate a monthly payment for people above them. Recruiting another paying participant turns out to be valuable to the recruiter even when the opportunity turns out to be worthless to the person recruited. And friends and relatives become prospective customers (marks) for the business opportunity. The Federal Trade Commission says having a real product isn’t enough to make a multilevel marketing business legal. It’s how the compensation and incentives work that matters. Poor earnings on their own doesn’t mean it’s a pyramid scheme. But the economics here certainly look like one to me. The Earnings Disclosure Is Brutal Here is the full 2025 rank distribution: Rank    Share of active representatives    Average annualized earnings Representative    92.52%    $38.15 Bronze Builder    3.48%    $752.71 Silver Builder    1.34%    $2,497.37 Gold Builder    2.17%    $4,865.04 One-Star Director    0.33%    $28,517.55 Two-Star Director    0.06%    $76,733.94 Three-Star Director    0.06%    $127,496.47 Four-Star Director    0.02%    $255,404.52 Five-Star Director    0.01%    $517,001.78 Six-Star Director    0.01%    $1,088,633.37 This is before expenses. The $38.15 base rank average doesn’t cover two months of PlanNet’s monthly dues. In a February 2026 compliance post, PlanNet describes the disclosure as a “strong marketing tool.” It says “a small amount of extra effort” to reach Bronze Builder raises the average earnings, then points to the higher averages at Silver and Gold. The Target Market (‘Victims’) In a company-published recap of a 2022 Atlanta event, a representative describes helping people “move to the other side of the poverty line.” Another invokes the opportunity to “change your bloodline’s finances.” Here’s a sample, A 2024 company profile celebrates a single mother of five who says she had been living paycheck to paycheck before finding the opportunity. The Guardian reported recruitment aimed at mothers on maternity leave and women with chronic illnesses. The Sun’s August 2025 investigation described pressure to recruit and guilt about quitting. It also reported celebrity Jess Wright telling people unable to afford to “invest into your future, then this is exactly why you need this travel business”. Someone’s inability to afford a fee is being turned into an argument for paying it. But being shown the celebrity’s lifestyle tells you very little about your own likely return. It’s also not clear whether people actually receive the requisite training to sell travel, understand cancellation terms, handle client money, know the products, and fix problems. You’re Guaranteed A Profit! InteleTravel offers a first-year profit guarantee. It counts both earnings and the value of travel savings and privileges for the advisor. It covers fees paid to InteleTravel not all expenses or PlanNet fees. Eligibility includes specified training, a qualifying cruise or vacation-package sale, a completed hotel stay booking each quarter, and purchasing business cards within the first 90 days. The claim must be made within 30 days after the first anniversary. PlanNet’s policies: Prohibit selling or transferring the position you buy If you don’t keep paying, you lose your downline commissions You can’t make negative remarks about the company, its compensation plan or leadership. It’s An Old Business Model This isn’t an original business model. Evolution Travel and Archer Travel is another marketing network paired with a host agency. Evolution’s compensation plan combines travel commissions with sponsor payments and network ranks. It raises the same question about whether a participant is building a customer base for travel or a network of paying agents. YourTravelBiz, or YTB: was alleged to be a pyramid scheme built around selling travel websites. A 2009 settlement required $1 million in penalties, costs and restitution. The company’s securities filing says the settlement involved no admission or court findings of wrongdoing. One executive named in that filing was Andrew Cauthen, the Andy Cauthen whom PlanNet honored on his retirement as president in January 2026. WorldVentures: a travel club version of multilevel marketing. Its U.S. disclosure from July 2018 – June 2019 reported that 85.4% of representatives earned no commission. Norway’s regulator found it to be an illegal pyramid system. I’ve long argued that a good travel agent’s expertise has real value. Someone who knows a destination, understands a complicated itinerary or takes responsibility when things go wrong can earn their commission many times over. I don’t see how I’d ever want to work with a PlanetNet agent, and that’s a problem. Top travel advisors can still do well but this is not the broad-based business it once was because of a new thing called the internet. Topics on this pageInteleTravel.comMulti-level marketingPlannet Marketing Inc.PlanNet Sells The Dream Of A Travel BusinessPyramid schemeAtlantaFederal Trade CommissionRolex+3 more More From View from the Wing

Norway’s regulator found it to be an illegal pyramid system. I’ve long argued that a good travel agent’s expertise has real value. Someone who knows a destination, understands a complicated itinerary or takes responsibility when things go wrong can earn their commission many times over. I don’t see how I’d ever want to work with a PlanetNet agent, and that’s a problem. Top travel advisors can still do well but this is not the broad-based business it once was because of a new thing called the internet. PlanNet was launched in 2015 by founder Donald Bradley. It works with InteleTravel, a host travel agency. These are separate businesses: .

InteleTravel reported $1.52 billion in 2025 travel sales and 140,000 independent contractors. A conventional host agency charges fees or keeps part of an advisor’s commission in exchange for infrastructure and support. But the salient feature of PlanNet is the multilevel compensation for selling agency access.

You can be an InteleTravel advisor without joining the paid PlanNet representative program. However, InteleTravel’s sign-up page routes enrollment exclusively through PlanNet.

Here’s the current U.S. pricing from InteleTravel’s benefits page and PlanNet’s current policies and compensation plan. Using monthly billing, doing both costs $59.90 a month, or $718.80 over twelve months, before joining fees or other business expenses.

Here’s a video describing their commission structure:

InteleTravel advertises paying advisors 70%–80% of supplier commissions. A hypothetical $4,000 commissionable booking at a 10% supplier commission produces $400 so an advisor receiving 70% gets $280. You can make a living with enough customers and bookings.

PlanNet’s compensation plan pays for something different: Sell an InteleTravel agency subscription and receive $50. Personally sponsor a PlanNet representative who makes an agency sale and receive a $25 matching commission. A qualifying Gold Builder receives a $10 bonus on agency sales in their network, down to the next Gold Builder. Qualifying representatives receive $4 monthly per active agency subscription in their compensation matrix, potentially through nine levels. At least two active personal agency sales are required to qualify. Gold Builder requires nine active personal agency sales. Higher ranks and bonuses depend on building larger qualifying organizations. The plan also includes rings and a Rolex award. What triggers those payments is selling agency subscriptions. It’s not selling travel, it’s selling the ability to sell travel. Someone can keep paying for an agency, sell no travel, and still generate a monthly payment for people above them. Recruiting another paying participant turns out to be valuable to the recruiter even when the opportunity turns out to be worthless to the person recruited. And friends and relatives become prospective customers (marks) for the business opportunity. The Federal Trade Commission says having a real product isn’t enough to make a multilevel marketing business legal. It’s how the compensation and incentives work that matters. Poor earnings on their own doesn’t mean it’s a pyramid scheme. But the economics here certainly look like one to me. The Earnings Disclosure Is Brutal Here is the full 2025 rank distribution: Rank    Share of active representatives    Average annualized earnings Representative    92.52%    $38.15 Bronze Builder    3.48%    $752.71 Silver Builder    1.34%    $2,497.37 Gold Builder    2.17%    $4,865.04 One-Star Director    0.33%    $28,517.55 Two-Star Director    0.06%    $76,733.94 Three-Star Director    0.06%    $127,496.47 Four-Star Director    0.02%    $255,404.52 Five-Star Director    0.01%    $517,001.78 Six-Star Director    0.01%    $1,088,633.37 This is before expenses. The $38.15 base rank average doesn’t cover two months of PlanNet’s monthly dues. In a February 2026 compliance post, PlanNet describes the disclosure as a “strong marketing tool.” It says “a small amount of extra effort” to reach Bronze Builder raises the average earnings, then points to the higher averages at Silver and Gold. The Target Market (‘Victims’) In a company-published recap of a 2022 Atlanta event, a representative describes helping people “move to the other side of the poverty line.” Another invokes the opportunity to “change your bloodline’s finances.” Here’s a sample, A 2024 company profile celebrates a single mother of five who says she had been living paycheck to paycheck before finding the opportunity. The Guardian reported recruitment aimed at mothers on maternity leave and women with chronic illnesses. The Sun’s August 2025 investigation described pressure to recruit and guilt about quitting. It also reported celebrity Jess Wright telling people unable to afford to “invest into your future, then this is exactly why you need this travel business”. Someone’s inability to afford a fee is being turned into an argument for paying it. But being shown the celebrity’s lifestyle tells you very little about your own likely return. It’s also not clear whether people actually receive the requisite training to sell travel, understand cancellation terms, handle client money, know the products, and fix problems. You’re Guaranteed A Profit! InteleTravel offers a first-year profit guarantee. It counts both earnings and the value of travel savings and privileges for the advisor. It covers fees paid to InteleTravel not all expenses or PlanNet fees. Eligibility includes specified training, a qualifying cruise or vacation-package sale, a completed hotel stay booking each quarter, and purchasing business cards within the first 90 days. The claim must be made within 30 days after the first anniversary. PlanNet’s policies: Prohibit selling or transferring the position you buy If you don’t keep paying, you lose your downline commissions You can’t make negative remarks about the company, its compensation plan or leadership. It’s An Old Business Model This isn’t an original business model. Evolution Travel and Archer Travel is another marketing network paired with a host agency. Evolution’s compensation plan combines travel commissions with sponsor payments and network ranks. It raises the same question about whether a participant is building a customer base for travel or a network of paying agents. YourTravelBiz, or YTB: was alleged to be a pyramid scheme built around selling travel websites. A 2009 settlement required $1 million in penalties, costs and restitution. The company’s securities filing says the settlement involved no admission or court findings of wrongdoing. One executive named in that filing was Andrew Cauthen, the Andy Cauthen whom PlanNet honored on his retirement as president in January 2026. WorldVentures: a travel club version of multilevel marketing. Its U.S. disclosure from July 2018 – June 2019 reported that 85.4% of representatives earned no commission. Norway’s regulator found it to be an illegal pyramid system. I’ve long argued that a good travel agent’s expertise has real value. Someone who knows a destination, understands a complicated itinerary or takes responsibility when things go wrong can earn their commission many times over. I don’t see how I’d ever want to work with a PlanetNet agent, and that’s a problem. Top travel advisors can still do well but this is not the broad-based business it once was because of a new thing called the internet. PlanNet appears to offer a compelling employment opportunity for those who are willing to work hard in a fast-paced, guest-facing environment.

After reading this, I’m very uncomfortable with how it works. It smells all too much like Amway and other MLMs.

I remember the latin america targeted version. Vision travel.. 95% of the ‘agents’ didn’t sell travel at all and were completely clueless about the travel agent business. They were only selling the Pyramid/MLM. I think they are still around

Most MLM schemes focus on selling the opportunity to sell instead of product. This is how people on the bottom end up with a garage full of soap they can’t do anything with.

jack the ladd nails it, the product is the signup, not the trip. These pitches tend to lean on insider hotel rates, yet a free extension like RatePunk already shows the same room’s price across the big OTAs side by side, no membership needed. If someone pitches you, ask what share of reps booked a paying client last year

A couple years ago I decided I wanted to cash in on the deals and commissions that travel agents get. I signed up with a company called Cruise Brothers.

By it’s name you can guess that they focus on cruises, but the big difference between Cruise Brothers and the company above is that it cost me absolutely nothing. The commission’s aren’t great, but I have access to tremendous tools and tons of training so that I may, at some point, actually make a few bucks on it. Right now I’m focused on just getting good deals from my wife and I.

#6161. Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers Airport Review: Strong Furniture Store Vibes

For the next stop of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I had the chance to visit the Air Algerie VIP Lounge at Algiers Houari Boumediene International Airport (ALG). I had just landed from Montreal (YUL) in Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, and was connecting to Tunis (TUN) in Air Algerie’s A320 business class (a wet leased flight).

The Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers is actually pleasant enough. It’s quirky, as it has a ton of seating, and almost feels more like a furniture store than an airport lounge. But I appreciate that the space isn’t crowded, so it’s a nice enough place to pass some time. The food and drink selection is totally unremarkable and okay, so at least it’s not negatively memorable.

The Algiers Airport transit experience was interesting. Algeria is a country that really doesn’t want tourists (getting a visa is a pain), and Air Algerie doesn’t get much connecting international traffic, so not that many people are in international transit.

Upon landing from Montreal, I followed the signage in the direction of “Flight Connections.” Interestingly, I seemed to be among the only people on my flight with an international connection, as everyone else headed to immigration.

I ended up in the “transit room,” as it’s called. There my boarding pass was checked, and then I was given a form that I had to fill out. A form to transit internationally? Odd, but whatever. I then had to wait for an immigration officer to be ready, but he just seemed to be sitting in his window for several minutes without signaling he was ready, so I just waited.

After about five minutes, it was my turn. Then there was a security check, except the security guy clearly wasn’t quite ready yet for anyone, so he was caught off guard by me, and took a second to set things up.

All-in-all, it was a painless enough transit experience thanks to the lack of crowds, even if it was a bit bureaucratic. The Algiers Airport terminal is really big, and it just felt totally deserted during my early morning visit (when a lot of flights leave, in theory).

Once in the international departures area, it was easy to find the Air Algerie VIP Lounge, as there was signage for it right there. The lounge is in the center of the terminal, up a level, so you can either take the elevator, escalator, or stairs.

Once on the upper level, the entrance to the lounge was right there. I loved the Air Algerie Boeing 767 airplane model at the entrance. I’m not sure if this was intended to be a throwback, or if they just hadn’t bothered getting a new model in the nearly decade since the aircraft type was retired. I have a guess, but… 😉

The Air Algiers VIP Lounge Algiers is open 24/7, or something like that. The hours aren’t actually published, but the idea is that if there are flights, then the lounge should also be open.

The Air Algerie VIP Lounge is the primary lounge at Algiers Airport. So in addition to being open to premium passengers on Air Algerie, it also acts as the contract lounge for premium passengers on EgyptAir, Qatar Airways, Royal Jordanian, Saudia, Tunisair, and Turkish Airlines.

Oddly, the lounge isn’t open to Priority Pass members, despite clearly having the capacity to handle more passengers.

The Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers is quite a large facility, especially in relation to demand. The lounge basically consists of one large room, and it “opens up” into the rest of the terminal, as it’s essentially just on top of the main passenger concourse.

As I said above, the only way I can describe this lounge is as having very strong furniture store vibes, as there’s just a sea of couches and chairs, all of which are quite plush. I’ll let the pictures speak mostly for themselves.

The lounge was really quiet during my visit. There were maybe a total of a dozen people in the lounge, and I’d say fewer than half of those were passengers, and the remainder were airport staff having their morning coffee, and helping themselves to the buffet.

The lounge was quite well staffed — there were two staff members responsible for overseeing the buffet, while for reasons I can’t figure out, there were three people at the front desk of the lounge (I don’t think a single other person entered during my hour stay, so that strikes me as an overkill, but…).

The Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers has a self-serve food & drink selection.

When it comes to food, the selection included finger sandwiches, whole fruit, veggies, cheese, cold cuts, yogurt, cereal, pastries, etc.

There were also some hot options, none of which looked particularly appealing to me (and I also wondered for how long these items had been sitting around). This included eggs, sausage, potatoes, and veggies.

When it comes to drinks, this is a “dry” lounge (so there’s no alcohol). Options included coffee, tea, soft drinks, and water, all of which guests could help themselves to.

The Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers has bathrooms that are located just inside the entrance and to the right. They’re down a hall, right next to the kitchen area.

The men’s room had three sinks, three toilet stalls, and two urinals.

In theory there was also a shower suite, but as you can see below, not really.

The Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers was the best part of my Air Algerie experience, which isn’t saying a whole lot. The carrier’s flagship lounge is large, and has an okay selection of food and drinks. In an era where so many lounges are crowded, it’s at least nice to have a quiet space like this.

Admittedly this is otherwise a pretty uninteresting lounge, with few amenities, and a lack of variety when it comes to seating options. I definitely wouldn’t arrive early to use this lounge, but it’s also not a bad place to pass some time.

What do you make of the Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers?

It really does look like a furniture store, where you buy the floor models lol. But seems a lot better than your in-flight experiences!

Was at this lounge a couple of weeks ago. The title made me laugh because the best part is that the furniture is really big and comfortable. There are barcoloungers to spare. But the food isn’t great. But no food in Algiers was great. It’s also the BA contract lounge (they have daily flight).

Looks like they shopped the Levitz liquidation sale 20 years ago. But I’d still rather sit on a real sofa with a real chaise on a layover than whatever angular mess of a lounger United is pretending will be comfortable at its new IAH lounge.

From the look at Ben’s photo of the breakfast sausages, if he did not mention what they were then one may incorrectly assume they were a pile of ————. Though, due to how they were piled up that assumption with a quick glance could be considered accurate, haha.

If you've ever rented a car, you've probably been asked whether you want to pay extra for insurance at the counter. But depending on which credit card you have, you may already have some coverage.

Many travel rewards credit cards offer rental car insurance that can protect you against theft or damage to your rental vehicle, potentially saving you from paying extra for the rental company's collision damage waiver.

Here's how credit card rental car insurance works, what it covers and which cards offer some of the best protection.

These cards offer primary rental car coverage on eligible rentals. Coverage can vary by card, rental location and purpose.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

These cards offer primary car rental insurance, as long as you use your card to pay for the entire rental. Note that this isn’t an exhaustive list; you may find other cards offering primary insurance.

The , and each provide primary car rental insurance for rentals of up to 31 consecutive days. The personal cards are primary, while the business card is primary in the U.S. only for business rentals.

This policy covers theft, damage, valid loss-of-use charges, administrative fees and reasonable towing charges due to covered theft or damage.

Policy details vary slightly among the three cards, though. A key difference is the total amount that can be reimbursed for damages caused by theft or collision:

To learn more about each card, read our full reviews for the Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Reserve for Business.

The Capital One Venture X and Venture X Business both offer primary rental car insurance, though the coverage terms differ.

The personal Venture X provides reimbursement for theft and collision damage up to the actual cash value of eligible rental vehicles with an original manufacturer's suggested retail price of $75,000 or less. Coverage applies to rentals of up to 15 consecutive days in your country of residence or 31 consecutive days elsewhere.

Meanwhile, the Venture X Business provides primary coverage for eligible rentals made primarily for business purposes, covering theft and collision damage subject to the policy's valuation limits. Rentals of up to 31 consecutive days are eligible for coverage.

To learn more, read our full reviews of the Venture X and Venture X Business.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

Four of the Ink Business cards from Chase offer primary insurance when you rent for business purposes, providing reimbursement for theft and collision damage for most rental vehicles with an MSRP of $125,000 or less.

Each card provides reimbursement of up to $60,000 for theft and collision damage.

To learn more, read our guide to the Chase Ink Business cards.

United’s cobranded cards offer primary car rental insurance, though the business versions are primary only when you rent for business purposes. You need to decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card.

This insurance provides reimbursement of up to $60,000 for theft and collision damage for most rental vehicles with an MSRP of $125,000 or less.

To learn more, read our guide to the United cards.

Among the most important factors here is making sure you pay for your entire car rental bill with a credit card that has an auto collision damage waiver included in its benefits. You'll also want to decline any insurance offer from your rental car company.

Of course, terms and conditions vary, so always check your card's specific policies before you rent. This way, if you run into a problem, you'll know what's covered and what's not.

If you don’t follow these requirements, your credit card car rental insurance won’t take effect.

Related: All you need to know about using a debit card to rent a car

The car rental insurance from your credit card is technically called an “auto rental collision damage waiver.” This benefit provides reimbursement for damage due to collision or theft. The cash amount your card's insurance policy will cover can vary, so check your card's guide to benefits for specific details.

While some cards also cover loss-of-use and towing charges assessed by the rental company, policies from other credit cards only cover physical damage or theft of the rental vehicle. Knowing what your card will cover is important before you use it.

Additionally, some rental types and locations may not be eligible for coverage. Keep the following provisions in mind if you rely on credit card car rental insurance benefits:

If you have doubts about your car's eligibility, it's best practice to call the customer service number on your card. You can get more information and confirm that your policy covers your rental vehicle type in the country you’ll be visiting.

Related: My experience with Turo: Car rental convenience at a great price

Another important distinction is the difference between primary and secondary car rental insurance, as your card could offer one type or the other. Both types of insurance usually have maximum coverage amounts, so make sure these meet or exceed the total value of the car you’re renting.

If you get into an accident with your rental car and have primary insurance, you only need to file one claim. Generally, primary insurance will reimburse you for the rental car’s cash value or the cost to repair it, whichever is less.

Secondary insurance is different because it only reimburses you for the amount not covered by other types of insurance, such as travel insurance or personal car insurance. However, if you don’t own a car or carry a car insurance policy, most secondary insurance from credit cards will become primary.

Select American Express cards include secondary coverage for damage to or theft of an eligible rental car. If you want primary coverage, you can enroll an eligible Amex card in Premium Car Rental Protection before you rent. Amex charges a flat fee per eligible rental paid for with the enrolled card.

Related: Secondary rental car insurance: Best cards and what's covered

Many consumers focus on the number of points or miles they can earn and redeem when choosing a travel rewards card, but travel protections such as rental car insurance can also provide significant value.

However, reviewing your card’s policy details is essential to understand what is (and isn’t) covered. Don’t assume you’re covered for every possible mishap when you pay for a car rental with a credit card that offers insurance, as many exceptions and exclusions apply.

Ensure you know the details and how they relate to your rental location, vehicle type, length of rental period and other important issues so you won’t be surprised by a bill if your rental car has a problem.

Related: Readers say this credit card insurance provider isn’t reliable: Here’s what you need to know

#6158. NTSB Recovers Cockpit Voice Recorder From Miami Crash As On-Scene Investigation Ends

The on-scene phase of the investigation into the South Florida Learjet crash that occurred on November 1 has been completed. The National Transportation Safety Board ( NTSB) has now handed over the scene after a fatal crash earlier this month when a Learjet 60 crashed into the ground, killing all nine occupants on board

Federal investigators were able to successfully recover the aircraft's Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) from the wreckage; this has now been sent to the NTSB laboratory in the country's capital for readout and audio analysis.

Evidence has been found that reiterates the mid-air breakup indications. The NTSB Board Member, Tom Chapman, confirmed in the active investigations report that the investigators have found evidence that the plane had begun to break up in the air before it made impact. The debris, including a section of the plane's tail, was located more than 3.8 miles (6.11 km) from the crater left by the plane's high-speed trajectory in Greenacres, Florida.

Reviewing weather and atmospheric conditions, it is suggested that the jet encountered severe weather during its flight from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) to the Bahamas. The air traffic control audio recordings by co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras reported that there were icing conditions that caused severe turbulence over and above 700 feet (213 meters), which was before the jet issued a Mayday call.

The ultimate loss of control and detachment of the critical tail control surfaces rendered the plane uncontrollable, which ultimately led to the nose-down, high-speed descent that resulted in the plane's crash into a residential Florida roadway. The impact crater left by the Learjet's crash initially filled with water due to heavy rain, which initially slowed parts of the recovery until the water was pumped out.

With all physical wreckage now documented and components collected from the impact scene, the NTSB will now shift its focus to the data extraction and laboratory analysis of all the evidence. This will include the download and evaluation of the audio to be recovered from the voice recorder.

Mapping of the flight data and flight track relative to the severe convective storm cell that expanded on its flight path will enable a radar and meteorological reconstruction of the fatal flight. This will be undertaken at the same time a structural examination of the airframe is conducted, where the tail assemblies and other parts of the jet are analyzed to identify the ultimate sequence of the structure's failure.

It is expected that a preliminary report will be issued by the NTSB over the next few weeks; however, the probable cause of the incident will not be expected for up to two years. Details of the aircraft involved in the incident, as per data from Craft, are outlined below:

A Learjet 60 carrying nine people crashed in Greenacres, Florida, near Mar-a-Lago, after a dramatic nose-down descent and fiery impact

All nine occupants onboard the Learjet traveling from Austin to the Bahamas were identified as two crew members and seven passengers. The flight crew were Captain Jeff Gregory and Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras. Captain Gregory was a veteran aviator and the pilot in command of the jet. He lived in Gilbertsville, Pennsylvania, and had a background in charter and commercial aviation. Filgueiras was just 20 years of age and a Brazilian American pilot who grew up in Boca Raton, Florida.

Of the seven passengers was Adam Robinson, an Austin-based tech entrepreneur and the founder and CEO of software platforms Retention, RB2B and MoltSets. His wife, Helen Sharep, and their two children, Emma (4) and Charlie (2), also perished when the plane plummeted and crashed into the ground. Family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, alongside the family nanny Anita Maria Cetina, were also on board and sadly lost their lives.

The jet at the center of the incident is that of Bombardier Learjet 60, which carried registration N722BD. It is registered to LR60271 LLC of Wilmington, Delaware, and was operated by charter company Aurora Aviation.

#6157. Use Lyft For Work? How To Get 6%–8% Back, Plus Extra Airline Or Hotel Points

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

I have a personal preference for Lyft, as regular readers know. One of the things that I really like is that they have the best rewards in rideshare. But I didn’t realize things get even more lucrative for business travelers using a Lyft business profile. They have benefits, like:

keeping all of your regular rewards to use on personal or business rides. earning with Lyft’s airline or hotel partners goes up significantly for eligible business travelers. and pocketing 6% – 8% back in Lyft Credits on business profile rides, to use on your own rides later. That’s why it makes sense to sign up for a business account. Bonus, it lets you separate personal and business rides, which makes expense management easier (and you won’t mistakenly apply personal credits to reimbursable trips as I sometimes do by accident). Earn Lyft Credits On Top of Travel Rewards The original idea of a frequent flyer program was that you’d earn rewards on business travel. Your employer pays for a ticket, you benefit personally with your miles. That kept you loyal. This is really the same idea that the airlines pioneered about 45 years ago. When you ride for work, you can get Lyft Credits to use on your own trips later – 6% for standard rides taken with your business profile and 8% for premium, airport, and scheduled business profile rides. And you can do this even while earning with your preferred travel partner, and you earn those points or miles faster than you do with a personal account (where I’ve already been happy with the points-earning). How To Join I already use Lyft for business travel, so enrolling is a no-brainer since it’s fast and free and you accelerate your earnings. This also lets you bill a business card or directly to your employer and it integrates with popular expense tools. Lyft estimates that over half of business travelers forget to take advantage of automatic company expensing, leading to missed rewards and lack of visibility for organizations. Can We Just Appreciate Rideshare For A Moment? For most of my life there was no such thing as rideshare. For a brief time in Austin where I live, the city government chased it away, and I actually had to re-learn how to get to the airport. Now I pull up my Lyft app and I’m frustrated if I see that my driver is six minutes away. Six minutes. That’s my complaint. A stranger is coming to my exact location, in their personal car, because I touched glass. That’s sorcery with seatbelts. It used to be that you had to stand on the curb with your arm out like the Statue of Liberty, just waving at traffic. “Please! Someone! I have money and a destination!” And the taxis would just drive by. Sometimes they’d slow down just enough to let you experience hope before crushing it. You’d make eye contact with the driver. He’d look at you, look through you, and drive right past. And if it rained? You were done. Some cab would blast through a puddle and soak you like you’re Carrie Bradshaw in Sex and the City. Now you press a button and a tiny map shows you a little car cartoon coming toward you. You get in, you get out. Start to finish, it’s frictionless. And to top it off, you even get rewarded for it. Just by using a business profile, you can earn Lyft Credits and extra travel points or miles on rides your company is already paying for. George Clooney said it best in Up In The Air, “I don’t spend a nickel if I can help it unless it somehow benefits my mileage account.” Your company is spending the nickel. You might as well get the miles. Thanks, I have a business account on Uber and, after reading this, Lyft now. Nothing reminded me more of the great value of these services than during a recent out-of-town car breakdown. I could easily get to and from the repair shop in about 7 minutes more than if I could drive. For laughs, I looked up Uber selecting a ride home. They offered a $270 price for a 3 hour drive with a 7 minute wait. I wonder how much the driver gets before tip and after they pay for fuel on the 6-hour return. I also wonder if anyone would take it. I remember the world where I had to call the night before to schedule a taxi that was pretty good at arriving on time (rarely 5 or 10 minutes late). #6156. Atmos Rewards Credit Card Bonus Offers & Eligibility Rules Explained

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, and the program has three co-branded credit cards in the United States — the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card, Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card, and Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card — all of which are excellent.

In this post, I’d like to go over the details of the welcome offers on these cards. After that, I’ll talk a bit about card eligibility. Let me say up front that it’s possible to get more than one of these cards, so you’re probably eligible for one of these even if you already have a card in the portfolio.

Link: Learn about the best credit cards for Alaska Atmos Rewards

Bank of America and Alaska Air Group partner on issuing three co-branded credit cards, all with Atmos Rewards branding, replacing the previous Mileage Plan program. Let’s cover the details of the bonuses, plus the basics of why you may want to consider these cards.

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card has a $395 annual fee, and is the most premium personal card in the collection.

The card is offering a limited time welcome bonus where you can receive 100,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award with this offer. To qualify, spend $6,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account.

While this card has the highest annual fee of the three cards, it offers an amazing value proposition. Perks include the following, among other things:

Read a detailed review of the Atmos Rewards Summit Card.

The Atmos Rewards Ascent Card has a $95 annual fee, and is the more basic of the two personal cards in the collection.

The card is offering a limited time welcome bonus where you can receive 60,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $3,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account. You can earn an additional 20,000 bonus points after spending a total of $5,000 or more on purchases within the same 90-day period.

This is a great option for a low-fee card that still offers considerable value for someone who flies Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency. Some of the card’s perks include the following:

Read a detailed review of the Atmos Rewards Ascent Card.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has a minimum of a $95 annual fee ($70 for the account and $25 per card), and is the business card in the portfolio.

The card is offering a welcome bonus of 70,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after you make $4,000 or more in purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account.

The perks on this card are very similar to the perks on its personal card equivalent. These include the following, among other things:

Read a detailed review of the Atmos Rewards Business Card.

With the above out of the way, who is eligible for the welcome offers on the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, Atmos Rewards Ascent Card, and Atmos Rewards Business Card?

Let me start by stating that eligibility for all three Atmos Rewards cards (including the welcome offers) is considered independently. So if you already have the Atmos Rewards Ascent Card, you can apply for the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, and vice versa. The same is true for the Atmos Rewards Business Card. So rules can’t get easier in that regard.

How does card eligibility work if you have an existing Alaska Airlines Bank of America card, or Hawaiian Airlines Barclays card?

Let’s start with the easier part of the answer. If you have or have had either of the Hawaiian Airlines Barclays cards (whether personal or business) that doesn’t impact your ability to qualify for any of the Atmos Rewards cards, including the welcome bonuses.

Meanwhile if you have any former Alaska Airlines Bank of America cards, those cards have been converted (or are in the process of being converted) into one of these new Atmos Rewards cards:

So you may not be eligible for the bonus on one of those cards if you currently have it. However, you’d likely be eligible for the bonus on whichever card you don’t have.

What about if you’ve had one of the above cards in the past? Bank of America doesn’t generally have a “once in a lifetime” rule. Instead, you typically have to wait 24 months from when you closed a card before you can qualify for the bonus on a card again (though some report earning a bonus sooner than that).

However, that’s not a published rule, and you’ll find that offer terms call this a “one-time promotion” that’s “limited to customers opening a new account.”

Beyond the rules specific to the Atmos Rewards cards, what general things should you be aware of if applying for a Bank of America card? Here are the two most common Bank of America restrictions:

Neither of those rules seem to be totally consistently enforced, and in particular, that latter policy doesn’t seem consistent at all. For example, when I applied for Atmos Rewards cards last year, I had opened more than three new cards in the previous 12 months, and was still approved.

How hard are Bank of America cards to get approved for, in general? Obviously this is only based on anecdotal reports, but in my experience, Bank of America cards are generally quite easy to get approved for, and I also find they typically have quite large credit limits. However, the issuer can also be quirky with denials, especially based on the above two rules.

There’s no published credit score you need to get approved for Atmos Rewards credit cards, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts your approval odds. I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range — ideally I’d have a score of 700+ points, but people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

What’s the best play if you’re considering picking up an Atmos Rewards credit card, between the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, Atmos Rewards Ascent Card, and Atmos Rewards Business Card? Honestly, you can’t go wrong with any combination of cards here. A few thoughts:

For example, I’ve shared my experience getting approved for the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, and also my experience getting approved for the Atmos Rewards Business Card.

There are three Atmos Rewards credit cards, including the premium Atmos Rewards Summit Card, plus the Atmos Rewards Ascent Card and Atmos Rewards Business Card.

These are all worthwhile cards, so if you’re eligible for any of these cards, they’re worth considering. One thing that’s great is that eligibility requirements for these cards aren’t too strict, in the sense that you can qualify for each of these cards, and earn the welcome offers. Hopefully the above is a useful rundown of the rules surrounding getting approved for these cards.

Are there any Atmos Rewards credit card application questions I haven’t covered? If you’ve applied for one of these cards, what was your experience like?

#6154. World of Hyatt Free Night Awards: How To Earn, Redeem, Gift, & Maximize Them

In addition to being able to redeem World of Hyatt points for hotel stays, program members also have the opportunity to earn free night certificates, which can be redeemed for stays at hotels.

In this post, I want to talk about everything you need to know about World of Hyatt free night award certificates — how do you earn them, how can you redeem them, and what are the restrictions associated with them?

There are a variety of ways to earn World of Hyatt award free night certificates:

For some context on the potential value of these certificates:

Note that while World of Hyatt is pretty strict when it comes to the expiration date of free night awards, members can sometimes receive points in exchange for expired certificates. This isn’t a published policy, but rather is an unwritten courtesy that’s sometimes extended to members, so it’s not something you can count on, but it’s worth asking about. This generally only works for awards issued through Milestone Rewards perks, and not those issued through credit cards.

If you want to see your free night award certificates, just log into your World of Hyatt account. Once in there, click on the “Awards” section. There you’ll see how many awards you have, what kind of awards you have, and when they expire (you have to stay by the expiration date, and not just book by then).

You can generally expect that your free night awards will be deposited in your World of Hyatt account within a few weeks of completing eligible activity, though often even faster than that.

The process of redeeming your Hyatt free night awards is pretty easy, and can be done online. There are two ways you can approach this:

As you start to redeem World of Hyatt free night award certificates, there are a few things to note:

With that in mind, I think the easiest way to redeem is to just start searching on hyatt.com. Search availability for the city or hotel you want, and go through the process as if you’re trying to make a points booking, by clicking the “Use Points” button.

You’ll see the hotel results on the next page. You’ll want to select a hotel that shows the points cost as being within the range of the certificate you have (in other words, for a Category 1-4 free night certificate you’d want it to cost no more than 25,000 points per night).

For example, take the Hyatt Regency JFK Airport at Resorts World, which represents a good use of a free night certificate compared to the cash rate.

When you click through and view rates, you’ll be able to select whether you want to redeem your free night award certificate or points.

For what it’s worth, for a random one-night stay on a Friday at this hotel that I pulled up, the cheapest paid rate would be over $500 per night, including taxes and fees.

It’s pretty amazing that a free night certificate offered by the $95 annual fee World of Hyatt Credit Card can be used here.

There are a couple of situations in which you may want to book by phone:

Much like an award night booked using points, stays booked with free night award certificates are eligible for all World of Hyatt elite benefits. If you’re a Globalist member you’ll receive a suite upgrade subject to availability, complimentary breakfast, lounge access, etc. The only restriction is that you can’t redeem a suite upgrade award, club access award, or Guest of Honor award, for stays booked with free night awards (because you can’t stack certificates).

Furthermore, Hyatt stays booked with free night awards are eligible to earn elite qualifying nights, so they can help you jump to the next elite tier, or help you reach the next Milestone Rewards perk.

It’s possible to transfer your World of Hyatt free night awards to others. This is super easy to do. When you’re in the “Awards” section of your World of Hyatt account, just take a look at your free night awards.

To gift an award to another World of Hyatt member, just click the three dots next to the award you want to gift, click the “Gift Your Award” button, and then you’ll be able to transfer your award. You’ll just need the World of Hyatt number and last name of the World of Hyatt member who you’re gifting the award to.

The award will then instantly post to their account, and they can redeem it however they’d like, with the same expiration date.

I figure it makes sense to briefly share my strategy when it comes to redeeming Hyatt free night award certificates. To keep things simple, let me talk about Category 1-4 free night certificates.

While they can be redeemed at properties costing up to 25,000 points per night (in peak season), I wouldn’t value them that high, given the expiration date of the certificates (meanwhile points never expire in conjunction with activity).

Does it only make sense to redeem a Category 1-4 free night certificate at a Category 4 hotel, or under what circumstances could it make sense to redeem at a hotel that requires fewer points? My general approach is as follows:

For example, while I’ve typically used Category 1-4 free night certificates at Category 4 properties, I’ve also a couple of times redeemed them at Category 3 properties, when I wasn’t 100% sure I’d be able to use them otherwise. I think that’s ultimately still a great deal, especially if it’s a property where the cash rate would be high.

Everyone should consider their own situation, though. For example, some people consistently plan all of their travel six or more months in advance, and in that case you wouldn’t want to wait as long as I do to try to maximize certificates.

There are several ways to earn World of Hyatt free night certificates, whether it’s through the World of Hyatt Credit Card, or through the Milestone Rewards program. There’s lots of value to be had with these certificates, and I’ve consistently been able to maximize their value pretty well. Now you can even transfer them to others.

Hopefully the above answers any questions you may have about Hyatt free night award certificates, though if I missed anything, please let me know.

#6153. Florida Man Urinates Toward Family At Fort Lauderdale Airport Gate—Splashes Mother And 7-Year-Old

A mother and her 7-year-old son waiting for a flight at the Fort Lauderdale airport were splashed with urine when a man seated across from them exposed himself and began urinating in their direction on Tuesday morning, November 3. Deputies arrested the 48-year old local man on six charges. The arrest affidavit says this happened at gate E6, which tells me this is either an American Airlines or JetBlue passenger. The family said the man was facing them when he unbuttoned his pants and let loose. The father avoided the blast. “Several other passengers were present in the immediate area at the time of the incident,” Powell wrote. “As Raben exposed himself and began urinating, the surrounding passengers dispersed from the area.” The charges were: Battery involving an adult causing a child to come into contact with bodily fluids. Battery. Three counts of indecent exposure. Disorderly intoxication. Go figure: Florida has an actual felony specifically covering an adult knowingly causing, or attempting to cause, a child to come into contact with urine or certain other bodily substances by projecting or expelling them. They knew they needed this. It’s a third-degree felony, punishable by up to five years in prison. He was released on $5,000 bond. Airport surveillance footage of the incident has not been released. Local 10 News reporting on the Fort Lauderdale airport arrest “Urine trouble now, buddy,” one Reddit commenter offered. This happens more than you’d expect (or at least, more than anyone would hope). At Memphis airport a man urinated over a woman sleeping in the terminal. Earlier this year, an Air Canada passenger was filmed urinating on the floor at a Calgary gate while bystanders wondered whether he was sleepwalking. And once you’re on board, getting away becomes harder. A Frontier Airlines passenger who said urine ran onto his leg and shoes was offered a $75 voucher. I’ve been writing about this long enough that the New York Times once interviewed me about what to do when another passenger urinates on you. Nobody should be surprised that the perpetrator in this case was a Florida Man. Though the meme itself is somewhat self-perpetuating, sort of like the 2001 summer of the shark despite no evidence that there was actually any spike in shark attacks. The state’s public records law helps make arrest material accessible, though they’re not alone here. There’s actually academic scholarship arguing it’s our existing priors about Florida that make Florida stories more social shareable. #6152. 25 Best Credit Card Offers & Bonuses For Travel Rewards In November 2026

For those with access to credit cards in the United States, the single best way to rack up a lot of points quickly is by taking advantage of the best credit card welcome bonuses and offers. The credit card industry in the United States is lucrative (for banks, airlines, hotel groups, etc.), and the idea is that they often offer large upfront welcome offers and bonuses to incentivize people to apply.

So in this post, I’d like to share what I consider to be the best current credit card welcome bonuses and offers for earning travel rewards, across a variety of categories. The details of the best offers are always changing, so that’s why I think it’s useful to keep a current list with the best credit card welcome bonuses, which I try to constantly update to reflect offers.

I’ll share what I consider the 25 best credit card welcome offers right now to be, across five categories (business transferable points cards, personal transferable points cards, hotel cards, airline cards, and no annual fee cards). Before I do, let me just point out a few things:

Simply put, most people want to travel better, but don’t know how. One of the best ways to improve your travel experience is to pick up an excellent credit card that can add value to your wallet.

When applying for a credit card, consider three main points:

In this post I’m focusing primarily on the best credit card welcome bonuses, which can be one of the best ways to get rewarded quickly. Often a good credit card bonus will be enough to earn you an international ticket in first or business class, which many would otherwise assume is off limits.

Business credit cards tend to have among the most lucrative welcome offers of any cards out there, so if you’re eligible to apply for them, there are some incredible opportunities. Admittedly these cards often have large minimum spending requirements, but if you can unlock them, these cards can earn you an incredible amount of travel.

Below are what I consider to be the five best welcome offers on business cards that earn travel rewards. Specifically, these are focused on transferable points currencies, which give you the most flexibility (I’ll cover some airline and hotel business cards below, in separate sections).

Personal credit cards are of course the most popular for those looking to earn travel rewards for their credit card spending. These cards can be all over the place in terms of their annual fees and perks, but many are worth having.

Below are what I consider to be the five best welcome offers on personal cards that earn travel rewards. Specifically, these are focused on transferable points currencies, which give you the most flexibility (I’ll cover some airline and hotel personal cards below, in separate sections).

I’m a huge fan of hotel credit cards, given the incredible value they can offer on an ongoing basis. Even if you don’t spend a lot on these cards, there’s potentially value to having them, thanks to their perks, like hotel elite status, free night awards, and more.

Below are what I consider to be the five best welcome offers on hotel credit cards, including both personal and business cards.

There’s lots of merit to getting airline credit cards, given that they can offer priority perks and fee waivers for travel on airlines, and can also help you earn elite status.

Below are what I consider to be the five best welcome offers on airline credit cards, including both personal and business cards.

Admittedly the best credit card welcome offers are typically going to be on credit cards with annual fees. After all, those are typically the most perks-rich cards, and also the ones that card issuers most want to incentivize consumers to apply for. I recognize that some people just absolutely don’t want to pay an annual fee, so it’s worth compiling those offers as well.

Below are what I consider to be the five best welcome offers on no annual fee credit cards, including both personal and business cards.

Before applying for the best credit card welcome bonuses, makes sure you’re aware of the rules each bank has for credit card applications. One of the common misconceptions people have is that they think applying for credit cards will hurt their credit. The opposite is largely true, actually. Assuming you use your credit responsibly (and make payments on time, don’t utilize too much of your credit, etc.), applying for credit cards can actually help your credit.

However, if you are going to apply for credit cards, make sure you do so responsibly — only apply for them if you have self-control and won’t end up in debt, and try to pay your balance in full every month, or else the interest charges will negate any rewards earned.

Taking advantage of the best credit card welcome bonuses and offers is the fastest way to rack up travel rewards, in order to book first and business class flights, stay at luxury hotels, etc. The best offers are always changing, so it’s worth understanding what the best deals at any given point are.

Of course you’ll also want to consider picking cards that match your long term travel goals, as there’s lots of value to travel credit cards beyond just the welcome offers.

American Express Membership Rewards aren't just for travel anymore. Sports fans now have another way to put their points to use.

As of today, some American Express cardmembers can transfer Membership Rewards points to FanCash, the rewards currency of sports merchandise retailer Fanatics.

The new transfer option is part of a broader partnership between American Express and Fanatics, which also unveiled additional details about its upcoming cobranded credit card.

Eligible U.S. cardmembers can now transfer Membership Rewards points to FanCash at a rate of 1,000 points for $10 in FanCash, giving you a redemption value of 1 cent per point. You can find this option in the newly added Lifestyle section of Amex's transfer partners page.

Simply enter your Fanatics credentials to link your account, which only takes a few seconds.

Once transferred, FanCash can be used toward eligible purchases across the Fanatics ecosystem, including sports apparel, trading cards, collectibles and tickets.

However, this isn't necessarily the best use of your Amex points. At 1 cent apiece, you'd be getting just half of TPG's valuation of Membership Rewards points at 2 cents each, a value you can potentially achieve by transferring points to Amex's airline and hotel partners.

Still, this gives sports fans another option for redeeming their points, particularly if they don't have any upcoming travel plans.

Related: Best ways to use Amex Membership Rewards points

As announced earlier this year, American Express and Fanatics are also teaming up on a new cobranded credit card designed for sports fans.

The upcoming Fanatics American Express® Card will have no annual fee and earn 5% FanCash on eligible purchases across the Fanatics ecosystem, or 8% or more when shopping through the Fanatics app.

The card will also offer sports-focused perks and more than 500 trading card-inspired designs featuring professional athletes.

It's not yet available for applications, but interested consumers can join the waitlist.

The information for the Fanatics American Express Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The ability to transfer Amex points to FanCash gives sports fans another way to use their rewards, but the 1-cent-per-point value may not appeal to travelers looking to maximize their Membership Rewards points.

For those who regularly shop with Fanatics, however, the new transfer option could be a convenient way to put unused points toward their next purchase.

Related: American Express Membership Rewards: How to earn, redeem and transfer points

#6149. Washington Dulles Concourse E Opens, With Huge New United Club

United Airlines is on quite the roll when it comes to opening new concourses and lounges at its hubs. Just recently, I covered how a new United Club opened in Houston (IAH) Terminal B North. This is not only the biggest United Club in the world, but it’s the biggest airport lounge in all of the Americas.

There’s now another update, as we’re seeing the opening of a new United Club at Washington Dulles (IAD) Concourse E. This is the second biggest United Club in the entire system, and it’s also part of a long overdue new concourse for the airport. Let’s first talk about the new lounge, and then about the new concourse.

A brand new United Club is opening in Concourse E at Washington Dulles Airport. The new lounge is nearly 40,000 square feet, with seating for more than 600 customers, making it the carrier’s second largest United Club in the system. Crucially, this also increases United’s club and lounge space at the airport by nearly 70%.

The new lounge has a bar, two buffet stations, eight private phone rooms, complimentary Wi-Fi, and power access at nearly every seat. Unfortunately there are no showers or barista coffee.

As the design is described, it “reflects the character of the Washington, D.C. region through design elements inspired by the historic natural and built environment of the nation’s capital, like the iconic main Dulles terminal architecture, cherry blossoms and the Blue Ridge Mountains.”

The club is located across from gates E14 and E16, and it’s open daily from 5:30AM until 10PM, with an opening on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. The lounge follows the standard United Club access policies.

The opening of the new United Club is part of the larger opening of the new Concourse E at Washington Dulles. This is the first new concourse to open at the airport in two decades.

The new concourse is 435,000 square feet, and it has 14 new gates that will exclusively be used by United. United claims that these new gates will increase connectivity by nearly 30% during peak times. The concourse also has direct AeroTrain access, expansive new dining and retail options, and more.

It’s important to keep in mind what a mess United’s current facility at Washington Dulles is, which is what makes this all the more exciting. United primarily operates out of Concourses C and D, which were built as temporary facilities in 1985. 40+ years later, they’re still there. So this new concourse will be a massive boost to the United passenger experience.

We know that Dulles Airport is supposed to undergo a major modernization, which was unveiled by the Trump administration. However, the cost is astronomical (even by the typically inflated airport standards), and things are already well behind schedule.

As you’d expect, this press release has endless quotes from airline, airport, and Trump administration officials. There’s also a fair bit of spin here, like this, from Deputy Secretary of Transportation, Steven Bradbury:

“Under President Trump, America is building again. So far, the construction of United’s new Concourse E has supported 2,700 good paying jobs and brought $1.3 billion in local economic activity to the national capital region. USDOT’s broader partnership with MWAA and United on the Dulles Airport transformation is just beginning, with many more milestones on the horizon. The ultimate winner will be the American people who will enjoy a stunning new gateway to America’s capital for generations to come. Congratulations to MWAA and United for today’s grand unveiling, and we look forward to even greater results in the near future.”

Keep in mind that the “building” of this concourse started under the Biden administration, and not under the Trump administration.

Washington Dulles Airport’s new Concourse E opens to the public on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. The new concourse adds 14 gates for United, and most importantly, it looks like a real terminal, and not like a temporary facility. The concourse has a new United Club, which not only looks much improved, but also massively increases lounge capacity.

What do you make of Washington Dulles Airport’s new Concourse, and the new United Club?

#6148. Brit Jailed In Singapore After Hidden Camera Found In Airplane Lavatory

A man is facing quite some legal challenges after installing a hidden camera in an airplane lavatory, and then trying to control it remotely. Of course this is not only incredibly creepy and illegal, but if you’re going to do something like this, it probably shouldn’t be on a Singapore-bound flight, given the country’s strict laws.

The Straits Times has the story of how a 52-year-old British man has been jailed in Singapore, following an incident that happened on an October 7 flight from Osaka Kansai (KIX) to Singapore Changi (SIN). The man was traveling on a Boeing 787 belonging to Scoot, Singapore Airlines’ low cost subsidiary.

A short time after takeoff, the man reportedly installed a camera in the airplane lavatory, which had the function to be controlled remotely through an app on his phone. A short while later, a flight attendant, who was using the lavatory, found the hidden camera. She removed the device, and of course alerted the crew.

The passenger reportedly tried to remove the camera from the lavatory later, only to find that it was no longer there. The crew managed to figure out who it belonged to (it’s not entirely clear how), though in the meantime, he had already deleted the app on his phone, and all related pictures, to avoid detection.

He was detained upon arrival in Singapore, and his camera and phone were seized. The man was jailed, and his trial will take place in the coming weeks.

He faces charges of voyeurism and obstructing the course of justice. For voyeurism, one can be jailed for up to two years, fined, caned, or a combination of these punishments. For obstructing the course of justice, one can be jailed for up to seven years, fined, or both.

I’m not here to kink shame. People can conceptually be into whatever they want, as far as I’m concerned. The issue is when they non-consensually involve others in whatever that fantasy may be, especially when it violates the law (obviously). A few thoughts come to mind:

While not exactly the same thing, keep in mind that phones sold in South Korea have to make a sound when pictures or videos are taken, even if a phone is set to silent. That’s intended to combat illicit and covert photography of people, against their will. So obviously being creepy in this way is something that’s way more common than it should be…

A British national is facing some serious punishment in Singapore, after he installed hidden cameras in a lavatory of a Scoot Boeing 787. A flight attendant noticed these while using the lavatory, and removed the camera. He later came back to try to retrieve it, and was caught.

The man is now facing charges of voyeurism and obstructing the course of justice, and could be looking at years in jail.

What do you make of this Scoot hidden camera incident?

#6147. Marriott Becomes Giant Anti-ICE Billboard As L.A. Protesters Project ‘Blood Money’ Onto Its Walls

Protesters turned a the Warner Center Marriott Woodland Hills into a giant anti-ICE billboard Sunday night, projecting “Marriott takes blood money from ICE” onto its exterior while the hotel’s own logo remained lit up beside it. Spotted at Woodland Hills Marriott where ICE is reportedly staying. — Raider (@iwillnotbesilenced.bsky.social) November 9, 2026 The messages include “Marriott houses the Gestapo,” “Marriott loves Trump” (with a heart), and “Marriott devours your tax dollars for fascism.” The closing message is: “We beat you before. We will beat you again.” Woodland Hills Indivisible had publicized the allegation on November 6, saying its community network had confirmed agents were staying there. A separate event listing advertised an “ICE OUT OF MARRIOTT” demonstration for Sunday evening, and here’s footage of the protest. This was posted on BlueSky, so naturally replies support a Marriott boycott, with one commenter listing out the brands because even Marriott execs can’t name them all. Another offers, “Projector resistance is an underappreciated art form.” And someone asks, “Motel 6 forget to leave the lights on?” I covered Motel 6 properties handing guest lists to ICE, and the chain’s subsequent $7.6 million settlement. Reporting your own guests to immigration authorities is a very different business strategy than renting rooms to the federal government. The Trump Hotel Got This Treatment, Too This immediately brings to mind the projections I wrote about at the former Trump International Hotel in Washington, D.C. in 2017. Artist Robin Bell projected “Emoluments Welcome” and “Pay Trump Bribes Here,” with an arrow pointing toward the entrance. He also displayed the Constitution’s emoluments clause. Projecting Light Isn’t Trespassing So can someone actually do this? In Wilson v. Interlake Steel, California’s Supreme Court said nondamaging intrusions of light, noise, or odor aren’t trespass. However, Light shining into occupied rooms would be nuisance if it’s sufficiently substantial and unreasonable. Actually putting the projection equipment on hotel property or blocking access could be actionable. And LA’s sign ordinance could be implicated – Los Angeles includes projected images in its sign definitions, with restrictions on supergraphic signs. I think it’s an interesting legal queston whether a temporary political display can be restricted based on a municipal sign ordinance but a neutral time, place and manner restriction seems plausible. Renting Rooms To Agents Isn’t The Same As Running A Detention Center The hotel is in HM Alpha Hotels & Resorts’ management portfolio. When HM Alpha announced taking over management, it identified the property as part of Southwest Value Partners’ portfolio. The hotel’s operator makes booking decisions, but a protest aimed at the Marriott name can spread the cost across the brand. Customers generally book a Marriott, not a particular real estate investment firm’s management arrangement. Still, renting an agent a room doesn’t establish that Marriott “loves Trump.” Back in 2019, Marriott, Hilton and Choice said they wouldn’t turn their hotels into immigration detention facilities. Marriott was also criticized for hosting a Customs and Border Protection trade symposium at the Marriott Marquis Chicago. I supported then-CEO Arne Sorenson’s argument that renting meeting space doesn’t mean endorsing a group’s views. Hotels shouldn’t need to agree with their guests’ politics before handing over a room key. I also covered Hilton telling properties to stop housing detained children, followed by government records showing children held at Hilton, Marriott and Choice properties. And Marriott’s neutrality claim looked awfully selective when a Prague hotel rejected a Uyghur conference. In January, Hilton removed a Minnesota Hampton Inn from its system after it continued refusing Homeland Security bookings. I’m not sure that refusing these bookings is something that the property would even be allowed to do, though post-midterms a lot of this is probably up in the air. And indeed the President himself has just walked back his own administration’s tough on immigration stance. (HT: Paul H) Topics on this pageProtestArne M. The hotel is in HM Alpha Hotels & Resorts’ management portfolio. When HM Alpha announced taking over management, it identified the property as part of Southwest Value Partners’ portfolio.

The hotel’s operator makes booking decisions, but a protest aimed at the Marriott name can spread the cost across the brand. Customers generally book a Marriott, not a particular real estate investment firm’s management arrangement. Still, renting an agent a room doesn’t establish that Marriott “loves Trump.”

Back in 2019, Marriott, Hilton and Choice said they wouldn’t turn their hotels into immigration detention facilities. Marriott was also criticized for hosting a Customs and Border Protection trade symposium at the Marriott Marquis Chicago.

I supported then-CEO Arne Sorenson’s argument that renting meeting space doesn’t mean endorsing a group’s views. Hotels shouldn’t need to agree with their guests’ politics before handing over a room key.

I also covered Hilton telling properties to stop housing detained children, followed by government records showing children held at Hilton, Marriott and Choice properties. And Marriott’s neutrality claim looked awfully selective when a Prague hotel rejected a Uyghur conference.

In January, Hilton removed a Minnesota Hampton Inn from its system after it continued refusing Homeland Security bookings. I’m not sure that refusing these bookings is something that the property would even be allowed to do, though post-midterms a lot of this is probably up in the air. And indeed the President himself has just walked back his own administration’s tough on immigration stance.
