#6145. Highest To Lowest: How To Get From JFK To Manhattan For Just $3

In the film Highest 2 Lowest (2025), starring Denzel Washington, legendary filmmaker Spike Lee portrays two distinct sides of New York City, depending on your altitude and bank account. Nowhere is that contrast more apparent than in the choices travelers face when commuting between Manhattan and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

Whether you are a visiting traveler or an NYC resident, navigating to and from the city’s primary international hub is a perpetual balancing act between cost, comfort, and time. Previously, I detailed what is literally and figuratively the “highest” mode of airport transit: Blade’s helicopter transfers (starting at $195 and easily topping $300, though rides can cost you nothing out of pocket using Bilt Cash). Each Bilt Cash award expires 12 months after you earn it, on the last day of that month.

In this Reader Story, I’m taking you down, subterranean, to the lowest option available: the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) $3 bus-to-subway hack.

Duke Ellington was onto something: “Take the ‘A’ Train.” However, he didn’t specify which A train branch, nor did he mention that a quick bus transfer might be involved!

Even some locals may ask: “Wait, isn’t the AirTrain $8.75, plus a $3 subway fare?” That’s true if you exit the AirTrain at Jamaica or Howard Beach. However, there is a lesser-known and dramatically cheaper workaround: just $3 total from JFK to nearly anywhere in NYC with the MTA, provided you don’t mind adding a few extra minutes to your journey.

For the reverse trip, take any Lefferts Blvd-bound A train, ensuring the destination sign explicitly says “Lefferts Blvd” rather than Far Rockaway or Rockaway Park. Importantly, Far Rockaway A trains often display “JFK Airport” on their digital side displays because most travelers use the more expensive $8.75 Howard Beach transfer route, so do not board those if you want the $3-only route. Once on the correct train, get off at Liberty Ave / Lefferts Blvd, exit to the street, locate the bus stop, catch a JFK-bound Q10 or Q80 bus to the Lefferts AirTrain station, and take the free AirTrain directly to your terminal.

If you type “JFK Airport” into Google Maps or Apple Maps, the app will almost never display the $3-only hack. Navigation algorithms prioritize minimizing the number of transit transfers over saving money, automatically suppressing the bus transfer in favor of the standard $8.75 AirTrain connection at Jamaica or Howard Beach.

Even typing “Lefferts Blvd AirTrain Station” into navigation apps often causes confusion because the AirTrain station and the Ozone Park A-train terminal are located roughly 1.5 miles apart.

To force your map app to show the correct route, search for the street-level bus-to-subway transfer point at “Lefferts Blvd & Liberty Ave.” From JFK, this will display the Q10 Rush or Q80 bus taking you to the A train turnstiles; from Manhattan, it will guide you on the Lefferts-bound A train directly to your bus connection.

Other than extreme weather events, strikes, and major crises, all three legs of this route—the AirTrain, the Q10/Q80 bus, and the A Train—operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, though timing varies. During daytime and peak hours (6:00 AM – 10:00 PM), AirTrain cars run every 7–10 minutes, Q10 and Q80 buses depart roughly every 8–15 minutes, and A trains run frequently as express services through Brooklyn and Manhattan.

However, late-night transit frequency changes significantly in NYC, so keep that in mind for overnight or early-morning flights: AirTrain headways drop to 15–20 minute intervals, late-night Q10/Q80 bus departures stretch to every 20–30 minutes, and the A train may shift to local-only service (check MTA Service Status for possible re-routings).

Thanks to the flat-fare structure of the New York City Subway (as opposed to distance-based transit networks found in cities like London, Tokyo, or Washington, D.C.), that single $3 fare (and free transfer) unlocks access to nearly the entire city once you pass through the turnstiles at the Ozone Park–Lefferts Boulevard station.

Because there are no exit turnstiles or zone caps inside the subway network, you can ride from Queens through Brooklyn, up Manhattan, and deep into the Bronx, all on that same initial $3 tap—as long as you stay within the fare-paid zone. And, if you exit the subway system in Lower Manhattan, you can walk over to Whitehall Terminal and board the free Staten Island Ferry to reach the fifth and final borough. While attempting to tap onto a Staten Island bus or the Staten Island Railway (SIR) on the other side would consume a second $3 fare (and likely break the 2-hour transfer clock), at least JFK to Manhattan for $3 remains one of the greatest transit bargains in the world.

All told—AirTrain, bus, and subway—you can get between JFK and Manhattan in about 75 to 90 minutes. Depending on brutal rush-hour highway traffic, you might even tie or beat a $100+ rideshare. That said, I would recommend this route exclusively for those traveling light (backpacks and carry-ons), willing to spend the extra time, and comfortable navigating city transit. But for the right traveler, it is a relatively safe, clean, reliable, and wildly affordable hack.

To put the $3 bus-to-subway hack into perspective, it helps to see how it stacks up against the other primary options for traveling between Manhattan and JFK:

Of course, there are other, less conventional ways of getting to and from JFK:

Whether taking a $300+ helicopter ride or a $3 bus-to-subway hack, commuting between JFK and Manhattan truly captures the two contrasting sides of New York City that Spike Lee brings to life in Highest 2 Lowest.

For light packers on a budget, the Lefferts Boulevard Q10 transfer stands as the undefeated champion of pure value. Duke Ellington was right all along—if you want to get to Sugar Hill or anywhere else in the city without breaking the bank, simply take the “A” train!

With so many options available, what’s your preferred way of getting to or from JFK, and which are your preferred payment methods to maximize value?

Nice writeup! On a similar note, in Vienna you can skip the (relatively) expensive CAT (city airport train) and take the RailJet RJ, REX, or S-Bahn line S7 to the city for less than a third of the price (4.60 or so vs 14.90, and it's faster too). The trains also may get you closer to where you actually need to go (e.g. the main train station) rather than Wien Mitte only for the CAT. Note thought that there is some construction affecting the REX and S7 lines for the next year so you either have to catch a RJ to the main station or get off the S7/REX at St. Marx and take the tram or bus from there until the work is completed.

There are actually 4 route options for JFK to Manhattan for the $3 MTA fare. All of these examples are from the Lefferts Blvd long term parking AirTrain station. 1. Q10/Q80 bus to A train at Ozone Park - Lefferts Blvd (the route mentioned in this article) 2. Q80 bus to Kew Gardens and get the E or F train to Manhattan 3. B15 bus to New Lots and get the 3 train to Manhattan 4. Walk to Aquaduct - North Conduit Ave (relatively short walk, < 10 minutes) and get the A train to Manhattan. This is the least desirable option, unless you're against switching between bus and train.

Alternatively, take the same Q10 bus and go to the last stop then catch the F train that goes many places, among them Midtown East in Manhattan. In the reverse direction, you may get a seat on the Q10 bus, too, because it's the terminus of the bus route.

Travelers on United Airlines Flight 1252 from Washington to Chicago on Tuesday are in for a surprise.

They will be the first to depart from the spacious new E Gates at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), the first piece of the airport’s more than $20 billion redevelopment and the future center of United’s hub operation at the airport.

“It’s much more spacious,” Andrew Nocella, the chief commercial officer of United, said at a ribbon cutting on Monday. “The gate hold areas are large so there’s plenty of places to sit and there are all kinds of new, great restaurants to enjoy.”

In the news: United went big on credit cards in 2026. More changes are coming, MileagePlus boss says

Nocella added: “It’s the tip of the iceberg to the future development of Dulles.”

The redevelopment calls for the extension of the E Gates far to the west with room for up to 50 gates. The rest of IAD will also get a needed upgrade, including the modernization and expansion of Eero Saarinen's iconic terminal, an extension of the AeroTrain and a new international arrivals facility. The aim is to open all of this by the mid-2030s.

“This is the first step to retiring Concourse C-D [and] eliminating mobile lounges — someday," said Jack Potter, the CEO of IAD operator the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority.

For now, though, the focus at Dulles is on the new E Gates. They're located directly above the AeroTrain station for Concourse C. That is possible because the station was built in 2010, a long walk to the south of the existing Concourse C with the plan to eventually build a concourse above it.

Travelers coming from the train enter the E Gates in a large, high-ceilinged atrium with the new United Club immediately to their right. At 40,000 square feet, the new lounge is the second largest in United's system after the one recently opened at Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH).

United's massive new Houston club: Inside the largest airline lounge in America

The look and feel of the lounge draws its aesthetic from the Washington, D.C., area. The entryway is inspired by the Washington Metro's vaulted subway stations; a cherry blossom mobile hangs in the central seating area; and a Blue Ridge Mountain-themed mural is painted on one of the walls.

"Lounges are very important to our customers," said Nocella. "You can see no design detail was left untouched" in the new E Gates lounge.

From the E Gates atrium, travelers make their way down the concourse itself. Gate areas are interspersed with concessions along the length. And, above, a sterile hallway takes arriving international travelers to the end of the concourse where they can board a mobile lounge to the international arrivals facility in the main terminal.

United will operate both international and domestic flights from the E Gates, Nocella said.

And, for design enthusiasts, the authority used Saarinen's original font for the gate numbers in the new concourse.

The E Gates will allow United to grow its hub at IAD. The airline plans to grow departures by about 20% next summer to around 300 daily flights, up from 250 earlier this year, Nocella said.

United will operate up to roughly 275 departures from IAD in November, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. In June 2027, the number jumps to as many as 290 a day though schedules remain in flux.

What the E Gates will not do is replace the six ground-level gates at the end of Concourse A — gates A1 to A6 — used by United Express regional jets. This was the original plan when the project was approved in the early 2020s.

Instead, United will use the new E Gates to "take the pressure off the C and D facility," Nocella said.

Potter, when asked when the airport authority will close the ground-level A Gates, said: "They’ll stay open until construction has proceeded sufficiently such that they can be relocated."

The authority aims to complete the build out of Concourse E, and the first phase of Concourse G further to the south, by 2030, Potter added.

United plans to expand its IAD hub to around 400 daily departures with all the new gates, Nocella said.

Asked when the airline would grow to 400 departures, he smiled and said they will unveil that at a "different announcement."

#6143. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

I’ve been looking forward not just to spending a big initial bonus – now 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first 3 months of account opening – but to making the most out of all of the credits that come with the Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees.) As a new cardholder I dove into the specifics of the benefits. So here’s what to expect.

The Citi Strata EliteSM Card offers an annual $200 Splurge Credit. You receive up to $200 back on retailers including 1stDibs, American Airlines, Best Buy, Future Personal Training, and Live Nation. This benefit is on a calendar year basis. So during your first cardmember year you can actually claim it twice – once during the remainder of 2026, and again at the start of 2027. You can redeem it across one or more transactions. You don’t need to try to max it out in a single transaction – you won’t simply lose the remainder. In order to use the credit you first need to register for it and select up to two merchants at a time you’d like to use the credit for. The selection applies immediately (in fact, as of 12 a.m. Eastern time on the day you made the selection.) It may take up to to billing cycles to receive the credit. The credits can be used at two of 1stDibs; Live Nation; Best Buy; American Airlines; Future Personal Training. Bear in mind that some transactions won’t qualify – it’s based on the merchant of record: American Airlines or American Airlines Vacations needs to bill for the splurge credit to count. If you book related products and services with a different merchant of record (which even includes AAdvantage status renewal) those won’t count. Live Nation purchases need to be made at livenation.com or ticketmaster.com- – and for events held in the United States – third party fulfilled purchases won’t trigger the credit. The credit is super easy to use. I’ll just use the card for an American Airlines ticket. (This needs to be booked directly, not through Citi Travel or another travel portal.) Don’t have a booking right away and you’re about to hit end of year? Avoid basic economy fares, but buy a non-refundable ticket. If you cancel the ticket you’ll retain an American Airlines trip credit for future use. Or select Best Buy and make a purchase there. $100 Semi-Annual Blacklane Credit Blacklane sets up car services for you all over the world. It’s mostly pre-reserved. They’re in a lot more places than Uber and you’re getting a professional driver. At airports you’ll usually have them meet you at baggage claim and assist with luggage, for instance. And you’re going to get more consistently nice vehicles and better service than rideshare. They track your flight, arrive in advance and wait for you for an allowable time (like an hour). The card offers a $200 credit each year with Blacklane – $100 January – June and $100 July – December. No registration is required, just pay for Blacklane trips with the card and the statement credits trigger automatically. In London, Paris and Dubai I use Wheely. Most of the time in the U.S. I’ll use rideshare. But with my family, arriving after a couple of weeks abroad, I may want a car service pickup because the Austin airport makes you schlepp across the road and through a parking structure, changing levels, to reach rideshare pickup. Pre-arranged cars park by the terminal, and the driver is there to help with luggage. Pricing varies by airport and trip, but it’s often competitive with premium Uber services like BlackSUV. $300 Hotel Benefit Each year, Citi Strata Elite Card offers a $300 hotel credit for stays of two or more nights that are prepaid through Citi Travel. (Prepaid rates can still be cancellable and refundable.) The credit must be redeemed by the primary cardmember and is by calendar year (based on when you book, not the dates of your stay). A new cardmember could use the credit now and again at the start of 2027, so twice in their first cardmember year. $300 will be applied to your booking when you make the reservation – it’s not a statement credit that posts later. You can also use it across multiple transactions, e.g. if you had a 2-night stay that totaled only $200 you’d still have $100 to use later. While the card earns 12x on hotels you use it to pay for with Citi Travel, you don’t earn points on the charges covered by this credit. Consider these OTA bookings. Pricing can vary and you’re often getting the same rate as elsewhere – but not discounted rates like AAA, or member rates. You also aren’t usually entitled to hotel loyalty points, elite stay credit, or elite benefits. Priority Pass The card offers a Priority Pass Select membership for the primary cardmember and any authorized users (which are $75 each), valid for unlimited visits and including up to two complimentary guests.. It does not cover credits at restaurants and similar non-lounge offerings like markets that are linked to Priority Pass. You don’t need to have your physical or even digital Priority Pass membership for access – rather uniquely lounges are supposed to accept your Strata Elite card as the Priority Pass card itself. That means, unlike other issuers, you don’t have to activate Priority Pass membership. Marco Polo Lounge, Venice Admirals Club Passes The card comes with 4 Admirals Club passes per calendar year (so twice in cardmember year one, for eight passes total). Each set of four has to be used during the calendar year in which they’re issued, and expire if unused. They are available to the primary cardmember and include one guest 18 years or older plus up to 3 children under 18. They can be redeemed for additional adult companions as well. Requires same day boarding pass (departing or arriving) for an American or oneworld partner airline flight. Valid for 24 hours, and can be used at multiple lounges on the same day. The passes are deposited to your AAdvanage wallet and can be scanned by the Admirals Club front desk for entry. Upon card account closure, unused passes are forfeit. Admirals Club Washington National Airport E Concourse Applying For This Card Was An Easy Decision Citi’s new premium card is pretty incredible in the first year, not just because of the strong initial bonus but also because of credits that are timed to calendar year rather than cardmember year. (Calendar year credits can be claimed twice in cardmember year one.) Honestly, I feel like this was a strategic error on Citi’s part. They’ve constructed a card that is a no-brainer to get. There’s just so much value to the customer up front. I’m not sure if it’ll be a keeper long-term or a card that’s best for your everyday spend (although it is very good). My take: apply for this card, reap the maximum benefits in year one, and then consider whether it’s right for you in the long-term. The Citi Strata EliteSM Card offers an annual $200 Splurge Credit. You receive up to $200 back on retailers including 1stDibs, American Airlines, Best Buy, Future Personal Training, and Live Nation.

This benefit is on a calendar year basis. So during your first cardmember year you can actually claim it twice – once during the remainder of 2026, and again at the start of 2027.

You can redeem it across one or more transactions. You don’t need to try to max it out in a single transaction – you won’t simply lose the remainder.

In order to use the credit you first need to register for it and select up to two merchants at a time you’d like to use the credit for. The selection applies immediately (in fact, as of 12 a.m. Eastern time on the day you made the selection.) It may take up to to billing cycles to receive the credit.

The credits can be used at two of 1stDibs; Live Nation; Best Buy; American Airlines; Future Personal Training. Bear in mind that some transactions won’t qualify – it’s based on the merchant of record:

American Airlines or American Airlines Vacations needs to bill for the splurge credit to count. If you book related products and services with a different merchant of record (which even includes AAdvantage status renewal) those won’t count.

Live Nation purchases need to be made at livenation.com or ticketmaster.com- – and for events held in the United States – third party fulfilled purchases won’t trigger the credit. The credit is super easy to use. I’ll just use the card for an American Airlines ticket. (This needs to be booked directly, not through Citi Travel or another travel portal.) Don’t have a booking right away and you’re about to hit end of year? Avoid basic economy fares, but buy a non-refundable ticket. If you cancel the ticket you’ll retain an American Airlines trip credit for future use. Or select Best Buy and make a purchase there. $100 Semi-Annual Blacklane Credit Blacklane sets up car services for you all over the world. It’s mostly pre-reserved. They’re in a lot more places than Uber and you’re getting a professional driver. At airports you’ll usually have them meet you at baggage claim and assist with luggage, for instance. And you’re going to get more consistently nice vehicles and better service than rideshare. They track your flight, arrive in advance and wait for you for an allowable time (like an hour). The card offers a $200 credit each year with Blacklane – $100 January – June and $100 July – December. No registration is required, just pay for Blacklane trips with the card and the statement credits trigger automatically. In London, Paris and Dubai I use Wheely. Most of the time in the U.S. I’ll use rideshare. But with my family, arriving after a couple of weeks abroad, I may want a car service pickup because the Austin airport makes you schlepp across the road and through a parking structure, changing levels, to reach rideshare pickup. Pre-arranged cars park by the terminal, and the driver is there to help with luggage. Pricing varies by airport and trip, but it’s often competitive with premium Uber services like BlackSUV. $300 Hotel Benefit Each year, Citi Strata Elite Card offers a $300 hotel credit for stays of two or more nights that are prepaid through Citi Travel. (Prepaid rates can still be cancellable and refundable.) The credit must be redeemed by the primary cardmember and is by calendar year (based on when you book, not the dates of your stay). A new cardmember could use the credit now and again at the start of 2027, so twice in their first cardmember year. $300 will be applied to your booking when you make the reservation – it’s not a statement credit that posts later. You can also use it across multiple transactions, e.g. if you had a 2-night stay that totaled only $200 you’d still have $100 to use later. While the card earns 12x on hotels you use it to pay for with Citi Travel, you don’t earn points on the charges covered by this credit. Consider these OTA bookings. Pricing can vary and you’re often getting the same rate as elsewhere – but not discounted rates like AAA, or member rates. You also aren’t usually entitled to hotel loyalty points, elite stay credit, or elite benefits. Priority Pass The card offers a Priority Pass Select membership for the primary cardmember and any authorized users (which are $75 each), valid for unlimited visits and including up to two complimentary guests.. It does not cover credits at restaurants and similar non-lounge offerings like markets that are linked to Priority Pass. You don’t need to have your physical or even digital Priority Pass membership for access – rather uniquely lounges are supposed to accept your Strata Elite card as the Priority Pass card itself. That means, unlike other issuers, you don’t have to activate Priority Pass membership. Marco Polo Lounge, Venice Admirals Club Passes The card comes with 4 Admirals Club passes per calendar year (so twice in cardmember year one, for eight passes total). Each set of four has to be used during the calendar year in which they’re issued, and expire if unused. They are available to the primary cardmember and include one guest 18 years or older plus up to 3 children under 18. They can be redeemed for additional adult companions as well. Requires same day boarding pass (departing or arriving) for an American or oneworld partner airline flight. Valid for 24 hours, and can be used at multiple lounges on the same day. The passes are deposited to your AAdvanage wallet and can be scanned by the Admirals Club front desk for entry. Upon card account closure, unused passes are forfeit. #6141. Amex Gold Card Bonus: As High As 100K Points Welcome Offer (Check Yours)

The American Express® Gold Card is one of Amex’s most compelling cards for earning Membership Rewards points, and it currently has a best-ever welcome offer that’s as high as 100,000 bonus points, making it a great time to apply. In this post, I’d like to go over all the details of the current Amex Gold Card bonus, including who is eligible, and why you might want to apply.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

The Amex Gold Card currently has a lucrative bonus, marketed as being as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards bonus points after spending $8,000 within the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the Amex Gold Card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. This means that to me, the 100,000 points are worth $1,700, making it among the best welcome offers out there. Of course that assumes you’re eligible for this offer, which not everyone will be.

As a point of comparison, previously the Amex Gold Card bonus offered up to 60,000 points, so this is a lot better. As a matter of fact, the current Amex Gold Card offer is potentially the best publicly available one that we’ve seen.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to roughly 20 airline and hotel partners, ranging from Air Canada Aeroplan, to Air France-KLM Flying Blue, All Nippon Airways Mileage Club, to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Just to give a couple of quick examples:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the welcome offer on the Amex Gold Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, you may not be eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had American Express Platinum Card® (learn more).

This is a reason to pick up the Amex Gold Card before you pick up the Amex Platinum Card. That’s because you’re potentially eligible for the Amex Platinum Card welcome offer if you have or have had the Amex Gold Card, while the inverse may not be true.

On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply. There are a couple of additional things to note:

Read more about Amex Gold Card application tips.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee (Rates & Fees). This is one of the most popular Amex cards for earning Membership Rewards points, given its excellent rewards structure and credits.

For one, it’s an amazing card in terms of the return on spending, especially for anyone who loves to eat (and who doesn’t?). The card offers the following Membership Rewards points multipliers for spending:

On top of that, the Amex Gold Card offers up to $424 in credits annually, which can help recoup much of the annual fee (or more than offset the annual fee, in some cases). These credits are with Uber, Resy, Dunkin’, and more, and are summarized in the below chart. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

The Amex Gold Card also offers Hertz Five Star status just for having the card (enrollment required), which can get you valuable perks.

Essentially, if you spend a lot on food (whether at restaurants or supermarkets) and if you can get some value out of the credits, I tend to think the Amex Gold Card is easy to justify.

Read a full review of the Amex Gold Card here.

The Amex Gold Card welcome offer is currently as high as 100,000 points upon completing minimum spending. The way this works, you have to fill out the application, and then you’ll see exactly what offer you’re eligible for. Then before there’s a hard pull, you can decide if you want to submit the application or not.

If you are eligible for the full Amex Gold Card bonus, this card is absolutely worth picking up. Beyond the huge welcome offer, this is one of the most rewarding cards for earning Membership Rewards points, and the card also offers credits and benefits that can help offset the annual fee. Amex doesn’t have that many super lucrative cards in terms of the number of points you can earn, and this is among my favorites.

Do you plan on picking up the Amex Gold Card with this welcome offer?

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: American Express® Gold Card (Rates & Fees).

#6139. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6138. Passenger Takes Another Man’s Aisle Seat To Sit With His Wife—Frontier Flight Attendant Lets Him Keep It

A Frontier Airlines passenger found another man in his assigned aisle seat. The man wanted to sit beside his wife, so he offered the passenger his middle seat two rows back. A flight attendant listened to a passenger’s plea to sit in his assigned seat but did nothing. The passenger finally gave up: “I just want to get home.” The seat stealer on flight 1550 from Atlanta to Jacksonville on Sunday got what he wanted. And the airline – which sells these seat assignments – left them to negotiate amongst themselves, creating a secondary market. The flight was full, a long-haired man in his 20s arrived at seat 28C, and a white-haired man in his 60s was already sitting there beside his wife. When the younger passenger pointed out that this was his assigned seat, the response was: “Well, I wanted to sit next to my wife. You can have my middle seat (30E).” The younger man waited. A flight attendant got involved and heard the story, the witness says. After nothing happened, he walked back to 30E and sat down. Several commenters say the displaced passenger should have insisted on his assignment or asked a second crewmember for help. Some suggest flight attendants shouldn’t get involved because unlike at Delta, American and United their pay at Frontier isn’t calculating including boarding time. Some think the best solution would be to stand in the aisle, refuse to move, and demand compensation. A couple can ask for a seat swap. They can offer money. They can ask a flight attendant for help finding two willing passengers. But stealing someone’s seat isn’t acceptable. Still, sometimes it’s permitted. I covered an American Airlines passenger whose paid aisle seat was occupied by a child. He said a flight attendant backed the family because “She got on the plane before you,” called him “the bad guy,” and threatened to remove him. It seems to me that at a minimum the passenger here is owed a refund for his seat fee. There’s no involuntary denied boarding. There’s no downgrade of class of service. So anything more than that is discretionary customer service on the part of the airline. Morally the passenger is owed more. I’d surely ask for another crewmember’s involvement if I got nowhere with the first flight attendant. Unfortunately, in the moment, it doesn’t matter whether the passenger is right or wrong. They’re at the mercy of what the crew says, even when the crewmember just shrugs. The seat stealer on flight 1550 from Atlanta to Jacksonville on Sunday got what he wanted. And the airline – which sells these seat assignments – left them to negotiate amongst themselves, creating a secondary market. The flight was full, a long-haired man in his 20s arrived at seat 28C, and a white-haired man in his 60s was already sitting there beside his wife.

When the younger passenger pointed out that this was his assigned seat, the response was:

“Well, I wanted to sit next to my wife. You can have my middle seat (30E).”

The younger man waited. A flight attendant got involved and heard the story, the witness says. After nothing happened, he walked back to 30E and sat down.

Several commenters say the displaced passenger should have insisted on his assignment or asked a second crewmember for help. Some suggest flight attendants shouldn’t get involved because unlike at Delta, American and United their pay at Frontier isn’t calculating including boarding time. Some think the best solution would be to stand in the aisle, refuse to move, and demand compensation.

A couple can ask for a seat swap. They can offer money. They can ask a flight attendant for help finding two willing passengers. But stealing someone’s seat isn’t acceptable. Still, sometimes it’s permitted.

I covered an American Airlines passenger whose paid aisle seat was occupied by a child. He said a flight attendant backed the family because “She got on the plane before you,” called him “the bad guy,” and threatened to remove him.

It seems to me that at a minimum the passenger here is owed a refund for his seat fee. There’s no involuntary denied boarding. There’s no downgrade of class of service. So anything more than that is discretionary customer service on the part of the airline. Morally the passenger is owed more.

I’d surely ask for another crewmember’s involvement if I got nowhere with the first flight attendant. Unfortunately, in the moment, it doesn’t matter whether the passenger is right or wrong. They’re at the mercy of what the crew says, even when the crewmember just shrugs.

#6137. Which Airlines Are Dry (No Alcohol)? Can You Bring Your Own Alcohol?

For many people, alcohol is an aspect of traveling by air that they enjoy. I’m not just talking about first or business class travel, where a glass of champagne might be part of the fun. Airports are also one of the few places where you can have a drink at 5AM and not be judged (too hard).

Admittedly customs differ around the globe, based on culture, religion, etc. In this post, I thought it would be interesting to talk a bit about dry airlines, as there’s a bit of nuance to this.

Which airlines don’t serve alcohol onboard? Which airlines don’t serve alcohol but let you bring your own alcohol? And does all of this even matter?

Let’s start by taking a look at the airlines that are dry, meaning that they don’t serve you alcohol. Here are the airlines that come to mind:

Admittedly that list isn’t totally exhaustive, since there are a countless number of small airlines out there. However, I think this covers the biggest and most interesting airlines that don’t serve alcohol (though if I missed any major ones, please let me know).

There’s an interesting twist to this. While some airlines are dry, they’ll let you bring your own alcohol onboard, and then you can consume it (within reason). The following three international carriers come to mind:

Now, it’s important to note that this isn’t without strings attached:

When I flew Kuwait Airways several years back, I wrote about how we brought a bottle of wine onboard, and they gladly let us consume it. It’s not that I couldn’t be without alcohol, but I was curious to experience a BYOB concept on a plane, since that was novel for me.

There’s an added layer of complexity to all of this, as there are some airlines that aren’t generally dry, but are dry on certain routes. Several situations come to mind (let me know if I’m missing any):

As you can tell, in some of the above situations, the lack of alcohol presumably has little to do with religion or concerns over behavior, and more to do with controlling costs.

People have different takes as to how “bad” it is to fly on a dry airline. On the one end of the spectrum, there are people who will avoid dry airlines at all costs. On the other end of the spectrum, you have billions of people who don’t drink alcohol at all, so this is a non-issue.

Personally I’m probably somewhere in the middle:

Regarding that last point, I do have to give credit to airlines that are dry, but still put effort into their drink selection. Take Saudia, for example, which goes above and beyond in terms of its non-alcoholic drink selection in premium cabins, with everything from cappuccinos and espressos, to excellent mocktails, to non-alcoholic wine.

Airlines often reflect their local customs and religions, so it’s not surprising that many airlines don’t serve alcohol onboard. If you definitely want alcohol when you fly, avoid airlines like Saudia. If you would like a drink when you fly, the good news is that some dry airlines actually let you bring your own alcohol, within certain limitations.

While the above doesn’t cover 100% of situations, hopefully it’s a useful, basic rundown of some of the bigger airlines that are dry.

How strongly do you feel about dry airlines? Does this policy impact your airline choice?

#6136. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a new mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half.  Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

There’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

There’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

“Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is currently streaming on Amazon.

#6135. Uber Wants You To Drive Yourself—Reserve Parking In 15 Cities, Earn 10% Back

Uber is launching parking reservations in 15 U.S. cities, letting you find a garage or lot, compare prices, and pay inside its app. Uber One members earn 10% back in credits on eligible bookings and of course Uber One comes with Amex Platinum. It’s a little weird to have self-service Uber. You supply the car. You do the driving. But they offer Uber Eats for pickup, so I guess? Still, even if it’s not gig workers and urban mobility, if the price and rebate are good, ok then. Where Uber Parking Is Available Uber’s November 9 launch covers Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, D.C. They plan to expand across the United States. This follows Uber’s acquisition of SpotHero, announced in February. SpotHero’s broader network has more than 13,000 garages, lots, and valet locations across over 400 cities in the U.S. and Canada. However, Uber’s parking page lists 7,000 facilities. Tap Parking in the Uber app, enter your destination and parking times, and compare the map’s prices. You can filter for self-parking or valet, garages or surface lots, and things like on-site staff. Enter your vehicle details and license plate, pay via your Uber Wallet, and follow the entry instructions on the parking pass. Uber already has your account and payment information. SpotHero had parking reservations. Now it’s in one place with Uber rebates. 10% Rebate, Including Taxes And Fees Uber One members earn 10% credits on eligible completed parking reservations including the parking charge, taxes, and fees. Credits generally arrive within 24 hours after the reservation. Not every location or reservation qualifies. Uber One costs $9.99 a month or $96 a year. Buying an annual membership solely for parking requires $960 in eligible annual parking purchases just to earn $96 in credits, assuming you use those credits at full value. So this is for someone who already has Uber One. Can You Use Amex Uber Cash? And Does Amazon Help? Uber Cash works at supported parking locations. Uber’s parking help page says so, and Uber’s American Express terms say: The Amex Benefit may be applied to any services to which Uber permits Uber Cash to be applied. So this is a new way to use monthly Uber credits ($15 monthly, plus another $20 in December). Consumer Gold offers $10 monthly. And you can get Uber One via Amex Platinum: up to $120 in statement credits per calendar year for membership fees charged directly to the card. Both monthly and annual plans qualify. (Consumer Centurion cards have a membership credit as well.) Keep Uber Cash off for the membership payment so Amex is charged and can reimburse it. Amazon Prime doesn’t unlock this. The new U.S. Amazon arrangement provides $0 delivery fees on eligible Uber Eats restaurant orders of $25 or more placed through Amazon, but doesn’t give you an Uber One membership. Those orders use a separate account and Uber One benefits don’t apply to them. Uber Isn’t The Only Option In This Market There are plenty of alternatives. Alternative   What To Compare SpotHero directly   The same underlying parking business, with a broader geographic footprint and hourly, monthly, event, and airport parking. ParkWhiz and BestParking   Other booking channels for prepaid garage and lot reservations, including event parking. ParkMobile and PayByPhone   Useful for paying for and extending parking in participating locations. ParkMobile also offers advance reservations. AirportParkingReservations.com and Way.com   Airport parking comparisons, including off-airport lots and hotel parking. Compare shuttle schedules, operating hours, and cancellation rules. The garage, hotel, event venue, or airport directly   Prepaid offers, parking packages, validation, and loyalty discounts that might beat an intermediary’s price. I’ve written about the economics of empty parking spaces: the garage already exists, and an unsold hour is revenue the operator never gets back. Advance booking can give operators a way to discount to people who compare prices while charging more to drivers who just show up. Uber says many participating locations offer rates below their drive-up prices. Read The Parking Pass Before You Pay Uber’s parking rules leave several decisions to the individual facility: Cancellation. Uber says most options can be canceled free before the start time, but the deadline shown for your reservation controls. Extensions. Most active reservations can be extended if space is available but don’t assume you can stay indefinitely at the original rate. Entry and exit. Follow the pass’s barcode, license plate, or attendant instructions. Most participating facilities don’t allow repeated entry and exit during one reservation. Vehicle restrictions and extra charges. Check height limits and oversized vehicle charges, along with early entry and late exit rules. Uber’s charge guidance flags additional fees. A reservation doesn’t imply a particular space is being held. SpotHero says it manages inventory with operators rather than physically holding a specific stall. If you arrive and can’t enter or the lot is full, Uber directs you to the parking pass’s help option. Good luck. There are two other launch limitations in Uber’s FAQ: business profiles aren’t supported, and Uber and SpotHero accounts can’t be linked. An Uber reservation won’t appear in your SpotHero account. The claim in the launch pitch that Americans spend an average of 17 hours a year looking for parking comes from a July 2017 study. It seems to me there’s very high variance in this. In fact, isn’t one solution just to Uber? Uber gets a transaction from people who choose to drive, then offers credits that encourage them to come back for a ride or food order. They also say they’ll explore using parking locations to stage autonomous vehicles between trips. They’re going to be losing their Waymo partnership so I wonder what that looks like? What I’d Really Like Is Uber Valet About a decade ago, Luxe offered a valet would meet you at your destination, take your car away to park it, and bring it back when you were ready. Zirx did, too. Walking into a restaurant while somebody dealt with your car was super value add! But it’s a tough business. Luxe ended its consumer valet service in 2017, and Volvo bought its technology, team, and other assets that September. Zirx stopped consumer valet service in February 2016. Attendants had to reach customers, park their cars, and return them, on top of paying for parking and insurance. Uber considered buying Luxe’s assets and engineers before Volvo did. Valet Network in New York advertises $10 parking, using street spaces. Apparently the service is in Carroll Gardens, Cobble Hill, and the Lower East Side and it’s another $3 to return the car. Ector offers something like this at French airports and train stations. That seems like an Uber feature, this is more like selling hotels through the app because they already have customers and their customers travel. I liked the old Travis vision for the company so much better. They had some growing up to do and maybe they wouldn’t have achieved everything before the VC cash ran out but this just isn’t that exciting of a vision, even if you have something new to do with existing Uber credits. Most active reservations can be extended if space is available but don’t assume you can stay indefinitely at the original rate. Entry and exit. Follow the pass’s barcode, license plate, or attendant instructions. Most participating facilities don’t allow repeated entry and exit during one reservation. Vehicle restrictions and extra charges. Check height limits and oversized vehicle charges, along with early entry and late exit rules. Uber’s charge guidance flags additional fees. A reservation doesn’t imply a particular space is being held. SpotHero says it manages inventory with operators rather than physically holding a specific stall. If you arrive and can’t enter or the lot is full, Uber directs you to the parking pass’s help option. Good luck. There are two other launch limitations in Uber’s FAQ: business profiles aren’t supported, and Uber and SpotHero accounts can’t be linked. An Uber reservation won’t appear in your SpotHero account. The claim in the launch pitch that Americans spend an average of 17 hours a year looking for parking comes from a July 2017 study. It seems to me there’s very high variance in this. In fact, isn’t one solution just to Uber? Uber gets a transaction from people who choose to drive, then offers credits that encourage them to come back for a ride or food order. They also say they’ll explore using parking locations to stage autonomous vehicles between trips. They’re going to be losing their Waymo partnership so I wonder what that looks like? What I’d Really Like Is Uber Valet About a decade ago, Luxe offered a valet would meet you at your destination, take your car away to park it, and bring it back when you were ready. Zirx did, too. Walking into a restaurant while somebody dealt with your car was super value add! But it’s a tough business. Luxe ended its consumer valet service in 2017, and Volvo bought its technology, team, and other assets that September. Zirx stopped consumer valet service in February 2016. Attendants had to reach customers, park their cars, and return them, on top of paying for parking and insurance. Uber considered buying Luxe’s assets and engineers before Volvo did. Valet Network in New York advertises $10 parking, using street spaces. Apparently the service is in Carroll Gardens, Cobble Hill, and the Lower East Side and it’s another $3 to return the car. Ector offers something like this at French airports and train stations. That seems like an Uber feature, this is more like selling hotels through the app because they already have customers and their customers travel. I liked the old Travis vision for the company so much better. They had some growing up to do and maybe they wouldn’t have achieved everything before the VC cash ran out but this just isn’t that exciting of a vision, even if you have something new to do with existing Uber credits. I’ve written about the economics of empty parking spaces: the garage already exists, and an unsold hour is revenue the operator never gets back. Advance booking can give operators a way to discount to people who compare prices while charging more to drivers who just show up. Uber says many participating locations offer rates below their drive-up prices.

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicansâ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who donât know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOPâs anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.Â

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurseâs office without parental consent.Â

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which hasÂ  been the central organizing principle of Trumpâs decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as âno new warsâ and âbringing prices down on day one,â but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, heâs even exceeded expectations.Â

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.Â

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOPâs nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the partyâs leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohioâs Republican nominee for governor.Â

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.Â

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of âlone-wolfâ terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.Â

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding âand worse,â and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America âuntil we can figure out what the hell is going on,â he executed his infamous âMuslim banâ days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trumpâs ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But sheâs a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trumpâs bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the stateâs governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesotaâs community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and thatâs saying something.

Somalia, he said, is âgarbage, a âsh*thouse countryâ that âstinks.â He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants donât work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to âfight backâ against the stateâs Somali population, writing that they âview you as weak and stupid people.âÂ

Another target of MAGAâs anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as âvery, very evil,â a âpsychopathâ who pushes âanti-white racial hatred.â This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.Â

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our âexceptionalâ characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to âwelfareâ and âbusingâ to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, âlaw and order,â as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about âwelfare queensâ during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in statesâ rights âÂ another dog whistle â in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his âbirtherâ campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the partyâs burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name âÂ Barack Hussein Obama â with a childish glee.Â

I donât think claiming that a whole African country is a âsh*thouseâ or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighborsâ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. Itâs just a matter of time. And if he does, Iâm sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGAâs staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.Â
